review_headline: The Same Old GTA.... Just Superficially Different & More Flawed. Also: Money, Where?
review_body:
The disappointment I now feel, having completed GTAV, was not what I expected to be feeling after being overwhelmed on my first day playing it. The moment I realised I could play full-on, completely optional tennis was a genuine 'WOW' moment where it hit me just how big the game is. And the the narrative being broken up between three characters - suggesting a more focused story than in past 'do jobs for random people/initial letters on map' GTA games - helped immerse me completely. But then it hit me: it's big yet an ultimately hollow experience where you get no rewards for your effort (yoga QTE...) and the vast majority of the side content just isn't fun. At all. The best example of the emptiness of it all is that you still cannot enter 99% of buildings, even in the 50GB+ PS4 version, leaving the world as a lifeless collection of tall buildings. And Rockstar's point black refusal to shift the gameplay of past GTA's to match GTAV's three-way story and heist focus meant the failings of the series' structure were highlighted, rather than being corrected.

Let me start with the most bothersome of GTAV's issues: money. In past GTA games, you began as nobody but then, slowly but surely, got more money from doing odd jobs for eccentric characters until becoming a rich career criminal. In GTAV, in spite of the entirely superficial changes mentioned above, you STILL spend all of the game doing missions for random individuals. The key difference is this: you get no money for doing missions in GTAV. NONE. You see, GTAV instead relied on 2-3 heist jobs (out of roughly 110+, including optional ones) that each give you a substantial amount of money. But, even so, it's nowhere near enough to buy anything other than weapons and a few of the less expensive properties until AFTER beating the game. So, basically, you do missions with no reward other than advancing the game, and only after beating the game (where you'll spend an hour buying everything, pointlessly, then either quit or play online) you get enough money to freely spend. The stupidity of this just blows my mind. And, worse yet, it seems like Rockstar nerfed the money given by side-activities, such as racing, so that you only get a few $100-1000 for winning--MAX. Then we come to buying properties: if you spend $100,000's buying a property, you get anywhere from $500-10,000 PER IN-GAME WEEK. Which is to say, you won't even get what you paid back by the end of the game. Only 2/15 unlock side-activities, only 1/15 gives you a real profit via side-activities, and if you don't do tedious kill/drive mini-missions when phoned for the properties you own, you get ZERO for that week, with no way of increasing your profit. You cannot even enter most of the properties you buy. I'm genuinely baffled by Rockstar defying common sense here. It's not as if you can do random heist missions to make money, or rob stores (I only found 1-2 in 60 hours that I could rob since they don't appear on map) for more than $300, either. The only real way you can make money in GTAV is to wait until the game is over and do Franklin's assassination missions post-game so you can manipulate stock prices (entirely artificial: can only profit at set points). THAT'S IT.

Next, we come to the second most irksome issue: the story. A three-way narrative suggested that GTAV would present three different distinctive character arcs that would eventually become one. What actually happened was Franklin (one of the three) - unnaturally - going from 'the hood' to becoming a sort of subservient sidekick to a white, rich, self-centered, family failure of a DSPGaming lookalike (with the goatee) in the form of Michael right at the start. Basically, Franklin starts out as the best character, with his own arc, before getting absorbed into Michael's arc. Until Trevor was introduced, with the promise of something more given by his psychotic-destructive self, the story was purely a black comedy centered around Michael'smid-life criminal crisis. But, in the end, Trevor only served to emphasise how little story there is and how padded it was, despite him being an unforgettable / brilliant character. He's introduced whilst fueled by anger over the apparent betrayal of his best friend, Michael, yet almost instantly becomes yet another black comedy prop for Michael's life: the questions he wanted to ask not being asked for some 20-30 missions, for no reason. And when the truth is revealed, AGAIN the inevitable gets delayed... just 'cause. At one point, you go from working for the FBI one minute, then working for a rich businessman connected to the FBI... then working for a movie director connected to the businessman. Which is to say, the structure and randomness of the previous GTA games is retained, with the three-way premise just being for decoration. And that angered me. When you reach the end and find yourself killing off a cast of insignificant nobodies for a Hollywood conclusion (unless you go for one of the two short/tacked-on alternate endings that bastardise Franklin's characterisation), if you're like me, you'll be left utterly underwhelmed. Pacing and story have always been Rockstar's main openworld failing, and this is doubly/triply true in the case of GTAV. As a black comedy, GTAV succeeds. As a crime drama, it fails.

If there's one moment where it hit home that GTAV was a disappointment, it was when I'd just got the mini-sub and was sailing around the map at excruciatingly slow speeds in an attempt to find 30/30 items, having purchased the one property that was worth buying in terms of profit. There were dolphins and sharks swimming in the unnecessary but very welcome underwater part of the map. But after finding myself stuck on a beach one too many times (when underwater, following sonar beeps, it's hard to see and easy to get marooned) and having to spend a silly amount of time sailing back from the one respawn point the mini-sub can be used from, like with the game-world as a whole, it struck me as how huge but empty it was. If you hit any sea life, they instantly go stiff and sink to the bottom, and there's no way to hunt anything, or even any side-activities such as stopping others hunting. No: you just keep chugging along, hoping something happens or it ends. And that was GTAV in a nutshell, for me. Even when I found myself absorbed in a rare side-activity of value, such as hunting on land, it quickly became a kick in the teeth after I'd spend 30mins trying to find animals and get under $1000 for a gold medal of no significance whatsoever. There was always something to detract from my enjoyment.

Also, GTAV is a surprisingly buggy game. And I'm not talking about just small things here: at one point I pressed the PS button to message a friend. When I returned to the game, I was back at the start, doing the prologue robbery. Luckily the game hadn't auto-saved or else I would've lost some 20hrs of gameplay. Others have had this happened and had to start over. But my troubles didn't end there: ever since that happened, the game would keep asking me to re-calibrate my screen, as if I was playing for the first time, and when I started playing all my settings would be reverted to the default settings. So, I'd have to change my target reticule and turn on subtitles. EVERY TIME. Worse yet, cars I'd spent $10,000's on and stored in my garages would vanish, then be back again the next time I played... then vanish completely. Hairstyles and facial hair would be there in one part of a scene, then not the next, or just revert to default after a scene. Vehicles, such as that damned drill, would get stuck on nothing and require restarting the mission. Just tapping characters with my car by accident would mean missions being failed. The list goes on. I don't know if the settings/garage issue is PS4-only, but many other people in forum threads have reported the same problems. Either way: it's shocking such a big title, whenre-released, has these issues. And that's saying nothing of other sandbox games where you can just use your phone to select vehicles you want to keep, or request they be delivered to you. GTAV expects you to drive to and from garages, or just order taxis everywhere. So outdated and easily corrected with effort.

And Rockstar provided one additional kick in the teeth in the form of trophies. Now, I know: trophies/achievements do not make or break a good game. But they're important to this generation of gamers and offer an incentive for replay value. There are two striking things about GTAV's trophies: the first is how few players bothered playing beyond the start. There were drastic drops between each story-related trophy, and by the end something like only 13% finished what is supposed to one of the greatest games ever made, which is a bit... odd. The second is that the BRONZE trophies for optional content had percentages as low as 0.9%. Having spent time getting as many trophies as I could, I ended with something like 24 bronzes and 3 silvers. Considering GTAV is a 30-60+ hour game, rivaling JRPGs in length, it just added to the unrewarding / pointless vibe the no-money-for-missions game itself gave off. I will never understand why games make every damned trophy a bronze; even for skill/effort/time requiring things. Bronze trophies should be for easy or unmissable things: not almost everything. GTAV was so stingy in terms of trophies I had to sleep 40 times in a row and run for FIVE MILES to get an optional silver. Other than that, you practically have to 100% the game - finding 100 unmarked collectibles for more bronzes - and/or play online.

The saddest thing about this is I don't hate GTAV. It's a good, entertaining sandbox game. The characterisation (aside from Franklin existing solely for an endgame choice) and dialogue are mostly outstanding; often making the cut-scenes worth enduring everything else for. Many of the optional freak missions are also fun, albeit short. But the flaws are so numerous and irritating that, by the end, I was playing it just to validate paying £40 for a re-release of a PS3 game... which, by the way, though obviously looking sharper and running better is far from 'next-gen'. Rockstar did some things right, such as adding skills (such as downgraded bullet-time from Max Payne) for each character to add individuality, yet they took so many obvious missteps it's hard for me to praise the game. The best I can say is that I love Trevor's psychotic self and the series has come a long way from GTA3's silent protagonist. The worst? That Rockstar were too cowardly to stray from their established formula, even with multiple characters and an almost non-existent heist focus leading the way. Let me put it this way: I enjoy going to GTAV's lap-dancing club as much as the next guy... it's just, I want something more to remember it by than a picture. And that's GTAV, in a nutshell: enjoyable but unmemorable. A jack of all trades but a master of none. Instead of terribly designed, needless parts such as drill-stealing stealth missions, more attention should've been put into perfecting what GTA is best at. The problem is, I don't think even Rockstar know what that is, anymore... though online play limited to 30-players max, chucked into the single-player world with added unimaginative competitive modes sure as hell ain't it.

review_headline: A retrospective look at the Game Boy Advance
review_body:
My love affair with handheld consoles ended with the Game Boy Color. Growing up my two brothers and I had our own Game Boys. It helped out on long road trips and when someone was playing the Nintendo or Super Nintendo and we were impatiently waiting for our turn. But after the Game Boy Color I lost my interest in handhelds and moved on to the PS2 and Xbox. So I never had one of these myself, however my brother has always had the latest Game Boy at the time of their releases. I remember playing both his Advance and SP and eventually his DS but I just didn't remember much about the Advance.

This year I decided to look at old Game Boys to add to my growing collection of outdated gaming consoles. I was impressed by the Advance's design and backwards compatibility. I think backwards compatibility is a big selling point for me whenever I buy any console. Its the reason why I got an Atari 7800 over the classic 2600. Upon testing it out the Advance is indeed backwards compatible with Game Boy and Game Boy Color games. I also appreciate that it allows you to stretch the image to fit the Advance's wider screen.

The design is another feature that caused me to choose the Advance over the SP. The design is similar to the PSP or Vita. Its not exactly something that could easily fit in your pocket but even though I don't have particularly large hands I wanted something that I felt was easier to grip and hold on to. Another benefit the Advance has over the SP is that the SP uses a rechargeable battery and requires an adapter. Anything that has a rechargeable battery will experience battery degradation over time making it unreliable for portable use which is the point of every handheld console ever made.

Now on to what I think is the Game Boy Advance's most notorious defect and something I would have been well aware of if I had bothered reading any reviews beforehand. The contrast on the display is so dark! It really is difficult to see. I have to have a lamp pointed right at it just to be able to define what I'm looking at. Unlike the original Game Boy you cannot control the contrast so its always going to need plenty of light. Obviously since the contrast is so dark the colors are going to look a bit muddy but I don't think its much of a problem. The colors aren't exactly vibrant but you can tell a red is a red and not purple. It also transfers colors from original Game Boy games allowing you to experience games in a way you never would have before. I think it goes without saying (especially if you read the other reviews here) that it also has no back light. This is a feature the SP rectified.

I'd hate to say it but if you've read this far and find value in my opinion then I'd suggest you pay a little extra for the SP. While it costs more on the used market it's worth it especially if you can get an adapter with the bundle. Being able to back light and increase the contrast is a definite benefit and an obvious oversight by Nintendo. Aside from that the SP does everything the Advantage does only better. Its smaller so it fits easier into pockets, the screen folds over so you don't scratch it when you do put it in your pocket, and its also backward compatible with the rest of the Game Boy library. I'd say the only flaw in its design is of course the rechargeable battery. The Game Boy DS is also backward compatible but only with Advance games, it has its own library of games as well. Ubi soft rushes games to release, but now that it's January, everything has been fixed except for the ONCE IN A BLUE MOON stutter. Though the load times are a little long, no game-breaking glitches here.

My only complaint is that Ubisoft opted to use British voice actors like they were making a playable Lés Miserables... This is the first time they've done this and it really detracts from the experience. At one point I even switched the language to French and turned on subtitles so I could immerse myself, but then I forgot that Ubisoft still bothers with the modern day side story. NOBODY cares Ubisoft. Really... We don't mind if you just drop that theme, We won't turn our noses up at you if your next game just pretended that subplot didn't exist. review_body: Perfect

I loved both DA:O and DA2, despite some of the latter's flaws. It was still fun! There are just so many problems with DA:I that the game becomes tedious and frustrating.

You can tell this is primarily a (bad) port from console, as they did little to accommodate PC controls. Controls and movement are just so clunky. You have to nearly be standing on a piece of loot to actually grab it--gone are the days of right-clicking and grabbing items.

Combat is a lesson in frustration. They hailed it as a great combination between DA:O strategic combat and DA2's actiony combat. This is completely not true. There is no easy way to control the AI players at all. If you want to use the horrible tactical view, you have to issue orders to each one individually. In the previous games, I would select them all and move them via right-click (yeah, no right click in this game) while using the hold command, so they would basically stay where I told them to go. Now, I have to tediously do it one at a time only to have them go to where I tell them then immediately run off once they get there. Telling them to hold also doesn't seem to work. One will hold, then the second I issue an order to another one, the first one runs off to do his own thing. And if they do happen to "hold" they will not auto-attack but just stand there and drool for a while.

The AI tactics system is basically gone. The only thing you can do is tell them whether or not they should use a command or not, but they took out the ability to tell it under what circumstances it should use them.

As for leveling, you can tell that this was originally supposed to be an MMO, as all of the tediousness of MMO play is present--collectibles and harvesting galore in order to later craft something halfway decent. After a while, I wanted to puke if I saw another elfroot I had to collect.

They also took away almost all character customization. You can't set your attributes (a fundamental thing to do in an RPG!), and the skill trees are fairly shallow--even after getting a specialization.

Story wise, the game is okay (the reason for 2 stars), though they definitely could have done a better job. Reappearances of some old characters from previous games was nostalgic and nice.attributes (a fundamental thing to do in an RPG!), and the skill trees are fairly shallow--even after getting a specialization.

review_headline: Best Action-RPG I've played in a while. A mix of Batman and Assassin's Creed
review_body:
Excellent game!
I have to tell you, I wasn't interested in this game in the least. I thought it looked okay, but nothing actually stood out to me about it. Seeing as it was a Lord of the Rings game I figured it would be mediocre at best. If you read the reviews and scores you will see I was wrong.

I picked this up and find it a very fun game to play. It was designed really well and I can't ask for more from it. The combat is good, the stealth aspects decent, and the overall production value of the game is high. The enemy army structure is quite an experience to deal with. Every character is random generated and unique in some way (they are random bundles of various characteristics which make them unique). They all seem to have their own personalities and story to go with it. It really makes the battles fun and not boring or repetative.

This game is one part Batman Arkham series and one part Assassin's Creed. If you ask me, this is exactly what the Assassin's Creed series should have become rather than degenerating down the path they have. I'm not here to knock the AC series, but that is just for some context of what this feels like. In the end, this is a fantastic action RPG. There is enough action and combat for a nice and exciting time, and enough skill/weapon power ups for a good RPG.

product_title: Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Summoner: Soul Hackers - Nintendo 3DS
review_headline: A Complex and Addictive Role Playing Treasure
review_body:
Shin Megami Tensei is still a series that seems to get little attention or acknowledgement in the United States. Aside from Persona 3 and 4's explosion of popularity in the past few years, the primary titles in the long running franchise don't strike a chord with as many people as the socially influenced games in the SMT canon.

Soul Hackers is a complex, intriguing experience that begs for your attention from the moment you start your first excursion into the game's introduction. As a person who cannot and will not ever truly appreciate the mind numbing premise of Pokemon, to feel emotionally attached and invested in the demons that you create friendships with in battle makes an engaging experience that I can't say I've seen replicated by anything outside of this series, and to win their loyalty by gift or by actions in combat makes it all the more interesting. The creature design, as always, is fantastic, and the characters are all memorable in their own ways, and they certainly are not a cliche for the genre.

Considering how old this title is, this experience has a timelessness that I don't think is present in newer Japanese RPGs, and the first person dungeon exploration gives it an atmosphere all its own. While this game might not be for everyone, give it a chance and you might figure out what made this series a landmark in Japan, and what we're missing out on with the other games in the franchise that haven't been localized yet. So far I've put in about 6 hours, and not one has felt like the slightest waste of time, and that hasn't been the case for me in ages.

product_title: Ar Nosurge: Ode to an Unborn Star - PlayStation 3
review_headline: better than I thought it would be
review_body: This game is a jrpg in line with Ar series (Ar Tonelico, Ar Qoga).  I have tried maybe the first Ar Tonelico awhile back, but wasn't really interested.  At the time of writing this should be the latest Ar game in the series.  I'm become a fan of the recent Atelier games from Gust, so was curious to see how this game is (as I think the idea for the games is interesting).  And I had began a gamefly subscription (game rental) service, saw this and thought I'd check it out.    I won't review in large details, but to summarize what to expect for this game, I recommend checking out other extremely positive/negative reviews on this game for more details, and most importantly checking out a youtube video to get an idea for battle gameplay, purification ceremony, diving, and to check out character models for Nay and Prim (they are the most awkwardly dressed) to get an idea for what to expect in this game.  Can expect to see most main characters in bathing suits / bikinis as well. It does touch on heavier topic of suicide, and has some edgier/risque material, which when combined with the other things mentioned makes this game more suitable for older teens, in my opinion.  Expect battle system to be easy and more casual, story details to not make complete sense, and if too much dialogue don't try to synthesize the best equipment all the time (as synthesizing triggers dialogue cutscenes).    To start, I like the games I play to typically be more 'clean' in terms of content, one as that's my preference, and two it makes a game easy to recommend to all ages to my friends (without having to try and review the entire game in my head to ensure it's appropriate for the person).    I had seen a youtube video of the gameplay, and having played an earlier entry in the game, I realized this game would be 'edgier' and more risque content-wise than the Atelier series.    Story and Characters: 8.3/10  (some gamplay elements mentioned)  The main concepts of the Ar series is that there are special females who have the ability to wield Song Magic, power through singing of different songs.  I forget the term for these beings, but they tend to have a partner (the main characters) that defends them while they build up power in battle to wield the Song magic.  Song Magic is created (weaved) when strong emotions are felt, in a special process/technology called 'Diving', which allows a song magic wielders partner to Dive or see the secrets of their hearts, and resolve discord/confusion or some other issue that exists there.    The details can be a bit fuzzy, and some of the elements in the story may have you scratching your head as they don't all fit together perfectly, but this game is best played not thinking about the specifics too deeply.  Some say this is a fault, but a lot of JRPGs tend to leave some loose ends in their stories (good if it causes a player to ponder the world more and be more interested in it, bad if it means some of the concepts don't really work together or make sense).  Again, I did not dwell on it too deeply, and it was fun for taking it at face value.    The main character Delta has amnesia, and works with main female protgaonist Casty or \\"Cassy\\" as a Song Magic wielder.  These two are childhood friends and help patrol a human city to protect it from 'alien invaders' known as the Sharl, who appeared out of nowhere and started abducting humans.  While a soldier, Delta has not had many tasks assigned to him as of late, until suddenly the leader (Great Empress) assigns you and Cass to investigate a Sharl/human estate, a faction of humans who have accepted the Sharl as messengers from God and co-exist with them (and are not forcefully abducted).  There is a religious faction that also highlights those beliefs in that town.  The story from there develops slowly, I can't think of any major plot twists, and most of the tasks you are sent on follows the concept of different dimensions, the Sharls' goals, etc, which again I felt didn't make alot of sense, but the general task of saving the world and the relationships/diving of the characters I felt was the most interesting part of it all.  I enjoyed it, but it may be best not to expect a lot from it.  I did not understand why Cass would like/love a character like Delta, but, seeing it from a 'childhood friend whom she loves bc he was a good childhood friend' perspective, helped.  I hear this game is actually a sequel to (Ar Ciel Nosurge?), which was not releases in the US, which may explain why I did not understand the character's relation very well.  There is another main pair of characters (robot named Earthes and Song magic wielder, Ion), which you switch between.  This is usually done well, but near the end I felt a little of it was repetitive (not really necessary to 'replay' a segment of the story for the other party's perspective).  Most of the characters have interesting and unique personalities, some of it is voiced over, and I feel they typically chose the right times to voice the dialogue.  Most of the (English) voice acting worked very well and helped add to the story's impact.  A handy feature exists where certain key elements of dialogue can be explained mid-conversation (via a dictionary help guide), and you can view/re-read recent past dialogue in case you need to backtrack if you missed something important.    There is a lot of dialogue in this game, with cutscenes tending to appear at the end of talking to a shop owner (if a cutscene is available with a condition at times that all the latest items from this shop keeper was synthesized).  Some of this dialogue I felt suited the characters well and their personalities.  Other times, I did not care for the dialogue and just wanted to skip it.  It is a little excessive because almost all, or all synthesis of items results in a cutscene to talk about the item.  While some items this is worthwhile for and good conversation comes from it, others it felt like it no words needed to be said, and having the dialogue there cheapened the other quality conversations by making things too dialogue heavy or talking about an item that really has no importance in the story or otherwise.  I avoided this by purposefully not triggering cutscenes when I was tired of the dialogue and not trying to always have the latest synthesized equipment.  This works because the game is fairly easy in terms of difficulty, and was more enjoyable for me in the process.    The main enjoyment I got was the general sense (of saving the world) and from the Diving sections of the game where the characters grow. I also much like the idea of Song Magic, how Song/music holds power, feels like an interesting way to empower the female characters, with the male ones playing the traditional guardian / knight in shining armor role).  In creating Song Magic too, helping Cass and Ion sort through feelings and become more emotionally whole is a neat factor, and helps give character depth (rather than just seeing females for their physical appearance).  There are some fairly deep topics that this game goes into, which helps the game in presenting itself with strong emotions.  It does touch on some on suicide and some edgier/risque material, which I think add to making this game more suitable for older teens.  Some of the Diving scenes had interesting plot twists, but the impact is lessened because there was little if any foreshadowing leading up to it (which makes it feel like something that was added on arbitrarily rather than it being well thought out in terms of the characters' personalities and reasons behind their actions).    Graphics and character design: 7.8/10  Graphics are 3D models, they are not cutting edge, but they are workable and fairly well animated in conveying the needed emotions.  Most of the character designs and clothing are good, most of the girls look like they are 12-15 years old, which is particularly awkward because character models Prim and Nay wear what looks like low hanging underwear that covers only their nether regions.  It would have been much better had they instead were appropriately clothed in stylish clothing instead, like some of the recent Atelier games or like character Nelo.  There are a couple of bath scenes, but these have been blurred / less detailed since this is a Teen game.    Gameplay: 6.9/10  Depends on the style you like, if you want a deep and engaging battle system you won't find that here.  The game is quite easy and doesn't require much grinding, which is good if you're shorter on time and don't like grinding or battling same enemies multiple times to level up.  There is some grinding involved, but the level of experience and DP (Dive points) you obtain progressively as you go through the game increases at a rate where you shouldn't need to stop to battle (unless you want more DP or until you're closer to the end of the game).  The battle system mainly consists of Delta or Earthes fighting 'waves' of enemies, with a meter for Song Magic building at the top.  The top displays a general number of waves left to battle, with a highlight of red if that enemy will be destroyed (if Song Magic were to be used at that moment). Song magic ends the battle, and based on how big the gauge is, it can wipe out some or all of the remaining waves of enemies.  Each general map area you arrive in, there are a certain number of waves of enemies in it (or number of random battle encounters).  When a battle is encountered, you have a set number of turns to clear out as many waves as you can (or, to use Song Magic to end the battle).  If you defeat all enemies who are about to attack you, you 'gain' an extra turn (or all your attack options are refilled).  This is beneficial in a sense, where if you don't like to encounter a lot of random battles, you can clear out all the waves in one go so that you can freely explore the area (less grindy).  The actions involved in battling consist of an available action in the standard square,triangle, circle, x buttons.  Holding R1 can bring up some more options which uses up some of the charge gauge.  While the battles are pretty fast paced (which is good) and is generally less grindy than other RPG's (also good, in my book), the actions can get pretty repetitive after awhile.  The system is not very dynamic because it is so repetitive and all battles will generally involve the same combination of presses.    There is some synthesis (item creation) in this game, but it should not be compared to the Atelier games vast crafting system with levels/grades of item qualities and effects.  The synthesis is fairly bare bones, and if you go through cutscenes moderately and do not try to get the best equipment, you should always have the needed items to synthesize the next item (or to synthesize the pre-reqs).    There are not a lot of context-sensitive options.  So, you may see that some equipment improves Burst Effect or Singing Magic, but you cannot use a help menu to highlight the ability to see what it does. A number of menu options I am confused on still, but since I don't need it for battles, I just equip the best (or seemingly best) stuff I can as I get it and that works.    There is mention of alternate costumes in the game, and you can collect them, but from what I read on a FAQ, the secret boss to actually enable the switching of costumes was left out of this version, so it is not available in this version of the game (which is unfortunate).    When Diving is done, you can gain 'thought crystals' to power up your characters by inserting/equipping them on certain parts of your characters' bodies (hand,feet,head,breast/chest,stomach?) during a purification ceremony, which is the main characters sitting/standing in a bath together in swimsuits, essentially.  In other Ar games (from what I've seen) they tend to make it more awkward by heavily innuating sex references, here is less so which I think is better.    Music: 8.5/10  The music is very good, setting the mood well.  Different key moments involve the use of song magic, and typically the songs chosen add to the impact of what is going on (the songs seem to be sung in japanese, being an english speaker I don't know if the lyrics add additional impact).  Unfortunately the soundtrack is not available for a cheap price anywhere at this time.    Overall score 79/100  As a rental and going in with lower expectations (having not liked the previous Ar games) it was much better than I expected, and I was able to get into it and feel some of the powerful emotion it conveys.  Content-wise, it skirts the line between T and OT, but seems more suitable for Older Teens rather than Teen.  Character models and world aesthetics are generally pretty good, but Nay and Prim's costumes should have been re-done, they are awkward and make the game difficult to recommend / play around friends.  Battle gameplay is faster and less grindy (and experience and Dive Point accrual scales well for a good pacing), but also becomes stale easily.  Many battle abilities are not explained, though w low difficulty this was not a problem (but also removes any depth that was there).  Story is a bit muddled but interesting at face value.  Dive scenes are well done and interesting, though some of the plot twists need foreshadowing to add impact, and to make it more believable (per the character's actions/thoughts) and not feel like it was just tacked on.  There are too many dialogue scenes (particularly, after synthesizing an item) which only feels to interrupt the pacing rather than add and benefit to the story, and makes the good dialogue cutscenes less memorable.  Music is excellent, voice acting is great and the dialogue was voiced over at the right times.  Some of the more risque or deep dark topics mentioned may've been better left out since this game is rated T, but other deep topics discussed (Cass [Stairway to Heaven]) were handled surprisingly well.  Would've been nice to have costume changeoption available (since it is not in this version) and available from the start, since the models are already coded in the game it seems like a missed bonus.  Wish the soundtrack was more freely available, either physically or as download via Amazon or itunes.  Buying the limited edition to get it would be an expensive endeavor.    I think this is a step or two forward for the Ar series, and decided to review in hopes that the things I like propagate in future entries.

review_headline: Amiibo:Train them to be your partners or unstoppable monsters.
review_body:
This figure is similar to Skylanders and Disney Infinity,in that you scan them into the game when you put them on an NFC touch point.However,amiibo work quite differently.They come as different Nintendo characters and work with Super Smash Bros. for Wii U.No other accessories are required(unless you have a 3DS,which will get an amiibo peripheral next year)to use them.All you do is scan them into the game from the GamePad.From there,you can name them and choose who owns them.Along with that,you can customize them with equipment(which changes their stats)and special moves(you'll have to unlock these in Smash Bros.).When you first buy amiibo figures,they are at level 1.They learn from fighting others(including you or CPUs)and impressively pick up techniques and tactics from other players.Amiibo max out their stats(which they gain by leveling up)at level 50,where they become nearly unstoppable.My Link,Samus,Luigi,and Fox amiibos were put into a free-for-all 8-player Smash battle and completely demolished the level 9 CPUs(which means they fight on the same level as a human player due to me training them)and started fighting each other after finishing off the CPUs quickly.It's amazing how fast and well the amiibo learn.

As for the look of the Link amiibo,he looks great.My only complaints with it are that the sword is too flimsy and that you can't use amiibo in modes other than Smash.But it's still a great collectable figure,even if you don't have Smash Bros. or even a Wii U.

iv been waiting since 1997 for Square Enix to make an open world Final Fantasy game and FINALLY its here. i LOVE the open endedness of this game and how you get to complete it however you want. dont care about saving people or the storyline??? spend your time exploring, fighting monsters (or running from them) and save No One, its Literally up to you. its like Skyrim mixed with Final Fantasy, a dream come true. i LOVE the button-mash combat and how easily you can switch between character sets in combat. i LOVE the fact that theres only FOUR Medium sized maps to focus on and theyre completely open and filled with casual-but-constant combat situations. i LOVE THE MUSIC and how seemlessly it flows with the beautiful environments. the outfits, the weapons, the customization, just the whole STYLE of this game is Amazing and i cant get enough of it.

my only SMALL ISSUE with this game is the process of \\"saving a soul\\". instead of doing a stupid favor or task for someone, why not let us get to know side characters in the world and then choose who we want to save??? and then maybe later we could see them in the Ark or on a new planet????? this would have been interesting and fit perfectly into the sci-fi theme of the game (which i LOVE because its actually Factual Sci-Fi). but like said, this is a small issue in an otherwise GREAT GAME thats mostly about Fun Combat and Experience.

if you look at my reviews, im really critical of games and RARELY ever give a game 5 stars....but this little game is a MASTERPIECE and is a COMPLETE STEAL for the cheap price its at right now. it got boring after about 40 hours for me....but its totally worth a buy. THANK YOU SQUARE ENIX AND I CANT WAIT FOR THE NEXT OPEN WORLD FINAL FANTASY!!!

Honestly, as far as pokemon goes, this is one of the better ones. Graphics are at their best while still keeping in style, the world seems a little more alive with pokemon jumping out of the grass, and if you liked any of the previous games in the series, you’ll probably enjoy this one.

What keeps this game from being amazing is that we’ve played it several times before. And not just the original ruby and sapphire, I mean every iteration.

You’re a kid, get one of the three starters, catch and evolve some pokemon, collect some badges, stop an evil team, beat the elite four. Sound familiar? And really it’s not bad –great if it’s your first or second encounter with the franchise- put if you’ve been playing since the beginning, just don’t expect the world to move.

Is it worth buying? Yeah I’d say so. You’ll still put plenty of time into it, train up a cool team, and see a couple small features that are new (seeing pokemon pop up in the grass is fun). And if you don’t buy it, there’s always the next one.

An engaging story with interesting gameplay and lovable, fleshed-out characters. This is the most fun I've had playing a game in a long time. This game really takes me back to Dragon Age: Origins, and I found it acceptably challenging, even on lower difficulties. It's very easy to lose myself in this game, and just as difficult to stop playing. Besides that, it's an absolutely beautiful game, with rich and colorful worlds, and I found the characters endearing and dynamic. I'm not going to go into a detailed and potentially spoiler-y description about the story; just suffice it to say that I think it's awesome and any fan of Dragon Age or RPGs should give it a shot.

My only complaints are more like minor gripes, mainly due to small glitches. I've had the game freeze a couple of times, but considering I've put 90+ hours into it, that's not terrible. The loading times are a bit long, and sometimes things take a bit to render properly. I've also had what I call "jumping characters", where they have some dodgy movement or suddenly appear. These things aren't that big a deal for me, hence the five-star rating, but I thought to mention them in case they are a big deal for someone else.

review_headline: That's both a good and bad thing
review_body:
Very difficult, old-school game.

This game feels straight out of 1996. That's both a good and bad thing. The good is its creepy, gives you very limited supplies, and requires some skill to get through. The game doesn't beat itself like so many do today, which people unfortunately expect or else they rate it a bad game.

The bad is that its sometimes clunky, and unforgiving with checkpoint placement at points. This sometimes exacerbates the games already difficult setting.

Regardless, it is nothing more than freshing to finally play a game that gives a true challenge, crazy story, and fun experience in one package. Most of the negative reviews on here seem to be from people who expect the game to play itself without putting any stress on the player.

I really can't recommend this game enough. Its a great experience that is a breathe of fresh air compared to how recycled, uninspired, and sequel happy the game industry has become.

product_title: This War of Mine (PC DVD) (UK IMPORT)
review_body:
NOTE: As of right now, you can get this game on GOG for 19.99 and they have a 30-day money-back guarantee.

IN SHORT: I should not have believed the hype of the 5-star reviews found on the web. Nor should you. Especially suspect are the positive reviews which don't mention any of the many flaws in this game. Some of this review will deal with technical problems and how they affect game-play, so below is what I am trying to play it on.

MY COMPUTERS (the two out of 5 on which I have tried playing this game):

1. 3-year old Alienware gaming desktop that still devours all games I throw at it without breaking a sweat (except this game that is; this game just stutters with micro-freezes of 2-5 seconds and crashes regularly - about every two turns - which is ironic because as you start the game its intro screen displays Alienware logo.)
2. Brand new Origin PC gaming laptop that devours all old and new games without breaking a sweat (except this one - this game just stutters and crashes regularly)

=========================================

INTRODUCTION

I normally do not write reviews for average, mediocre games. I only write a review if a game either immensely pleases or deeply angers and/or offends me. \\"This War of Mine\\" is one such disappointment. Below I explain why I am so greatly disappointed and support my opinions of this game with game-play examples (you may call them \\"spoilers\\", but as far as I am concerned - there is nothing to spoil - you cannot spoil something that is already bad).

First things first:

I originally bought this game from GOG - before it was made available anywhere else. I wanted to support what I thought was a noble idea of alerting the the world to the horrors of war. Now, 11Bit Studios, the developer of This War of Mine (hereinafter TWoM), claimed they wanted to show the true and ugly side of war - the suffering of innocent civilians caught in the war zone without the means of escape and practically no means of surviving... Have they succeeded? Let's find out.

Over the past ten days or so I tried playing TWoM for a total of approximately 20 hours, possibly more (that includes many reloads/restarts due to the game crashing AND/OR due to other bugs and nonsensical events and outcomes resulting in death of some or all of my survivor toons through no fault of mine).

I believe that since this is a game (not a movie or a documentary) the player's actions should be the main deciding factor in how things play out. Whether your toons live or die should not be forced on you by unnatural events that don't blend organically into the game, nor should there be setups/outcomes that are designed from the start to ruin all your efforts as the player. Most setups in TWoM are such that whatever you do you are unable to ensure that all your toons survive. As already mentioned, if I wanted to see the inevitable suffering and death of the helpless in a war zone I would probably watch a documentary. Playing a game where the player can't affect the outcome 90% of the time is a dumb idea, I think.

And though a survival game is supposed to be hard and bad things can and should be happening to civilians in a war zone, what does happen SHOULD MAKE SENSE.

For example, it makes sense that a stray artillery shell could hit your shelter, create a new breach in the wall forcing your toons to work on securing the shelter once again. It makes sense that the rubble resulting from the shelling could hit one or several of your toons wounding or killing them. But you will not encounter events like this in TWoM. Instead, you will encounter events (such as described in the game-play examples below) that make little or no sense... Like, your toons cannot just have an argument if there's some (imaginary) misunderstanding. No, Sir. If you are doing well as the player, your toons will often develop baseless interpersonal conflicts of which there are NO warnings and which (conflicts) manifest themselves only when your toons fight. Yep, they don't have arguments. They always FIGHT each other literally to the death.. with weapons often resulting in someone becoming wounded or severely wounded basically ruining your chances of completing the game with all of them alive and well...

I gave this game enough chances to work, but it failed not only on the technical level, but as a PC game as well. Now I am inclined to think that the developer has used this sensitive, heart-breaking issue to abuse the higher aspirations of some members of the gaming community only to grab some cash - it is hard for me to believe the developer honestly thinks that TWoM actually does what it (supposedly) was intended to do, namely to bring the message home that all wars should be stopped because behind the democratic, nationalistic or whatever slogans hundreds of thousands and even millions of absolutely innocent people get crippled, killed, displaced, orphaned and otherwise hurt. So, if the game fails to do what was intended (and this game does fail at that), why release it? Right?

TWoM's genre is difficult to define: It is partly \\"The (original) Sims\\", partly a rogue-like (as in the player cannot save), partly an adventure (as in you have to go scavenge for supplies and solve unimaginative puzzles), partly a turn-based RPG (as there are hints of character transformation and interaction and the game is divided into 24-hour \\"turns\\"), partly an action side-scroller (as in you can choose combat or stealth while scavenging), partly a narrative (as in you read chat bubbles and thoughts of your survivor toons in the form of \\"journal entries\\")... and it fails in all of this:

- your survivor Sims become very annoying very quickly and fail to evoke any feelings of compassion or commiseration (especially those who whine about lack of coffee and cigarettes as if these things are absolutely essential to survival)
- you cannot save your progress, the game saves automatically once per turn - and this is bad because the game CRASHES a lot (details below)
- role-paying is basically non-existent
- adventuring and solving \\"puzzles\\" is primitive
- narrative is bland and colorless and it feels like a seventh-graders' uninspired composition.
- the game is full of completely unrealistic, nonsensical constraints (too many to list, but I will give a few examples below) which tie the player's hands.
- game mechanics, game design decisions and in-game events often defy common sense and logic therefore making your \\"survival\\" experience nothing but learning the right sequence of crafting actions
- due to bad game design, bugs and technical problems the immersion is constantly broken
- this is supposed to be a survival game, but in reality it is a Sims-like crafting game, nothing more. Some would argue that TWoM is not about crafting. Those who suggest it are in error because EVERYTHING you do (and you do only three things in this game 95% of the time - scavenge, barter and craft, other than that you eat and you sleep) has one purpose and one purpose only: build (craft) higher-end stuff and more of it. Later in the game this includes food, vegetables, cigarettes, coffee, bandages, medications, bullets, weapons, etc.

Amazingly, thanks to the hype and the unorthodox theme the game sold an insane number of copies and paid for its development two days after the launch. However, just because McDonald's sells billions of cheeseburgers every year it does not mean that junk food is good or those cheeseburgers are healthy.

That said, let's get down to business of reviewing this game in-depth.

=========================================

I. The Good

There are a couple of things about this game which are actually VERY GOOD:

1. The visual representation of a ruined city isawesome. Very beautiful I would say even in spite of the gruesome and gloomy atmosphere. The character models and animations are completely natural and realistic.

2. The music (though not brilliant or genius) is good. The sounds of distant gunfire and explosions are extremely well done.

=========================================

II. THE BAD (not sure if these are conscious design decisions or just bugs, but regardless - these ruin the game)

BAM! - you are dead (Part I):

And so, Pavle went to scout the Sniper Junction and got shot. He is lethally wounded and I bandage him and let him stay in bed for a couple of days so he can recover. In the mean time Marko scouts the Hospital which is still in operation complete with doctors and nurses. While there, Marko (who is not sick or wounded) approaches a nurse to see if she has anything to say or offer. She says that he does not appear to be in need of medical attention. You figure - well, had he been wounded, she would probably patch him up. The next night you put Marko on guard duty and as Pavle is no longer lethally wounded but only severely wounded you send him to the Hospital. Unarmed, barely moving civilian Pavle approaches the hospital... and BAM! For no reason and without a warning the Hospital guard shoots him DEAD. If you want to finish the game with all your toons making it, you have to... Restart. Yes, you will also want to restart because the death is immediately saved and the night ends and you cannot reload from the point when Pavle was still alive. This seems to be a BUG. Why would the Hospital guard shoot a badly wounded, unarmed civilian who came to the Hospital for help?

BAM! - you are dead (Part II):

And so Marko goes to the Garage. As he approaches, quietly and cautiously, invariably the Garage owner comes outside. He has the barter icon on him and says he needs medications for his sick father (since I've restarted the game a number of times already and this is not my first trip to the Garage, I know he needs the meds, so Marko has some on him). We trade. The Garage owner is happy. There's a lot of trash to scavenge through there (not private property, just stuff lying around and up for grabs). So the next night I send Marko there once more. Again, the Garage owner comes out and this time he says - \\"What do you think you are doing sneaking around here?!\\" and pulls out a shotgun... And BAM! Shoots Marko on the spot (and I thought we were friends after we helped your father, you think). If you are quick and lucky, you can have Marko run away... and now you have two lethally or severely wounded survivors with very small chances of 'beating' the game. Restart.

Your stuff is safer OUT THERE:

Suppose you find a lot of valuable food, bandages and medications and you bring them home. The next time your shelter is raided much or all of this valuable stuff will be stolen by the raiders. So just leave it \\"out there\\" where you found it. YOU are the only scavenger in the world. Your stuff will remain \\"out there\\" forever until you need it very badly. Then you can go there and get it. Now, (BUG) I usually collect all the stuff I find and store it in the same pile of trash for easy access later. Once, when I came for the stuff, the pile was completely gone (but this happened only once, the rest of the time it just stays there indefinitely).

You are not supposed to \\"win\\" (Part I):

Imagine you are doing well. No one is sad, depressed, wounded or sick. You have sealed all the breaches in the shelter and even installed a security door complete with an alarm system... but (BUG) the game does not always register that. You check your shelter status and it says that \\"we have breaches in the walls, our place is not secure and we must be constantly on guard\\". Next night you get raided and some of your toons are wounded, sad and depressed. Restart. Why restart? Because this BUG, not my poor decisions or careless actions harmed my toons and ruined their chances of surviving.

You are not supposed to \\"win\\" (Part II):

Imagine you are doing well. No one is sad or depressed. The next morning your scavenger returns you get the shelter status update: Bruno fought with Pavle. Bruno has an ugly deep wound. This looks very serious... and you go WTF??? Where did THAT fight come from? There's been no indication of any disagreements or conflicts between Pavle and Bruno. Restart.

Time is... relative, you know (Part I):

The game is on a timer. 12-hour timer for the DAY and 12-hour timer for the NIGHT. It takes 1 hour to build a new bed, a half-hour to prepare some firewood to use in the heater... your shelter is 4 stories high and has 15 rooms in it. Each room appears to be about 5-6 meters across... and if you send a toon from the bedroom on the ground floor to the top floor, he has to cross 3 rooms, climb a ladder and walk up 1 flight of stairs. If you send him there at walking speed it will take him close to TWO hours to get there. If you send him running it will take ONE WHOLE HOUR.

Time is... relative, you know (Part II):

Suppose Bruno is depressed and a chat bubble icon pops up over his head - he wants to be comforted. You send his best buddy Marko to talk to Bruno. Marko takes 2 hours to reach Bruno. Then the following \\"meaningful\\" conversation takes place (I kid you not):

- Bruno, you mustn't give up!
- Yes, I know, but...
- Bruno, we need you, you must hold on!
- I know, but it is getting so hard!
- Bruno, I am there for you!
- No, leave me alone!
- Bruno, talk to me!
- I don't want to talk to you. Leave me alone!
- Bruno, I am not leaving until you talk to me.

Then Marko and Bruno just sit there with the chat bubble icon displaying \\"in progress\\" animation. After a while they stand up. Pep-talk is done. Bruno is still depressed. The entire affair has taken SIX hours + the TWO hours that it took Marko to get to Bruno. The day is over. Wasted.

I should not have become a writer:

The journal entries (called characters' 'bio' in this game) are pathetic. They are completely uninspired and usually contain zero useful information and are not at all emotionally charged. Example (Marko, day 15): \\"I am glad we decided to help our neighbor in need. Supporting each other is important\\". Well, thank you, developer, for fortune-cookie wisdom. That was DEEP.

A cup of coffee and a cigarette anyone(?)(Part I):

Some of your toons just CAN'T frigging live without coffee or cigarettes (which are very expensive to trade for and when scavenging take up inventory space which is very limited). If you don't provide coffee and cigarettes, your addicted toons become sad, depressed or worse - broken, at which point you can no longer control those toons. They won't eat, they won't take medications, you cannot bandage them if they are wounded... and they will DIE! Or they will leave the shelter and rob you blind of the most valuable things you have. Restart.

A cup of coffee and a cigarette anyone(?)(Part II):

Not only your toons simply can't possibly survive without coffee and/or cigarettes, they don't know how to ration them and whatever is available will be binge-drunk and binge-smoked whereas, knowing how difficult it is to find these things they could cut back a bit and stretch the supplies.

All toons are created equal but some are more equal than the others (Part I):

And so Marko goes to the Supermarket. The description of the Supermarket on the map says \\"Danger\\", so Marko takes an axe with him. Once there, he spies through a crack in the door that a soldier is harassing a girl who is scavenging for some food demanding sexual favors from her in exchange for food. She refuses. As the soldier begins to assault the girl, Marko charges him from behind and drives his heavy fireman's axe right through the soldier's back. The soldier's health bar drops from 100% to something like 5%. By any logic, that soldier should drop to his knees and start vomiting blood in the near-death agony, but that does not happen. For reasons unknown Marko takes a couple of steps back (without any input from me), just out of the melee range of his axe, as the soldier (still standing upright like the axe through his back never happened) begins to turn around. The soldier has an assault rifle. I promptly click on the soldier again hoping Marko can finish him off with another axe hit. Marko runs up to the soldier and stops. I click again - same result. Soldier hits Marko with his rifle's butt-stock. Marko is immediately wounded, sags and slouches and is clearly hurting badly. Another click on the soldier - nothing. Soldier hits Marko again and again and in the end Marko is DEAD. So, it seems, the soldier can handle an axe through his back - no problem, which, of course, is nonsense. (TO BE FAIR, later I accidentally found out that I was not fighting the soldier \\"correctly\\". While in all games I know spamming click-to-attack results in your toon attacking the enemy as often as possible, this is not the case in TWoM. Here, you click the enemy only once and then watch the fight unfold. If you spam-attack your toon's action will be spam-reset and he/she will never attack. Who designed this? At least they could include some manner of tutorial here...)

All toons are created equal but some are more equal than the others (Part II):

The toon selection when you start the game is NOT random. You have preset groups of one to four toons. If you want a 'fighting chance' to see all your toons through the survival game and make sure none of them die, you want the 'blessed trio' of Marko (experienced scavenger with the second largest inventory space in the game), Bruno (a good cook who takes fewer ingredients to prepare meals) and Pavle (a fast runner - which is basically useless, but he is part of this preset trio). You should also hope that along the way a useful fourth toon asks to stay with you in your shelter. You should hope that this is either Marin (a handyman who takes a lot less stuff to craft stuff) or Katia (bargaining skills) or Zlata (comforts everyone and raises everyone's spirits) or Boris who is very strong and can guard the place and also has the largest inventory space of all the toons in the game. Anyone else will just be the ruin of your survivor team.

All toons are created equal but some are more equal than the others (Part III):

When starting a new game,

- If you get the elderly mathematician + kindergarten teacher (loves children) - Restart. They cannot craft anything efficiently and have the smallest inventories
- If you get Roman (ex-soldier, military trained, could be a good guard for your shelter) and Katia - Restart, because just as you begin to think you are doing well, for NO REASON Roman will \\"fight with Katia\\" and she will be badly wounded ruining your chances of seeing this survival effort through.
- If you get Emilia (a talented lawyer) - Restart. She will quickly and invariably get slightly sick -> sick -> severely ill -> terminally ill... AS WELL AS slightly wounded -> wounded -> severely wounded -> lethally wounded... AS WELL AS sad -> depressed -> broken. Then she will either die or run away after robbing you blind.

Persistent visitors:

Should the kids knock on your door you know they want your medications for their mother. If you have 3 bottles of pills, they will ask for 3, if you have 2, they will ask for 2, if you have 1 they will ask for one - you have to give them ALL your meds. If you don't, your toons will become sad or depressed and undermine your efforts to help them survive. So, knowing that and not willing to give away all your meds you can try to ignore the kids knocking on your door... but the kids will NEVER go away. They come at 10 am and every 10 seconds there's bang-bang-bang on your door until 8 pm when the night cycle begins.

Don't be such a crybaby:

All your toons are annoyingly whiny. They will always and constantly say ONLY the following:

- I am hungry (and you should keep them \\"hungry\\" and feed them ONLY when they become \\"very hungry\\" because otherwise you will run out of food and they will become \\"starving\\" and therefore you will most likely have to ... Restart)

- I would not mind another helping (of food)
- We need food! (yeah, like I didn't know)
- I am tired
- I need bandages! (even if \\"slightly wounded\\" - I don't know what it means... A couple of scrapes and bruises?)
- I haven't slept in days
- I need coffee!
- I haven't smoked in days!
- This is just getting too hard!
- Not a good day...

They spam these (and a few other similar) complaints all day long. I am not simplifying here. That's pretty much all they say and in exactly those words ... (other than the degenerate pep-talk presented earlier). Well, sometimes they can say something like

- We might make it. Let's keep it up
- Not a bad day (if they are content that they helped a neighbor)

Hey, can we talk, please, I beg of you(!?):

NOPE, even your toons living in the same shelter cannot talk to each other at all (except the above example of primitive pep-talk when someone is depressed). You cannot talk to any NPCs out there either. You can click the barter icon which brings up the barter screen or you can fight the NPCs. That's all. Once, my scavenger was running home from the St.Mary's Church (he did not steal anything or anything like that, did not even look at any private property, did not hurt anyone either). When running past the priest... well, I don't know, he probably accidentally stepped on the priest's toе or something. Before I knew it they were fighting for no reason at all. The priest started it. Immediately, I clicked on the space away from the priest to break it up. The priest did not insist on continuing to fight (my scavenger hit him with the shovel pretty hard - by the way, the shovel was NOT equipped by me, it became automatically equipped when the priest started the fight)... Could I break it up? Could I come up to the priest, apologize for whatever it was that I did? NOPE. Can this be undone, forgotten, worked out somehow? NOPE. Instead, the priest-loving refugees from the basement under the church started running at my scavenger and attacking him. Done. The place is now off-limits (including the ability to barter with the priest) unless you want to kill everyone there (including the priest).

These are just a few examples of the \\"depth\\" and \\"ingenuity\\" of this game's design and writing.

=========================================

III. THE UGLY

GAME CRASHES (why this is so very bad):
NOTE that many reviewers complain about the game crashes, not just me.

Now, the game turn is a 24-hour period divided into DAY and NIGHT cycles.

During the DAY your toons craft - they build beds, cook food, seal the breaches in the walls, etc. - there are a lot of tedious (and fairly complicated) tasks to perform. The complexity of these tasks lies in the need to keep track of multiple ingredients/components/parts used in crafting - how much of what you have, how much you will need tomorrow, how much you've spent... but there is no easy way to track any of this. Still, you MUST be excessively efficient because if you are not, some or all of your toons will soon become sick, wounded, depressed or even broken and therefore uncontrollable... and/or some or all of them will die and you will have to restart the game.

Also, during the DAY random events take place - a trader may or may not stop by,said trader will or will not have what you need, a neighbor may or may not gift you some food or ask you for help, a new survivor may or may not come and ask to join your crew, etc. (By the way, the game tells you that you cannot leave your shelter during the day because snipers are hunting anyone and everyone, but NPCs have no problem with that - children will come to your door asking for medications for their mother, traders will come to barter, neighbors will come asking for help boarding up their windows and so on. ONLY YOU cannot step outside during the day.. well, sometimes you \\"kind of\\" can, for example, if you agree to help that neighbor with her windows.. AND if you do, the toon you send will simply disappear until the next morning and in the morning he/she will return safely - snipers or not.)

Now, the player CANNOT SAVE game progress. It is automatically saved at the end of the NIGHT cycle if you are done scavenging and send your scavenger home or if he/she is killed. And so, you go through another DAY doing all of the above... and the next night before your scavenger goes out the game CRASHES. So you have to reload and re-do the last DAY, but you really CAN'T because unlike the day BEFORE THE CRASH (when the night was calm, your shelter was not raided, no one got sick or wounded, a trader showed up bringing stuff you needed)... the day AFTER THE CRASH everything could be exactly the other way around... and through no fault of yours the situation of your survivor toons suddenly turns from promising and hopeful to impossible and desperate... and you thought you were doing so well. Oh, well.

(By the way, the night cycle is 12 hours. Even if you are revisiting an already scouted location which allows you to load up on supplies by 10 pm your scavenger cannot make another trip that night and he/she will return home at 7 am as if he finished scavenging at 5 am and not 7 hours earlier)

BOTTOM LINE: THE GAME THAT DOES NOT ALLOW YOU TO SAVE HAS NO RIGHT TO CRASH. Period.

And this is what you get with this game... Good luck.

======================================
WHAT OTHERS HAVE SAID ABOUT THIS GAME:
======================================

2/5 stars: Emotionally good. Frustratingly bad. by Grogger

The game sets a great tone and atmosphere, conveying the feeling of hopelessness and loss, surviving and success. Often leaving you in situations where you have to make tough decisions which both you and your characters have to live with, characters you may like or hate and have to keep alive.

Though it goes downhill steadily in execution, some of the gameplay mechanics are far to contrived, it is often not clear when you are making you character do something that could get them killed in situations it clearly should tell you. Unfortunately, due to the game being pretty inconsistent it's hard to even say if many of the problems are very poor design or just huge bugs that have been overlooked.

Due to it's flaws, regardless of if they're preposterous design or blatant bugs, the result is you will often go through a lot to keep your characters alive only to have them killed off due to the flaws in the game rather than any fault of your own. When this happens, the game wears thin quickly.

In it's current form I would give it 5/10, if the bugs/bad design are corrected it could go up to 7/10. Currently the game spoils to much of it's positives.

1/5 stars: Neat Concept, Poor Game by Nystur

Glitches, nonsensical crafting, unfinished writing, permanent death, no save feature, a lack of realism, preaching to the player, and unbelievable quirks ruin the game. Examples/explanations:

--Glitches: [1a.] Good glitch: Want to keep your stuff safe from raiders? Don't loot one of the cabinets in your base. As long as something stays in it at all times, you can use it to hide your stuff. [1b.] Bad glitch: If you board up your base entirely, it sometimes won't register that you did.

--Nonsensical Crafting: [2.] Finding things to barricade doors and windows wouldn't be difficult: they'd litter the ground. It's a city full of ruined, wooden buildings and furniture. The effort you have to go through to collect them often seems unrealistic, and it cheapens the gritty feel of the game.

--Unfinished Writing: [3.] Donating medical supplies to the hospital deletes them from your inventory, but does little else. Donating doesn't appear in the what-you-did slideshow at the end, etc.

--Permanent Death and No Save Feature [4.] The game auto-saves when a night is done, and if a night-time raid fails due to a character death. Since there are many glitches/issues in the game, this is an irritating problem.

--Preaching to the Player [5.] Characters disdain violent actions, and monologue text about how bad they are.

--Unbelievable Quirks/Lack of Realism [6a.] Addictions depress characters if you don't indulge them. [6b.] Item weight isn't considered. For example, 10 inventory slots could = 20 pieces of lumber or 100 sugar cubes. (The sugar cubes would weigh about 0.66lbs total. The lumber would obviously be heavier/cumbersome.) [6c.] If a character becomes \\"broken\\", they're unplayable and unable to move due to depression. Shortly, they'll flee, robbing the group and leaving them to die. The person will somehow do this even if too sick/weak to flee. The sudden betrayal makes no sense: they gave up on life, but then they're motivated to survive at the cost of everyone else?

==============================

First of all, I played this game on PC with a Xbox controller. So the review is not reflective of the PC UI.

I have put in about 30 hours and I can honestly say I am enjoying it more and more. I would not say it is a stepdown from DAO. And here is why:
1 The map is huge, beautiful and well-designed. There are tons of things to do and areas to explore. It is truly enjoyable to walk around.
2 Leading the Inquisition is fun. It offers you a lot of room to act the way you want and the war-table is awesome.
3 High-quality and intriguing side request.
4 Lots lots lots of code index, songs, notes, and information.
5 Cool weapons and armor design.

review_headline: I think this may be the worst video game I've ever played in my life.
review_body:
Let me preface with a couple of things. First off, I'm furious. I've been playing this game now for two days in "My Career" mode to learn & figure it out, and I haven't won a single match. Not one. Nothing. I've even gone in and set the game to its easiest settings and cranked reversals to where I should be murdering this game. Still nothing. It's the worst experience I've ever had playing a video game. The team who made this, and the people who, along the way, allowed this game to see the light of day should be fired from 2K Games. Secondly, I'm a HUGE video game player, I've had an Xbox Live account for over a decade and have hundreds (thousands?) of hours playing a variety of games from Borderlands to Skyrim to Battlefield to GTA... I was VERY excited to play this. I'm a huge wrestling fan and hadn't purchased a wrestling video game in probably ten years, but I have the WWE Network, and WWE did a great job of getting me excited to play (Pre-Ordered just to get Sting!).

Again, let me be clear, I'm not the guy who played 2K14 and created 250 CAWs with every single moveset meticulously pored over. I'm the guy who loves wrestling and video games and thought it'd be awesome to be The Rock or Stone Cold and lay the smack down on Ultimate Warrior and Sting. So I'm literally the most casual of casual gamer this game is targeting. I haven't owned one of these before so of course I went straight the tutorial... oh wait, there ISN'T a tutorial. Nope. No way to have someone even briefly explain to you how to grapple, move around the ring (how do I run?) how combinations are executed, how things happen in the ring... how to climb the ropes, etc. Nothing. If you're not familiar with the mechanics you are just out of luck and get to frustratingly teach yourself the basic mechanics of how to move around the environment on your own while getting your ass kicked.

Most frustrating of all is the HORRIBLE "reversal" mechanic. This idea that at seemingly arbitrarily decided nanoseconds during character interaction you have the briefest of opportunities to reverse what's coming, provided you can either use the Force or manipulate space/time. I've gone in and cranked these settings to the point where I should literally be able to reverse things every single time, but do you think that helped? I probably reverse a move 1 out of 20-25 times I'm provided a chance.

The resulting gameplay is an exercise in murderous frustration. The game simply is NOT fun. It's not even fun to lose, it's not fun to play, it's not remotely an entertaining experience.

If you're a hardcore player of these games and this is a routine purchase for you, then you're not the target of this review. You probably play these things in your sleep and enjoy them immensely. You haven't experienced anything that I've experienced and I'll completely acknowledge that. I'm just a casual gamer who thought this would be a fun way to vicariously live through some of my favorite wrestlers and spend some time dropping some Stone Cold Stunners on some Jabronies. This game is such a failure you can't even do that. If you're in my shoes and you're thinking about this as a diversion, look elsewhere. Giving this game 1 star is generous. Don't waste your money.
