review_headline: What if I had never been born???
review_body:
As human beings we occasionally wonder about the road not traveled. What if I just got on a bus and left right now? What if I had stuck with my first major, instead of switching? What if that car hadn't stopped? What if I had never been born?

Those types of questions are the premise of Chrono Cross, as the main character, Serge, stumbles into a world where he was already dead. What all those questions mean for all of us, we will never know, but Serge is at the center of something bigger than all the universes put together. What transpires is a dimension hopping plot about alternate futures and temporal paradoxes.

Things you need to know:

Firstly, while this is the sequel to [[ASIN:B001E27DLM Chrono Trigger]], it's not mandatory that you play the SNES/DS game. I can say that, because I had never played CT until I had beaten Chrono Cross. I think it's a fitting sequel, what could you do with a game that had nineteen different endings? The answer is a very creative solution which I shall not spoil.

Secondly, this game boasts 45 different playable characters. On the negative side, less than half of them are remotely interesting. In addition, despite having so many characters, very few can be combined to use special moves (Double Techs and Tripple Tech Skills, as they were called in Chrono Trigger). And as you play through the game, you might find the way they speak (although it's all in text, there is no voice acting in this game) annoying. Instead of programming different things for each of the characters to say, each of them says the same thing, but with a different verbal tic. This was done to save space on the disk.

Thirdly, the unique battle system/ leveling system. For the most part, you only gain levels by beating a boss character. Which means you can't grind until you're ten or twenty levels above everybody to breeze through the game the first time around. In addition to that, the individual battles take strategy. Sure, regular enemies are a breeze, but there's a lot of push-and-pull, risk-vs-reward in the difficult battles.

Each character has a Stamina Meter worth 7 points. You can use that Stamina to perform Physical Attacks, that come in three levels 1. Weak, 2. Strong, and 3. Fierce. Each hit that connects will raise your \\"Grid Level\\" by that many points. Your Magic Grid contains the spells that you can use in battle. But, using a Magic Spell will diminish your stamina by 7 points completely, and you can go into negative stamina points, which means it'll take longer to be back up to full Stamina.

This means, in the late game, if you need to heal a party member, it's not as easy as Casting Cure in Final Fantasy. You have to spend the stamina, to build up your Grid, to cast the spell, and most spells can only be cast once per battle. Sometimes it's smartest to have all your party use Defend, just to let your Stamina build back up.

Oh, sure, you could just pound X, going 1-2-3-Element, 1-2-3-Element, 1-2-3-Element! But, believe me, you'll hit the wall eventually. And, just a heads up, you can only get one Revive Element per play-through, so plan your battles correctly!

There's not much else to say without resorting to spoilers. Chrono Cross is an video game epic that should be uncovered as you go. Take the road less traveled, I say. Unlike real life, there's always NewGame+ Mode, where you could do it all over again.

If you've started collecting PS1 games, or JPRGs, Chrono Trigger deserves a spot in any collection.

review_headline: Fun But Not a Memorable Ride
review_body:
I'll just break it down into 2 simple parts: good and bad. Keep in mind these thoughts are based on my personal opinion. Fair warning: spoilers up ahead.

Good:

-Voice acting is great. Adds dimension to the main characters.
-Good gameplay. There's nothing more satisfying than the sound of a hard death blow to the head caused by Joel's iron pipe. Sniper option allows you to feel good about developing a good strategy to defeat villains.
-Fantastic environment design. Really gives you a sense of being alone (at times) in a post apocalyptic world. Running and frantically searching for an exit in a dark sewer system - I love it!
-Very well written story. I was heavily intrigued with the transition from Joel clinging to his last breath to Ellie hunting in the woods.
-Good emotional content. Death, betrayal, sense of humor...it's got a bit of everything to stimulate your senses.

Bad:

-Human villains are too generic. C'mon. You can do better than dirty jeans and a beanie and lines like, "You killed my pal, you're dead meat!"
-No exciting final battle. All I have to do is shoot a handful of robotic soldiers? That's it?! Would've been better if they saved bloaters for last.
-Ellie! Can this little potty mouth be any more annoying? Jesus. I can't stand Ellen Page as it is; her soul now has to haunt me in my video games? Dear Lord, please don't let her return if there is a sequel. Give us plenty of Bill.
-Creature design: Clickers. I can't help but think their heads are covered with candy corn. Infected are great.
-AI. Ok, this isn't bad per se. But it can be better. I can't help but laugh whenever I hide behind a counter, a villain spots Ellie standing in front of him, then proceeds to walk away as if he never saw her.

Overall it's a good game. It just didn't live up to the hype in my book. RE4 is safe from getting knocked off its throne. For now.

product_title: Corepad Mouse Skatez Pro Skatez for Universal Use (1 sheet)
review_headline: May need to be thicker for some mice
review_body:
As a previous reviewer mentioned the sheet is about the size of a baseball card, it measured roughly 10x7 cm (3.9x2.8 in). The material is fairly easy to work with and depending on the mouse there should be enough material for 2-5 replacements total.

However the issue is that many mouse manufacturers (Logitech MX, 518 and MK550 in this case) have been indenting the area where the Teflon sits. This helps to keep the Teflon from coming loose, and then a slightly thicker Teflon is used to make up for the increased depth. This meant that when the mouse feet were removed as instructed and replaced, the new Teflon from this sheet was flush with the mounts, and because of this was not any better than the worn out Teflon.

This issue was fixed by reattaching the original feet and installing much larger feet over the originals. Its not ideal because they may come loose more easily, and due to the larger cuts there will be fewer replacements from a sheet. However it does work for now and I'll update if there any issues with the feet staying.

review_headline: Not perfect but still fun to play
review_body:
Your sister has vanished on her wedding day and is presumed drowned. Your family is in mourning and the family home in ruins. It is up to you to access Luisa's memories and discover what really happened to her.

There are three ways to play \\"Grim Tales: The Bride\\": Casual Mode (significant game locations and interactions marked with sparkles); Advanced (no sparkles or extra clues); and Hard-core (no game hints, no min-game hints, and no sparkles). The game is untimed and there is no penalty for excessively clicking during hidden object scenes. There is a Strategy Guide (when playing in Casual Mode you can click the hint button if you don't know what to do next) and a Walk-through Guide. There is also a bonus game included in the Collector's Edition.

For the most part \\"Grim Tales: The Bride\\" is a nice hidden object/adventure game The storyline is a good one (although you don't want to think too much about it or the plot starts to make less sense - for example just when did Louisa disappear and why look for her now?). The game play is pretty good but a bit repetitious - you'll come across an item that is locked (you need to find lots of keys in this game), have to travel through several rooms to find the object, and then travel back to the original location to use the object you found. There is no map in this game but you really don't need one. The mini-games range from easy to semi-difficult. The hidden object scenes are just the right level of difficulty. The scenery is beautiful and there are some nice special effects - for example snow falling during a hidden object scene. The music adds a nice ambience to the game. Oddly enough, the dialogue is written and not spoken. The one thing I really didn't like was the abrupt ending of the game which seemed a bit anticlimactic (the same is true for the bonus game in the Collector's Edition).

\\"Grim Tales: The Bride\\" isn't perfect but it is still a fun game to play.

After beating the main story and most of the side quests, I clocked in around 135 hours. Now that is impressive and most of the quests were fun.

The game reminds me a lot of the original Dragon Age (also check that out, Ultimate Edition for under $20 bucks) without squad combat. You choose your race, gender, and appearance and then you're dead. A great and interesting concept that will have you guessing, literally, up until the very end. Who is your friend, who is an enemy, is this or that person lying?

The game has hours upon hours of great voice acting, a ton of books and lore to read about the world of Amalur. You can plow through the main story or really take your time and immerse yourself in the world which is a really interesting one. You can make your own weapons and armor or just buy some. Or maybe you want to make your own potions and gems for upgrades. You can do it all or not of it and still progress

The combat system is really great as well. You can choose to focus on being a melee fighter, a finesse combatant, or a mage. Or you can spend points in all 3 categories and be a hybrid fighter (my preferred method). You can equip one main weapon and a secondary weapon. So you can combine a sword with a bow (yawn) or get nutty and use a greatsword (giant body long sword) paired with chakrams which are flying discs of death. You can also equip magic spells and other talents once you level up enough to "buy" them

It's not all roses though. Money becomes useless after about 10-15 hours of game time because you'll have so much of it. I ended the game with over 18 million gold after having spent a lot before that. There is so much loot to find (like weapons, armor, gems, treasure) that you'll constantly be in the inventory. I probably spent at least 5 hours in the inventory over the course of the game selling, stashing, and rearranging all my loot.

Also some quests never seem to end. As an example (veryvery minor spoilers), some guys asks you to get him specific clothes and he'll pay you for them. When you give them to him he asks for more, and more, etc. It's annoying for gamers like me who like to finish a quest and get a result. The clothes and armor for some characters are limited in styles so it's hard to get something really unique. And all the clothes/weapons you can make look virtually the same.

With all that said, I'd still recommend this game to any RPG fan. Anybody who likes Fable, Zelda, and/or Dragon Age will find themselves right at home in the world of Amalur

Single player is available look for it in the multiplayer menu under STEAM WORKSHOP. Use the option to set up bot matches with scripted AI. You could set up an online server and padded it out with bots or bots and human slots.

The basic tutorial level which takes you through the different roles you can play Assault, Rifleman, Automatic Rifleman, Scout-Sniper, Sniper, Machine Gunner, Light Mortar, Flamethrower, Commander Squad Leader and Command Leader can be seen as a \\"mission\\" and not an easy one to master. The tutorial introduces you to the weapons and lets you practice with them via shooting at targets and makes sure you know how they work and what their capabilities are. The Commander part for example tutors you in the very specific methods of controlling squads. Again this can be seen as a mission within a mission. The curve is very steep and that in itself can also be seen as a challenge.

Then the maps Hanto, Saipan, Guadalcanal, Peleiu, Kwajalein and Iwo Jima can all be played as stated above with Bots. Each can be an objective or mission if you'd like.

review_headline: Why did they ruin Elder scrolls?
review_body:
I can't believe they decided to ruin this series. It's such a let down. In this game you will be doing the same things over and over again until it drives you insane! Finding gates to Oblivion, entering the gates, and finding the source of the gate so you can close it off. Over and over again. The armor and weapon choices are so basic that it's not even funny. It's got quite a bit, but it's all the same, just enchanted differently. No personality in equipment, items, people, or sidequests. And the storyline is just blah. One of the worst things I hated about this game was the fact that they took away the jump spells that were in Morrowind. One of the best things about Elder scrolls. I loved jumping 300 feet into the air and slowfalling back down whilst I'm fighting cliffracers in the air. That was awesome. Nothing awesome about Oblivion.
Invisibility makes it a joke. Way too easy! And I don't know how long I roamed around sometimes without running into hardly anything to fight or any new places. Just a bunch of trees, rocks, and hills. BORING! Oh...and turning into a vampire is absolutely stupid, and a waste of time. Vampirism works totally against you, and being a vampire is not in anyway enjoyable.
The basics of this game: turn invisible until you get strong, and then just decimate everything with a warhammer. No strategy at all. Zero.
All the running around that you have to do in this game is bound to give you a headache and make you sick to your stomach. I would recommend Morrowind over this game any day.

This Brief Review is for L.A. NOIRE \\"Greatest Hits\\" Edition.
This game is fantastic. It is genuinely surprising to me how poor many of the reviews have been for this game... and it is reasonably clear that most players weren't ready for the plunge. I am a big mystery fanatic, so please factor that in. This is the best solo story game I have played on a console for the following reasons:
1. Best use of environmental cues (and a very difficult set, IMHO, to have pulled off so well).
a. wonderful atmosphere / sensational music & radio
b. excellent cue mechanics and cut-scenes, etc.
2. Decent lie/doubt/truth mechanic: From reviews I had interpreted that this was \\"broken\\", but absolutely not the case.
3. Surprisingly decent action integration. There has never been a second where I didn't have something \\"critical\\" to do...
4. Unbelievable and smooth motion play.
5. No punches pulled MA rating, without gratuitous pandering (city corruption, racial themes, nudity of corpses, dead bodies, and high violence outcomes without prolonged silliness).
There are strong story influence leads from the great L.A. Confidential motion picture (and lesser Black Dahlia, from the great James Ellroy). I have never driven so consistently poorly in my life... but it is all in good fun. If I have any game-play complaints, it's that we should have more time to explore the city and make other venue determinations... I think the game is constantly trying to compensate zero-attention-spanners. Much higher replay value than the disappointing Hard Rain, and I would be overjoyed with any sequel.
Mature Audiences only for this one. All IMHO.

Up to four people can play on the same cartridge, but only the first person (most likely the owner of the game) fills the shoes of the mayor.

For those of you who played Wild World and might be worried that New Leaf has the same restrictions, it doesn't. The game gives the player as much freedom as it can within the boundaries of the game world. I don't want to spoil too many of the new things in this game because it was very fun to experience rather than have explained to me.

The bottom line is that veterans and newcomers alike will most likely enjoy this game. Veterans, such as myself, will enjoy it for all the changes and enhanced online play, newcomers will enjoy it because it's probably the best Animal Crossing game to date.

review_headline: High quality gamepad with an excellent layout. Falls short on support.
review_body:
I was very excited to play games on my Galaxy Note II and Windows PC with this controller. I did quite a bit of shopping and decided on the Nyko Playpad Pro because of its ergonomic design and similarity to popular console controllers. For $25.00, I couldn't say no.

Nyko's product description insists this controller functions under several different universal protocols, making it perfect for just about everything. The controller's communication type is controlled by a switch on the underside, and can be changed from HID (Human Interface Device), a universal game controller protocol; iCade, a protocol specifically for a set of iOS games; Mouse, which allows the controller to control a mouse cursor within the OS; and \\"APP,\\" specifically for routing the controller's input through Nyko's \\"Playground\\" application.

First things first: this is a great looking controller. The design closely resembles an Xbox controller. The analog sticks' resistance in both movement and pressing (yes, they can be pressed down just like on an Xbox controller) are appropriate. I have no complaints about the bumpers or triggers, but I wish the directional pad had more flexibility. It is a bit difficult to independently press one direction.

I was slobbering happy to set this up. It charged quickly and paired up with my phone right away. However, the triggers would not register in emulators no matter what I set the mode to. They would only work for left and right clicking in mouse mode. I tried pairing it up with my laptop's integrated Bluetooth 4.0 radio and although the Playpad Pro pairs with my computer, no input is registered. I tried using it on every different controller mode, pairing between switches, updating my drivers, etc. - Nothing. Very disappointing.

As a last resort to get the controller functioning 100% with my Note II, I downloaded the NYKO Playground application, despite its 2-star rating and reviews which warn that it may break bluetooth communication with the Playpad unless a factory reset is performed on the device. The configuration menu, appearance and stability of the application actually looked promising. It even \\"updated\\" my controller's firmware via Bluetooth. However, trying to configure a profile to use the controller did nothing more than put me in a circular process of unpairing, repairing, and restarting the application.

I still have high hopes for this controller. I gave it a generous three stars despite its shortcomings. While it is a relatively sturdy and attractive controller at the right price, it falls flat on its face in product support and ease of use. Nyko has a blatant chance to fix many of the common issues with this controller as they are obviously software-based. I, as well as many other owners of this product, can only hope it is in their interest (money-wise) to do so.

UPDATE: After reinstalling Bluetooth drivers again and re-pairing the Nyko PlayPad Pro with my PC, I got it to function normally with several emulators. I can switch seamlessly between HID and Mouse modes, but the triggers will only work for the latter and don't register in Windows as game controller buttons.

review_headline: Slow and Underpowered - Public Beta Version?
review_body:
I really wanted to like this console. I bought it off Amazon.ca and got it shipped the next day. Everything looked and felt good. The controller felt slightly cheap and overpriced at $49.99 by itself, but is a fantastic deal when bundled with the console.

The OUYA runs well, but refused to connect to my wired ethernet connection. I was forced to connect to my slow and distant Wifi instead, which undoubtedly made downloads and media streaming slower. Even the update seemed to take forever.

I was excited to go through the setup process and surprised that the controller was very responsive when typing in my info. I went to the DISCOVER menu to download a bunch of games. I was pleasantly surprised when playing Bombsquad and Vector. Fast, responsive simple games with no problems.

Things slowed to an absolute crawl with games like Beast Boxing and Flashout. Beast Boxing had a 4 second lag at times. To say it was unplayable is a gross understatement. Flashout took 3 attempts to load, and the menu itself was lagging by a few seconds. I never even succeeded in getting into the game. I tossed my controller on the table in frustration and noticed after a few seconds that the OUYA was still slowly registering my button presses on the screen. BRUTAL.

XBMC was also a nightmare, though admittedly this may be because my OUYA refuses to connect to my wired network. The menu lag wasn't too bad, but video slowed down to a crawl, and I suspect it wasn't just because of network buffering.

The simple games run quite well, but the more advanced games and media software are either completely stonewalled by bad OUYA software or outdated hardware, or a combination of both.

UPDATE: After a few days with the OUYA, my opinion of it hasn't gotten any better. It may have even gotten worse.
-A \\"simple\\" game like Vector now lags and stutters in later more complex levels, which is more frustrating than fun.
-The emulation performance for NES/SNES/Genesis is fantastic on the console itself, but the controller ergonomics are frustrating. The top edge of the \\"O\\" button frequently gets stuck under the cover plate if pushed a certain way, as do the other buttons to a much lesser extent. I also find it far too easy to accidentally push the center OUYA button when doing certain motions with the D-Pad (ie: dragon punch).
- The OUYA console seems to have better performance after a reboot, so I suspect it's not killing background tasks aggressively enough.
- XBMC performance still stutters noticeably at 720p, and very badly at 1080p. I thought this may have been a network performance issue, but it doesn't seem to have a big problem buffering. It's the video rendering that falls greatly behind. I've tried both the official XBMC download and the latest nightly builds.

review_headline: Great start for those new to Metro Series
review_body:
I have to say I loved the original metro 2033. The atmosphere, the story, and weapons. There were many flaws with the original that were greatly improved in Metro Last Light. There are a 5 main things that make this game good, along with a few small flaws.

1. The combat is well improved. Unlike the first Metro I didn't have to sit there and unload a full clip into an enemy to kill him. The AI are well improved to the point were sneaking is the greatest weapon in the game which seemed impossible in the first game.

2. Button mapping and interface are well improved. By pressing different buttons it brings up a nice screen that shows you your inventory nicely as well as buttons to push in order to access that part of the inventory. Also selecting the military grade ammo was even better instead of accidentally switching to it while pressing x you have to press two buttons to do it. It helped me so much knowing that i didn't accidentally switch to military rounds when i didn't want to.

3. The choice of action is greater and you have more options in how you approach your situation. You can sneak through the whole game without killing a single human, go guns blazing, sneak around a kill everything, or a combo of each. Also the two endings are back with a good and bad. Both are good endings and I didn't disappoint myself by which ending I got because both a good in their own ending.

4. Weapons are stealth abilities are greatly improved. You can now carry three weapons of your choice with you. Also at markets you can upgrade them there. No more hoping for a gun with the right attachments you want. You can decide what you want just there. The amount of weapons in this game are even more. From the previous metro to this one there was close to 5 more guns added giving players new game styles to try. You can snipe if you want to now which was missing from the last game. The stealth is greatly improved to the point where it is too easy at times. It is still hard deciding who to avoid or kill but it is easier to do so than in the previous game. There is even an added instant kill sneak kill or knock out.

5. The graphics are beautiful and could compete easily with some of the top graphical games out there. It can even lag on some better pcs which is scary.

Now aside from the many pros the cons are there but are minuscule. For example ammunition is limited. You can't just go and stock on as much ammo as you want to. I get it is a realistic shooter and people can't carry 1000 assault rifle rounds with them but come on it was fun having a lot of ammo especially for the mutants. Also the ranger mode was only a preorder bonus and the only information on public release suggest a 5 dollar fee which is crazy for an added difficulty level. Also the game seemed shorter compared to others out there and with no multiplayer aspect YET, the game could have been longer.

All in all this game is great game and for its appeal to many people its a great buy.

review_headline: As a newcomer to the series I enjoyed this one a lot!
review_body:
Final Fantasy XII is a great game. For starters people who are newer to the series will probably see the beauty of the game more than hardcore fans. I myself have played I,II,VII, and just finished XIII and I enjoyed myself greatly during my whole experience.

The Battle System: 4/5

First of all the battle system in 13 is different, something unlike anything I have ever used. I didn't think it was terrible though, you used more auto-triggers than anything else but shifting paradigms helped with player-character connection slightly. You don't get the feel that you are playing as each character by selecting their individual moves, but I got the feeling more of being a controlling force over my battle team which didn't bother me much I kind of enjoyed the change in things. I liked leveling, but the only drawback is that once characters can learn any role it's kind of difficult to stray from the main three roles they had in the beginning chapters. All in all I didn't mind the change of battle system and I actually thought it was strategic feeling more so than the older games.

The Story: 5/5

I am a person who loves a good, long, intriguing story in my games and every FF game gives this to me, or at least most have so far. Final Fantasy XIII has a great story-line with all around great characters (Minus Lightning's mood-swings and Hope's annoying moments). The story of Gran Pulse and Cocoon was interesting and the fight between Fal'cie, L'cie, and the worlds was just balanced and the settings were phenomenal. The ending will blow you away, well it did me because I just wasn't expecting it.

General Gameplay: 5/5

All in all the gameplay was fun. It's just a fun game, but only if you don't mind a bit of linearity. Clearly if you're used to the open-world FF games the linearity is going to be a little bit of an issue, but if you just let it slide then you'll actually have a great fun game. The movement controlscan be a little sticky at times also but nothing too major. Skipping cutscenes is a plus and the replay value seems good.

Graphics: 5/5

Even people who don't like the game admit that it's a beautiful game, and it is. The environments, the character detail, the overall graphics and cutscenes are just beautiful and if you don't like any other aspect of the game, it's worth a play just to see the awesome graphical work of the game.

Overall: 5/5

Final Fantasy XII is by no means perfect, but closely hits perfect on the head. In my opinion it was a game that had the guts to change it up. They switched the can for a bottle and got a reaction that fans and general gamers either hated or loved. I'm slowly becoming a fan of the series and have played enough of the games to know that XIII is different, but a great game and worth 14 bucks. Overall it's a beautiful game with an amazing story, setting, and a genuinely F'd up but pretty cool battle system that takes a strategic and open mind to work with.

product_title: Hyperkin RetroN 2 Gaming Console for SNES/ NES (Gray)
review_headline: Good system, but original is still the best
review_body:
I've now owned this system for 2 months and have played it avidly. Here's the breakdown.

GOOD:

-Plays practically all games. A few have mentioned some incompatibility issues with games like Starfox(SNES) and Super Mario 2(NES), but I own and play both on this system and both work well.

-This system allows you to use all types of controllers, including the originals for each respective system.

-It's much more affordable than tracking down a good WORKING NES and SNES.

-The system is simple and is reliable.

BAD:

-The controllers are junk, the buttons are far too stiff and unresponsive. It makes for some frustrating gameplay. I use the originals for each system and they work flawlessly.

-The system feels cheap. It's very light and slides easily. Remember this if your cord is too short.

-The system does not like being moved, even a little, while a game is playing. I can't tell you how many times I pulled the cord on my controller just a little too hard, moved the system and then had the game seize up.

-SNES Eject button is hit or miss. Sometimes it works great, other times it may as well not exist.

-NES games are hard to get out. Be sure to pull them straight out! Don't want to hurt your games! (NES Eject button would have been nice, even if it might have been hit or miss.)

MEH:

-Sound quality is ok. Most games sound perfectly fine, but there are some cutouts here and there. Nothing terribly noticeable.

-Picture quality is ok, looks very dated on a large screen TV. This is probably due to having to use component video and isn't the systems fault, so I don't consider it an actual issue as it would still exist on an original NES or SNES.

OVERALL:

This is good system for those who want to experience retro gaming or relive it. Finding a good NES or SNES can be difficult and expensive and these retro systems offer an affordable solution.

My verdict?

Buy it.
Get some original NES and SNES controllers.
Have fun with it, but if you come across a good NES and SNES system for an affordable price, don't hesitate to make this your backup.

review_headline: I liked it except for the part where it stopped working after 2 weeks.
review_body: I ordered the guitar and a couple of guitar hero software packs for my Wii.  I had a little trouble getting it to work at first but then after that it was great......for about two weeks.  Then it stopped working.  And now I can't play it anymore, can't find another guitar in any local stores, and I am afraid to buy another one online because I have no confidence that it will work any better than this one.  Not sure what to do at this point.......  :(
The seller sent out the game right away and the game was in better condition than described. My son and I love playing this game. The characters are cute and the game is a lot of fun.

I'm gonna list the cons first since they seem more significant.

Cons:

NETWORK CONNECTIVITY: When I first hooked it up, it detected my wifi connection correctly, and began downloading a firmware update. After a minute or two with no progress in the download bar, I got a message saying that my connection failed. My Ouya is about 30 ft and two walls from my wireless router, but I've never had a problem with any of my other devices, so I chalked it up to early firmware. Luckily (or so I thought) I had a wired connection to my desktop nearby and plugged that in. Started the update process again, and after downloading approximately half the update, I got the connection failed message again! I moved the unit and a spare tv near my router and tried a direct ethernet connection with a different cable, which still failed complete the download, and finally a wifi connection from 3ft away from the router that finally managed to pull down the entire firmware update. After completing the update and moving back to it's original location, it still drops wired ethernet connections whenever I try and download a game/update, but manages to maintain the wireless connection, although it's very slow. I originally bought this to use as an XBMC movie streamer in the bedroom, and thought that any games it could play would be an added bonus of sorts. It streams movies just fine when it's close to my router, but it's basically useless to me due to it's slow and inconsistent network capabilities. It's possible this can be fixed by a firmware update, but it could also be a hardware/design issue.

D-PAD: The D-pad is a little weird, there's not as much give on the right as there is on the left.

ANALOG STICKS: The analog sticks feel/sound like they are grinding on something when in use, which doesn't really bother me as it is, but I wonder if this will dissipate over time, and/or eventually break.

PERFORMANCE: If I download somethingin the background (which took an hour for the 12MB Canabalt) navigating menus becomes much less responsive, this also seems to affect more graphically intensive games. This one I'm sure they can fix using a firmware update, but it's a problem as it is.

Pros:

INTERFACE: The interface is okay, reasonably simple and responsive as long as nothing else is going on.

CONTROLLER ERGONOMICS: I had none of the issues with the face plates or sticky buttons that early reviews had. Controller feels good in the hands, and is similar in layout to an Xbox 360 controller.

To sum up, I recommend potential buyers to wait on this one. The Ouya has potential, but too many rough edges to make it worth the risk. The networking issues in particular, from what I've experienced and read about from others, might be a deal breaker for many. It's totally possible that they will fix many of these issues with firmware updates, but I'd bet that the next version of the Ouya is where we see this concept fully fleshed out (If that ever happens).

NOTE: I ordered direct from the OUYA website, so my Ouya is not a Kickstarter backer edition.

-Dolby Surround Sound button toggle
-Master, and bass volume control
-Digital line for higher quality audio
The X11 Headset Features:
-Chat and Game Volume Control
-USB Power Supply Core
-Audio In and Audio Out Jack

Sound quality is not the greatest, but it is a vast improvement from TV speakers, or even a surround sound system. Setup and breakdown is a bit more complex than other headsets with the addition of the DSS box, but is still easily manageable. The headset itself is multipurpose, with the microphone supporting full computer recording capabilities for commentaries, Skype calls and other audio conditions.

Overall, the DX11s are one of the best buys for any headset user looking for the best bang for his buck.

product_title: Nintendo 3DS with Super Mario 3D Land - Flame Red
review_body:
I can't review all the technical aspects of this game system, but as a parent I can address some of the concerns that others might have in terms of buying this for a child.
My son received the 3DS for his 9th birthday. I was concerned about too much 3D exposure but the parental controls allow you to limit that or even turn the 3D slide off altogether. My son cannot access the parental controls to change that without a 4-digit pin code that only I know. Same goes for internet access and game levels (i.e. he could not put in a game rated above what I've set his rating limits for), plus Netflix shows. He can still play his older DS games on this system (but be aware that they will not appear in 3D). The convincing factor for us buying it for him was when we realized that most of the new games that are being released weren't compatible with his DSi. These portable gaming systems are great for long car rides, office waiting rooms, etc. My son has been very happy with his 3DS. I don't find that the battery dies any faster than his regular DSi, and it was nice to find that the chargers we already had fit in the 3DS. There is also a hard rubber case you can buy to go around the 3DS that has its own backup battery power, and when the 3DS battery dies it will convert to the case' battery power to supplement.

Sonic Generations was made to please fans of both classic and modern Sonic. You'll race through levels from various Sonic games throughout the ages, experiencing waves and waves of nostalgia as you go. But this game relies upon far more than fond memories. Here's my breakdown:

Story:
If you must know, Dr. Eggman and Dr. Robutnik have teamed up to mess up time. As the 2 Sonics, you'll race through the worlds at top speed to restore places and rescue friends. Speaking of Sonic's friends, you'll cringe every time they have a dialogue. It's that bad. Anyways, no one plays these games for story, so I'll just dock a point for lame voice acting.
Score: 4/5

Graphics/Setting:
What I've always appreciated about Sonic games is the fact that they don't follow the whole photo-realistic craze. You'll dash through bright, refreshing environments that take you all over Sonic's history, starting with Green Hill Zone way back from Sonic the Hedgehog 1 to Planet Wisp from the recent Sonic Colors. The more familiar you are with Sonic games, the more you'll get out of Generations because of nostalgia, but anyone will enjoy it regardless. Speaking of nostalgia, this game does NOT play it safe by merely copying and pasting the levels it draws from. These are levels with obviously similar themes, but redesigned structure, so they feel both old and new in the best possible ways. And it's always a pleasure to play modern versions of classic levels and vice versa. The levels feel just right no matter which Sonic you play as.
Score: 5/5

Gameplay:
As classic Sonic, you'll utilize the famous spin dash, smash in TV boxes containing rings and powerups, and bounce off enemies on your way to the familiar banner at the end of the level. As modern Sonic, you'll boost at break-neck speeds, homing-attack bots, and stomp your way to the giant ring goal. A quick note: don't worry about moving so fast that you won't be able to see obstacles coming;the game is pretty fair about reaction time. However, you'll still need to know levels inside and out for a smooth run, and this applies to both Sonics. The game mixes things up by giving you optional skills. These are welcome enhancements that do things like give you the signature fire/water/lightning shields or make you brake faster. The number of skills you can equip is limited, so you'll have to strategize which skills to use for which levels. Levels themselves are a blast to play. You'll never tire of discovering and taking shortcuts, all the while listening to the incredible soundtracks provided for each version of levels. Even better, YOU CAN CHANGE the soundtracks for levels by choosing from unlocked music in the gallery! If you're still not convinced about this game I have 2 words for you: Super Sonics.
Score: 5/5

Missions:
And here is where Sega could have gone with the policy \\"less is more.\\" When you're not zipping through the 18 main levels, you might be engaging in not-so-fun side missions. These have you collecting a certain number of rings or making it to the goal with limited time. There are even some that feature a friend. These missions are nowhere near as fun as the main stages and there are 30 of these that completionists will feel obligated to muddle through. At least they offer soundtracks and artwork upon beating them. One of my favorite things about Generations, though, are the red rings. There are 5 of these in each main level and collecting all 5 yield skills to use. The best part is that you'll get hints on where these are found, and they usually are found on shortcut routes, serving as a guide for the quickest way through a stage. Very clever, Sega.
Score: 4/5

Overall:
This is such a remarkable game, and it's a well-needed break from the myriad of realistic-looking shooter games flooding the console market nowadays. This game will test your skills as you race through beautiful, well-designed worlds, learning shortcuts and memorizing routes. Classic and modern Sonic are both great fun to play as. Skill sets add a welcome strategic element to gameplay, and the soundtrack is stellar. My few complaints are somewhat tedious side missions and lame friend characters. These are easy to overlook in the grand scheme of things. Trust me, from the moment you start up this game, greeted by the unforgettable Genesis era menu music, you'll be enchanted. Beware! Nostalgia awaits!
Overall score: 4.5/5

Remember Me is destined to be overlooked, which is unfortunate.

I'm about mid-way into the game, and it is a fantastic and hypnotic game, captivating me with it's beautiful and heavily detailed world. The setting is the first thing you'll notice; vivid, unconventional colors blot this world, and it is a feast for the eyes.

Combat works and plays out like Batman, but not quite as fluid. The ability to change up your combos makes for a refreshing experience each time. Enemies are can be quite tough in numbers--especially when they differ in types, forcing you to use different tactics for various enemies. Button mashing won't get you very far.

The platforming and exploration are the weakest links, as they are far too scripted. You never get a sense that you're in immediate danger from scaling walls. And exploration is so linear, so confined, which is a shame considering Neo-Paris is a major sight to behold.

Memory Remixes are the star of Remember Me, setting it apart from other action/adventure games. Basically, you can hack into peoples memories and alter things, changing the outcome of their behavior. It's fun to mess around and experiment. Not to mention, the memory remixes give great insight into Nilin's character; you really get a sense that she is conflicted with the ethics of what she is doing, which, in my opinion, makes her a very human character to whom we can relate.

The story... I won't elaborate about it. You really need to experience it for yourself because it will blow you away. Some of the writing is awful, though. But most of it works.

Overall, fantastic game. The story and lore are the strongest aspects. The game play is, for the most part, solid. Remember Me is a game you don't want to miss.

review_headline: A tour de force in disappointment
review_body:
Turok is disappointing for multiple reasons, but perhaps even more so because parts of the game really aren't so bad. There are some occasions when the game opens up a bit and offers us some large outdoor arenas to do battle in with sneaky vantage points scattered around the level. It's brilliantly satisfying to sit back with the bow and arrow (which should be in more shooters), picking off the occasional soldier while watching a dinosaur wreak havoc with the rest of the group. In fact, taken as a pure shooter, it can be quite entertaining. The guns are satisfyingly potent and the action often pacey and intense. Despite the fundamental awfulness of most of the game mechanics, there were moments while playing Turok that I realized I was having fun. Unfortunately these moments are few and far between.

The story is incredibly derivative and cliche ridden \\"borrowing\\" from almost every 1980s action movie. This is made worst by the fact that the game takes itself seriously. These flaws might have even worked in the games favor had they taken a tongue in cheek approach. The story essentially sees the title character Turok (who is now a generic space marine) going up against his mentor after he turned bad for reasons that aren't exactly clear. There is an odd-couple paradigm to the story too. Your main ally is Slater (voiced by Ron Perlman). Apparently he blames you for the death of his brother some years ago, but this isn't really explained that well either, and the result is that you simply don't care. Odd-couple pairings only work with fabulous writing. This just makes you want to shoot your companion in the head, but you can't, because he's plot-essential. It gets tiresome very quick.

One of the worst aspects of the game is the AI. It is horrible. Your \\"buddy\\" Slater insists you hang back and follow his lead, then will not move a muscle until you have cleared out an entire area in front of him or until you have stood in one particular spot that triggers him to continue. Slater runs into you, blocks your path, and just occasionally hovers in mid-air. The AI of the enemy is a little bit better. The enemy goons take cover and work as a team for the most part.

One would think a vast jungle-covered planet should have presented a wealth of opportunity for open planing gameplay. Unfortunately the developers have created a corridor shooter, then replaced the walls with rocks and the ceiling with a skybox. Checkpoint placement is the cardinal sin the developers make when it comes to level design. The placement of checkpoints in this game really defies logic. In harder parts of the game checkpoints are simply too spread out meaning you sometimes have to redo lengthy sections of the game even on lower difficulties (I remember one particular elevator sequence that brought me to the edge of rage quit numerous times). Strangely enough checkpoints seem to be in an abundance at easier parts of the game where they are totally unnecessary.

The graphics is something of a mixed bag. The game renders some things very well such as the glimmer of the sun's rays on a metallic surface or the animations of the characters during the cut-scenes. However most other areas it fails staggeringly. Reflection effects are applied to pretty much everything other than grass, meaning the otherwise pretty dinosaurs often resemble cellophane-wrapped children's toys. The art style is very generic, appearing to be a sloppy mish-mash of Gears of War, Killzone and Unreal Tournament whilst retaining non of the aesthetically pleasing aspects of either.

There are far better shooters around, meaning there's very little reason to spend money on this one. I still look at the Turok franchise with fond memories but if this is the future of the series, then perhaps our memories is where it should have remained.

It's another iteration of ZUMA loosely tied together with a story line as you work your way around an island, but hey.. it is ZUMA and it is fun.

The ease of using the stylus rather than directional buttons makes it much more user friendly and enjoyable.

In terms of the story, DOAD is between DOA4 and DOA5. Character design is still based on DOA4. Strongly hope that Team Ninja will make a DOA for 3DS based on DOA5 character design.

As for the game itself, DOAD continues with the classic rock-paper-scissors system of all previous DOA versions. It is a whole lot easier to learn and play DOA than let's say Street Fighter because at least we don't need to learn how to do the dragon punch and/or charged moves. Most importantly, to fully enjoy SFIV, it is better to play with a joystick on a game console/PC. The joypad on 3DS just isn't as much fun as the joystick. That's why I consider DOAD is better than SFIV3D.

If you are new to DOA series, DOAD has a chronicle mode that basically teaches you everything you need to know about playing DOAD, such as the stories of previous 4 versions of DOA and the basic fighting mechanisms that you need to know. The best part I like about DOAD is that the chronicle mode has several high-detailed, 3D videos that fully utilized 3DS upper screen's resolution, so it is very enjoyable to watch those videos in 3D.

I got this game late, so I missed all the DLC and most of the throwdowns. After I finished all the arcade, survival, tag challenges, etc., the internet play has become the major part of this game. The good thing is that there are still a lot of people playing DOAD online, so it is very easy to find opponents around the world or in the same region. This allows me to play DOAD regularly even nowadays. After all, you want the bang for the buck.

review_headline: The weakest link - not very compelling
review_body:
ACIII is easily the weakest offering so far from Ubisoft in the AC franchise - and it stands out as such.

I have been a fan of the franchise since it started and have pretty much enjoyed all of the games so far, with Brotherhood and Revelations sort of getting a little bit weaker on the spectrum of enjoyment, but still thoroughly playable and enjoyable. Unfortunately, I found ACIII to be far less enjoyable to play than any of the other games - and this disappointed me because I always thought that Ubisoft adhered to a good template with each of the other games.

**SPOILER ALERT**

It really seems that there was something missing in this game. For starters, the way it begins (and, really, through about Sequence 4 or 5) is VERY rocky. They really risked alienating a LOT of their fans and players by having the player start out as a Templar, and sort of \\"punking\\" us by showing us that who we were playing as - dum dum DUM! - a baddie! Muahahahahaaaaa!!
Yeah. This almost made me throw up. I wouldn't suggest throwing this sort of curve-ball out to your fans again, Ubisoft.

And - if that weren't bad enough - when you eventually DO get to play as Connor (the protagonist) you start out as a child. So you are forced by the game maker to undertake several missions/sequences as child-Connor and adolescent-Connor before even getting to embark on your assassin training/becoming an assassin.
This fact REALLY spoiled the game for me. It went from punking me to being VERY slow to get going.....

Controlling assassin-Connor also made for a very disheartening experience. He was unwieldy, clumsy, and rarely did he feel like he was interested in sneaking about or doing anything clever. Very few missions actually required assassinating people - most of them just involved either shooting a pistol at the Main Baddie, or hiding in piles of hay or grass and avoiding guards while you get to where you can \\"touch the thing\\".

Story and character-wise, ACIII falls very short, too, unfortunately. After training to become an Assassin in a very improbable way (which basically means bullying an old black man to let you live in his house and show you what's what), Connor grows up to be a very unlikable person in my opinion. And let me just say - I GET that he is Native American and has been cast as angsty and angry at the white men taking over his village. I get that. But that DOESN'T mean that it translates well into the playable-character/protagonist of a game like ACIII.

Connor basically gets through the game pouting, sulking, being rude to people and going against the wishes of folks who are trying to help him. He is very simple minded and yet very complex, and has some of the weirdest and most sour one-liners I have ever heard in a game. The storyline also doesn't help - as it basically seemed to me a random bunch of \\"let's make them do this next!\\" missions that were *barely* connected to each other, which led you to simply just go through the motions until you finally got to the end.

The ending mission where you chase Charles Lee and kill him (well, after burning, falling, getting impaled, shooting him, waking up, limping for a few miles, following him to a bar, sit with him and drink wordlessly, and then STAB the living daylights out of him) was SO improbable and random that it felt like a five-year-old had devised it. It was like watching a French farce.

The end of the ending with real-world Minerva and Juno arguing about which solution Connor was to take was very anti-climactic, because I THOUGHT I was going to be actually OFFERED a choice at the end (ala-Mass Effect-style), but in the end Desmond just makes his decision and \\"touches the thing\\", and then the game is over.

There is a little thing that happens at the end where you get thrown back into Boston in the animus, and Desmond's voice tell you to triangulate stuff topick up weird things.....no idea what that's all about. I googled it and apparently it's just for game hacks like \\"crazy weather\\" and \\"thunder-when-you-kill-people\\", so I was like -_- , eject game.

So, yeah. Not the best in the ACIII franchise, unfortunately. Here's hoping that next-gen Black Flag makes up for it!

From start to finish - I played it with the painted-on smile of a lifelong AC fan - but I was living in denial. It's awful. review_headline: Impressively huge with solid combat, but weak writing lets down the game
review_body:
Dragon Age: Origins is BioWare's reflective look at their own origin (so to speak). It's a big, broad, swords and sorcery epic meant to evoke memories of the Baldur's Gate series, where BioWare got started in RPGs. It's also in 3D, with streamlined controls, inventory management and in-engine cut-scenes. It's BioWare's attempt to blend their original, more hardcore RPGs with their later, stripped-back and more cinematic games like the Mass Effect series. It's a game that tries to balance the old with the new and does not quite succeed.

Which is not to say it doesn't have a go. The game is huge, taking upwards of 50 hours to complete. Cleverly, the game reorganises its opening two hour prologue based on your race and class: a dwaven noble starts in a separate location to a human mage, with a totally different cast of supporting characters, enemies and opening quests. The fact that you can replay the game several times and get a different opening, with the various versions not aligning until you reach Ostagar, is quite clever and rewards replaying the game. Indeed, the choices in these sections reverberate throughout the whole game, with your eventual return to your starting location allowing you to address unfinished business. It's the game's main selling point and is something that is handled very well, making it all the more bemusing that the concept was completely chucked out the window for the two sequels.

As is traditional with BioWare games, your main character is fully customisable but the supporting cast are set in stone. You can accumulate up to ten companion characters throughout the course of the game and take three of them with you on missions. Your inactive party members hang out at a campsite you can periodically visit to exchange information, form friendships (and even romantic relationships) and improve everyone's equipment. The game has a reputation system for each character, and winning their trust will give you bonuses in combat and open up additional questlines. It's a nice idea but also one that's easy to neglect. The game also treats morally ambiguous sorceress Morrigan and sarcastic warrior Alistair as almost the secondary main characters, each with huge roles to play in the endgame, which is rather bizarre if you've just gone through 95% of the game favouring other characters instead. All of the companion characters are nicely-developed, though it's far from the strongest cast BioWare have produced for a game and some self-derivation can be detected: Shale is awesome, for example, but feels a little too reminiscent of Knights of the Old Republic's HK-47.

You spend the game doing what you usually do in a BioWare games: a broad variety of quests, varying from the mundane to the epic, and getting into lots of conversations and fights. A lot of fights: you seem to spend the overwhelming majority of the game in combat, and violence seems to be the solution to almost every problem in the game. There's a few quests based on diplomacy and dialogue, and a few fights can be avoided through intimidating or persuading the enemy, but otherwise be prepared to do a ton of fighting. Fortunately, the old 'hit space to pause' option is still present and correct, allowing you to assign orders to characters and take stock of the battle as it develops. A quickbar allows easy access to abilities, spells and weapons. Combat is generally satisfying, although health spells feel a little weak (at high level they restore so few hit-points it's almost not worth bothering with them). The biggest weakness is positioning: enemy units can clip or shove past your units with ease, making it impossible to create bottlenecks in corridors and engage the enemy with warriors whilst wizards and ranged fighters engage from afar. This seriously limits tactical options and can make fighting large numbers of tough enemies particularly difficult. Some abilities also feel overpowered: the enemy's ability to encase your characters in null-magic zones where healing magic simply does not work can result in total party wipe-outs all too easily.

In technical terms, the game is okay. Graphically it looks solid on PC (but a bit washed-out on consoles) and mods are available to improve textures further. The game is a bit flaky on multi-core PCs but runs fine if you assign it to run on just one core. Camera control is a bit of an issue: the PC version allows you to play the game from an overhead viewpoint (reminiscent of Neverwinter Nights except, bizarrely for a seven years-newer game, far less customisable) but you can't zoom out very far, and enemies often engage you from outside this viewing range. Switching to the over-the-shoulder view (which the consoles are limited to) is great for spotting distant enemies and engaging them at range, but is useless for melee. You can switch between them easily enough, but it feels a bit annoying you can't stay in the viewpoint you favour throughout the game. The overhead view also sometimes seems to get confused on whether it should be 'locked onto' your selected character or allowing you to free-roam.

The writing is a mixed bag. A lot of dialogue in the game is obvious, expositionary and risible, not helped by severely variable voice acting (Claudia Black is the standout as Morrigan). There are attempts at nuanced characterisation - key villain Loghain has his reasons for doing what he's doing, though he's such an unrepentant martinet that most players will feel zero sympathy for him - but they mostly fall flat. The game also makes a nod towards gritty realism through its political infighting and bloody combat, though the game goes completely over-the-top with your characters walking out of fights covered head-to-foot in gore. The political angle also doesn't work very well due to the politics being rather boring and it's difficult to care about Ferelden when you spend most of the game hearing about how isolationist and racist it is, riven by internal conflicts with few genuinely good people in positions of authority.

Despite the clunky writing, poor camera controls and focus on violence as the solution to just about everything, the game just about manages to keep its head above water. It's satisfyingly huge and the worldbuilding is derivative (a mash-up of standard fantasy tropes with more than a bit of inspiration from George R.R. Martin) but somewhat interesting. The differing opening sections of the game give some good replay value. Combat is solid if unspectacular. There's a germ of a really good game here, but there's also an overwhelming feeling of blandness and predictability that rears its head all too often.

Dragon Age: Origins (***½) is a very solid game from BioWare, although it's self-reflection on BioWare's past is rather pointless: the Baldur's Gate series is still extremely playable and frankly on almost every front bar the technical one are better games than Dragon Age. For those simply after a big, enjoyable fantasy RPG, Dragon Age certainly fits the bill. Its ambition is impressive and even in failing to fully achieve it, it's still very playable and worth a look.

In the realm of 8-bit graphics and extremely limited storage space, Nintendo RPGs (and other RPGs of the time) had a difficult time telling expansive, immersive stories. Dragon Warrior IV, released in the US in 1992, tried to buck this trend with a unique approach to unraveling the game's overarching narrative. Instead of focusing on just one character or one group of characters, Dragon Warrior IV tells its fragmented story in chapters, which the gamer takes on one at a time. When all's said and done, the chapters' events and characters culminate in an amazing endgame. Even though Dragon Warrior IV approached the act of storytelling in a unique way, most of Dragon Warrior's gameplay conventions remained unchanged. It's a good thing, too, since this was the last Dragon Warrior game to appear in the United States for nearly a decade. American gamers weren't privy to subsequent releases until Dragon Warrior VII hit the PlayStation in 2001.

review_headline: Feels like an imitation with bad touch controls.
review_body:
I'm a huge uncharted fan and was really looking forward to this game. Unfortunately you can tell that Naughty Dog did not make this game. Everything besides the graphics are sup-par compared to the ps3 games. Also Sony Bend added a lot of inane touch controls and puzzles that were never fun in my eyes.

So lets talk about the good things. The graphics in this game are awesome. If you squint your eyes a little it's like you are playing a PS3 game. Also the soundtrack is pretty dang good. The tracks usually fit the theme of the location you are in and pumped me up during fights. That's about it for things I thought were on the same level as its bigger brothers.

Now for the mediocre to bad. The biggest thing I play Uncharted games for is character and story, this game falls short at both. The writing is just not as good as the other games, the new characters they introduce are stereotypes and forgettable (except for Marisa Chase. Shes not bad but nowhere near Elaina or Chloe.) The overall story is similar to 1 and 2 but it has none of the great set pieces. (such as the train sequence in 2).

Combat design, it's all over the place. Sometimes it can be fun. The controls work well enough..mostly. The enemy A.I. is a bit crap. They take tons of damage and either stay in cover or run straight at you. The game also relies on this thing where you shoot while climbing way to often. It's just not very fun.

The touch controls. OMG I want to throw my Vita every time they come on screen and that's allot. So yeah be prepared to touch the screen anytime you non stealth melee fight, slip while climbing, doing any puzzle (and they are all crap), and charcoal rubbing. Also remember that dumb sixaxis balance thing from the first game when you walk across narrow things? That's back, I have no idea why.

There's a ton of other things I could gripe and complain about but I did still finish the game. I think what made me the angriest is that this could have been great with only a few tweaks. Add an option for no touch controls. Not hard. Higher better writers. Okay Hard but if you've never done a game like this before c'mon hire pro's.

I honestly hope that Sony Bend learned what they did wrong with this game and gets another crack at it. I believe they could make a great uncharted. review_headline: IT'S MAX PAYNE MEETS MIAMI VICE!
review_body:
Sadly, most of the game's detractors are correct. I really liked the original Max Payne and loved Max Payne 2. I've played both many times over. Here we have Max Payne 3 and it is quite a departure from the first 2. For starters, Max doesn't slowly wend his way thru the New York streets but has been transplanted to Sao Paulo, Brazil of all places! Not too sure how great an idea this was and it begs the question, why not just stay in New York? Consequently, that slick gritty Noir feel is lacking in this game. Truly this is more like Max meets Miami Vice. I find it annoying that all the baddies are rattling off Portuguese(The Brazilian language) and, unless you understand it, they might as well be speaking Chinese. It made me realize that Portuguese isn't as close to Spanish as I thought. I know some Spanish and couldn't make heads or tails out of what these guys were saying. Much of this could be forgiven but the game simply doesn't play like the others. In MP1 & 2 you controlled Max as he made his way thru the streets of NY. In this game most of the time there will be a (too long) cut-scene followed by Max being positioned behind a desk or some such object and you will have to fight it out with mucho bad guys. And be prepared to die... a lot! You will make your way thru a bunch of bad guys only to come across a second wave and realize you're out of painkillers and your health is low...then dead! Hit retry and start that section over again because this game has those hated checkpoints, no quick-saves folks! I played it on normal difficulty but, unless you're pretty good with shooters like this and can take dying a whole bunch of times, you might want to try easy mode.

There are many little annoyances that make things unfun. You'll be looking for that crappy white reticule to aim properly. This had me curse the game many times. It's tiny and can be hard to see depending on the background. Also, more often than not Max will be dumped amongst a ton of guys holding his pistol even though he was just using a machine gun before the cut-scene. And yes, there are way too many cut-scenes in this damn game. They tried too hard to make this feel like a movie or something. Note to game developers-Don't take anymore playing time away from the player than necessary. Seriously, almost every time Max approaches a slightly open door, you lose control and the cut-scene takes over. It gets to be quite tiresome. On the plus side the graphics are truly stunning. About halfway thru, Max shaves his head(why?) and begins in the slums of Sao Paulo and I marveled at all the visual detail. But, of course, graphics alone can't save a game. Maybe if there were quick-saves instead of checkpoints my rating would be higher. But overall I found myself too pissed half the time to say I enjoyed this game. I also don't like so much control being taken away from me, the gamer. My advice is wait until it goes on sale. I got it off Steam when they were having a 75% off sale so it only cost me $9.99. I certainly wouldn't pay $40 for it.

review_headline: I only have one complaint and it is a big one
review_body:
The Bad: When you play a game you need to be able to have several save files.
You start a profile and then from beginning to end the game saves automatically. There was one part that I thought was so awesome I wanted to watch it again so I literally just turned the system off....it still saved.
The game just has so many great boss fights that you should be able to save right before and go back to fight them anytime you want.
The manual should have had more information on what some of the stats mean. You either have to look it up online or figure it out as you play.

The great:
Weapons, weapons, and weapons. You have so many options. You can carry different scythes as opposed to one primary weapon in the first Darksiders. You can also choose a secondary weapon raging from claws to hammers and clubs.
You can change you armor to change your stats. Just pause if need to change armor for more magic defense (resistance.) Equipment changes stats (def, resistance, arcane (magic power), health and wrath regen options, increased chance of items after killing enemies, increased experience.)
I like them bringing in a level system. I never really liked the concept of putting you're experience into leveling up your weapon. The skill tree is nice. You can pick and choose you abilities and if you get tired of it, you can go see Vulgrim to reset them and reassign your points as much as you want.
The wrath system is much better. You don't have to work as hard to accumulate wrath and if you have trouble attacking you still have the option of using wrath potions (think of an ether from Final Fantasy series).
The controls can be kind of annoying because when you're fighting you might accidentally use your potions because you're so used to using the D pad controls to switch secondary weapons.
The fighting system is just as good as the first. I actually like it better because I like Death being able to jump and flip around rather thanjust dash like War. It plays a lot like Prince of Persia. (If you've played it you will occasionally die because you use a different button for wall running.)

The awesome: New game+ I haven't played many newer games to see how much of a comeback it's made but it automatically made me think of the hours I would spend playing Chrono Trigger. If you don't know what that means it basically means you start a new game with the same stats and weapons that you just beat the game with.

Then something I thought was pretty neat was that as you changed your equipment it changed on the actual character and each piece had things that made it unique.

The storyline is pretty good. I think a lot of people complain about the story because even though the goal is the same you end up going about it in a different way.
Some of the fights are kind of disappointing. The last boss was nowhere near as hard as he should have been. I beat him on the first round when there were others that I got killed by several times.

If they remade it with a save system like the first Darksiders, this game would be near perfect.
It breaks the heart to know that if you want to fight an epic boss fight again you have to play through to get to them again.

product_title: Sid Meier's Civilization V: Brave New World
review_body:
Brave New World introduces 9 new civilizations, new scenarios, new units/buildings, and a few new mechanics to the game world.

The biggest changes are revolving around the new Trade Route system, new cultural victory, introduction of ideology, and World Congress.

Trade Routes:
When you start a new game you can create a trade route using a unit called a Caravan. The number of trade routes you can create increases as you progress your civilization through the game. You can also gain additional trade routes through the construction of specific wonders. Trade Routes may be sent from one of your cities to another or from one of your cities to another civilization or city-state. When choosing where to send the Trade Route you will be shown the benefits of each option for your civilization as well as the other civilization/city-state (if applicable). For instance: You receive +1 Science, +2 Gold, while they receive +1 Science, +1 Gold, or something similar. You can also pressure other civilizations to convert to your religion through these trade routes.

New Cultural Victory:
The new culture system is much more dynamic than it was previously; evolving from a number you gained every turn amplified by buildings/wonders to a system that is much more interactive. Buildings like museums now have slots for different kinds of great works that are created by the three types of special cultural units, the 'Great Artist', 'Great Writer', and 'Great Musician'. The Great works created by the Artists, Writers, and Musician all boost your civilization's tourism output. Tourism is a new resource helps you gain sway over the other civilizations by making them envious of your great works of art, writing, or music. You can also swap the great works you have with another civilization if you find yourself with an abundance of one type but lacking another. Another new aspect of culture is the introduction of Archaeologists, who can find artifactsfrom ancient battles that occurred earlier in your game to boost your culture/tourism.

Ideology:
Once you reach the modern era (or construct 3 factories, whichever comes first) you can choose an ideology (Freedom/Order/Autocracy) which helps guide your civilization for the later parts of the game. Whichever you choose will either bring you closer with other civilizations with the same choice, or may drive you away from civilizations that chose a different ideology.

World Congress:
The World Congress (and later the United Nations) is possibly my favorite new aspect of the expansion. Throughout the later part of the game you vote along with your fellow civilizations on many different things. You can tax large standing armies if one civilization is bullying the others, you can choose who is going to hold the world games, you can limit particular resources, vote on nuclear weapon usage, and MANY other things. It makes you interact with civilizations that you usually would not contact often and adds another layer of strategy and makes the end of the game much more interesting.

If you enjoyed Civilization V, I would say this is a great buy. It adds more layers to the game and makes the later stages of the game much more interesting and fun to play. I really enjoy the game I played through, and will update this review as needed.

*PS* - This game includes the religion and espionage mechanics that were in the Gods & Kings expansion, so you DO NOT need to buy that expansion to get this one! If you did choose to skip the Gods & Kings expansion, however, you will be without the civilizations/wonders/scenarios that are introduced in that expansion. So while you can play this expansion only previously owning the original Civilization V, you will not receive all of the content within Gods & Kings.

EDIT - 7/10/2013 - Expanded on the PS note to include additional information regarding the Gods & Kings expansion.
*Thanks to Mike for the feedback on the PS note.

review_body:
There are a ton of these out there. They all come from China and are of dubious quality. But this one is being sold at a really good price, and it works as it should. Keep in mind that you will need to use a cable to connect the headphone jack on the back of this device to your TV or audio system. My TV has shoddy component connections, so the picture would keep going out. Using this, I can hook it up to a free HDMI port and it works great! I get the same picture, if not a tiny bit crisper than with the component cables, and it is definitely better looking than with the Wii's included RCA cable.
My only gripe is that the connection is a bit tight when you are plugging it into the Wii. But it doesn't matter once it is all done, and it will prevent it from getting pulled out.

review_headline: LIPSTICK ON A PIG (A BLACK MARK ON 2K GAMES)
review_body: I'm afraid I'm no longer a big fan of 2K Games, or of this (Bioshock Infinite), their latest version of a truly legendary game.  Yes, its got much of the same gorgeous graphics, but it lacks the dark and deeply haunting (blood and guts) allure of Bioshock I and/or Bioshock II, and worst of all, as crazy as it may sound, it has a completely dysfunctional 'SAVE' function. Two players of differing abilities or skills cannot reasonably hope to play this game without screwing up the game of the other player, because the game 'autosaves' the game progress only at past Checkpoints, and it offers no way to save the game in multiple registers or under multiple players names. This means that the next (but different) player must OVERWRITE the game created by the earlier player or begin an all-new game which autosaves to the very same register as the earlier player (i.e., he/she cannot reload a previously saved game in their name). This has to be one of the single biggest flaws I've ever encountered in any video game in over 20-years of gaming. For a game of this quality and price, that is as sophisticated as it is, to have been released by 2K Games with this glaring and monumental flaw, is simply amateurish and inexcusable in my book. Shame on you, 2K Games!

i was bored and happen to hear the tile Dragon Age mentioned in passing. I looked it up here and found out I could get it for a pretty cheap price (at the time of this review). And I loved it from beginning to last. The game includes all the important DLCs in one package, which is a big plus for the price.

I loved my companion characters and i liked being able to chat with them in camp or in town. The decisions i made were important to how the story unfolded and every time I play I have the chance to change the way a scene plays. You can choose from several classes and backstories and changes some of the options open to you in your decision making. In short this game is heavy on the player decisions and party management.

Fighting was a pretty simple matter and could be as complicated or simple as you like. the quickbar allows you to assign techniques and spells and potions so that they are close at hand. Digging through your inventory for the best equipment gets a little tedious and more than once I wanted to just have a place to dump all the extra junk where it would be safe because I was simply convinced something would be important later.

More than anything though this game made me fall in love with the world of Dragon Age itself. I was intrigued by the origin of the Darkspawn. The legends of Andraste and the Chantry's rise to power felt authentic to me as being a plausible religion and the stranglehold on magic was something that (though in other stories in other series) was a first time encounter for me. It just feels like that, despite the magic and dragons and monsters, that this could be a real place. I wouldn't go so far as to say it's on the same par as the Tolkien world building but given a few years it could get to that amount of detail. Here's hoping this series stays a good thing.

It's sad because Lara is done so well! Over all though it's very well done and I'm very pleased with this game!!

review_headline: Really great fun for kids and adults
review_body:
We've been playing this game with our grandchildren for about 4 years now, and they are 12 years old now. They could beat their grandpa and me when they were 8 years old, so I would say even a 7-year-old could play it.

There are 25 mini-games to play, and it keeps score of each one to determine the final winner of the whole game. You can also choose to play fewer mini-games and play practice rounds where you select which games come up. If you want to play just your favorites, you can customize the \\"big\\" game by choosing whichever mini-games you want to play. There's also the option of using a memory card to save the information, but we don't bother with that.

There are four monkeys, so you can have up to four players (or even play alone). You'll have a great time playing Island War, Elephant Baseball, Monkey Bongo, Rain Dance, Primate Penalties, Rocket Riders, and lots of other creative games. Each game requires some skill of quick visual recognition and hand/eye coordination.

This bundle pack comes with four controllers that are connected and then plug into one port on your Playstation 2. Some games will have you using all four color buttons while other games require just the big red button. If you are playing with a much younger child, maybe 5 or 6 years old, you could opt to only play the mini-games that use the big red button, thereby not requiring as much coordination.

There are 3 or 4 other games (Buzz! Junior Robo Jam for example) that you can buy for the Playstation 2 that use these same controllers, so you can just buy the stand-alone games (software) after buying this bundle

This game is genuinely just as much fun for adults as it is for kids, and I don't say that about too many games.
