I loved 4 except for the fact that it dragged on and i always felt as if I had to rush because I knew I would die if I stuck around too long. 5 was just aggravating in some situations even though in both it was awesome to carry a Rocket Launcher (solves all problems).
Now, to the matter at hand after I have made my background and point, this game is by far the best. I don't care what anyone says, bargain bin is bullshit. I have given up on Resident Evil games fast and numerous times. This is a completely different story. What they have done is actually listen to the fans. Before knifing seemed as a last resort type of thing. Now you don't have to be scared to melee if you are surrounded. It's a stupid with response but still a good try. Three precise hits usually kill a zombie and they are the only ways I have found to kill the armor plated zombies. Leon's campaign is definitely for the Resident Evil 4 fan who misses zombies (which would be me). Chris is a lot like RE5's closing chapters where all freaking enemies had guns but more fast paced. Jake's is basically all out bad ass and over powered enemies. Can't comment much on the 4th character but she is definitely story and puzzle based for those old old fans but of course it's in 3rd person. When I first saw they were coming out with a SIXTH RE game i practically laughed. But me, I like to give everything a try and another installment in a horror classic is a must for me. After playing it I would recommend it to anyone that was a fan of the old RE games. New fans, stick to COD (I know I will), but definitely rent it and give it a try. It's a little broken in some places but not anymore than the previous RE games and definitely not game breaking type of broken. Just maneuvers built in that could use some tweaks.
Also I would like to point out that this is the only RE game that I have liked from start to at least for Leon's campaign at where I am. So far. I'm just sick and tired of seeing 1 star reviews. review_headline: Without Naughty Dog to head up development Sony Bend lacks that special something.
review_body:
A powerful new handheld, one of Sony's best franchises, and a whole new adventure at release sounds like the perfect recipe for an incredible game right? Sadly that isn't the guess as SCE Bend Studio seems to have left something out of Uncharted: Golden Abyss while their own additions to Naughty Dog's perfect formula leaves plenty to be desired.

Diving in the first thing I noticed were the visuals. Rarely did I see the frame-rate dip, there was no screen tearing, everything looked beautiful on my shiny new Vita. This was Uncharted in the palm of my hand. Environments pulled you in with many vistas showcasing the surrounding jungles, mountain tops looming in the distance, the sun setting just behind a distant peak throwing out a reddish hue of the fading day. The jungle floor expanded well beyond my view with ambient sounds further pulling me into the experience. Birds chirped, creatures could be heard in the distance, if there was one thing Bend got right it was the environments.

The original voice cast is back as well to add whole other layer to this. Drake often chimes in with his quips and thoughts about the situation, sometimes mirroring my own thoughts with exasperation over the next challenge. The voice work is strong, with characters regularly communicating just like the PS3 entries. Sully and Drake go back and forth as you paddle down a river, poking fun at one another over their mistakes. Often Drake subtly flirts with the new love interest Marissa Chase as they scale what most would deem impossible. Drake can even be heard muttering under his breath when dealing with his old friend Dante as the two have many differing opinions.

So where do things go wrong? A number of areas really. What you find is a series of little annoyances that quickly add up detracting from the overall experience here. Sony Bend played it safe with Golden Abyss, never striving to outdo what Naughty Dog had already done as well. They seem content to live in the PS3's shadow and often avoid situations where they could have pushed that bar just a little higher.

Issues start to arise early on via the Vita's new control elements. In some aspects I loved how Sony Bend implemented these with things like using the gyroscope for aiming. Whether sniping or just looking down the sights making quick adjustments by moving the unit itself was a breeze to do and greatly increased my accuracy allowing minimal changes without having to rely on an analog stick. This was a perfect fit for Uncharted and something I hope to see more games do. It's responsive, easy to use, and easy to understand.

At the same time though this experience is marred with an odd hit detection system. Often I would get a head shot, or rather it should have been a head shot but I would see my enemy simply stumble before pressing their attack. Other times my shot would miss entirely for no reason at all. The over the shoulder aiming we've all come to know and love from Drake often felt like it lacked a true line of sight or your target as well. I would zero in on a target, squeeze the trigger, then see my shot hit a rock that was apparently between the barrel of my rifle and my target yet from my perspective it looked like a clear shot.

The touch screen is the worst offender for the new controls. Often Sony Bend relies on this to do things like boost up your partner to an area you couldn't normally reach by doing a quick scene and requiring you to swipe upwards on your screen. You do this constantly and it gets old fast. Drake this time comes equipped with a machete but the only time it is useable is to cut down bamboo which acts as a barrier to get to a treasure. Standing there waiting for you to complete a three part sequence of swipes Drake will suddenly spring into action cutting down the bamboo so you may seek your prize.

Fight scenes also incorporate touch controls that often go unrecognized for some reason.Most of the time this results in Drake getting punched and you having the choice to either run or try for another melee take down. There are several fights that are basically QTE cutscenes which rely on this mechanic and the results are less than desirable. Again the issue of not recognizing my swipes across the screen would result in a failed attack or it would end with Drake's death and my going back to the start of the cutscene.

Drake will often take Charcoal rubbings to get a better picture of long worn ruins and symbols. This mechanic works well enough but doesn't really add anything to overall the experience beyond 30 seconds of rubbing the Vita's screen. Also this acts as another form of collectible throughout the game.

Navigating where you climb can be done via the touchscreen and I was surprised at how well this worked. Trace your path and Drake follows it perfectly. Plenty of times I would use this instead of just holding the analog stick left or right and waiting for Drake to reach the end.

Despite the issues laid out above gun fights in Golden Abyss do a lot to keep you in the action. Enemies attempt to flank your position, drop grenades at your feet to push you out of cover, employ a wide variety of weaponry to keep you on your toes, and provide some nice action packed moments. The AI here could use some work as enemies wouldn't notice dead bodies laying around when I was sneaking about or would often stroll right up to where they knew I was hiding only to be grabbed and quickly taken out one at a time. Still the gun fights were a blast and definitely brought that Uncharted goodness we all know.

The story lags though and badly. Never doing much to push boundaries and lacking that Uncharted twist at the end this felt like a by the numbers story. I kept waiting for that ancient evil to come into play yet it never happened, leaving you to only do battle with a few different types of gun wielding baddies and nothing super natural.

One moment stood out in particular to me where Sony Bend could have given their audience a new look at Drake. As you paddle across an underground lake Drake's past is brought up and I got a little excited thinking we'd learn a little more about our hero. Instead Sony Bend shied away instantly with Drake's remark \\"This lake isn't big enough for my story.\\" Apparently it was big enough for another five minutes of Chase rambling on about the Spanish and the temple, the entire time I'm swiping my finger over the touch screen to keep them paddling. This was a wasted opportunity if I ever saw one.

Set pieces are fun but not on the same level as the PS3. With caves collapsing around you, trying to outrun explosives, and other such things Golden Abyss tries to keep you moving forward during this sections but I noticed Drake lacked that frantic run, stumbling over himself as he scrambled to make it to safety. It was somewhat jarring to hear Drake screaming \\"We have to move! Now!\\" yet he's jogging along at a light pace. A minor complaint yes but then again this is what Golden Abyss is about.

There are numerous times where the on screen actions don't seem to make sense and pull you out of the experience. At one point while traveling with Sully you end up separated from each other, each taking two paths that involve you helping one another to advance. The problem here is that Drake and Sully are often talking to each other, yelling across the map yet none of the enemies take notice of this at all.

A few times I even managed to sneak up on an enemy while Drake was rambling to whatever NPC was accompanying him during that section. I was a little baffled how a guard couldn't hear Drake talking about Sully ruining the GPS the entire time he is slipping up behind him to snap his neck.

The NPCs actually brought the experience down I thought. Not through being underdeveloped or uninteresting but by simply being there. Drake is often tag teaming situations with Sully, Chase, or Dante and all three can do exactly what Drake does. They follow his every step climbing through the same areas, keeping up just fine and this seems to take away from Drake being the hero. I often looked at his ability to climb as something special, yet here everyone has this ability.

Other points they hinder you from advancing before you take out some enemies. At one point I was climbing a rope with Chase taking the lead when she suddenly stopped climbing so I could take out a group of enemies shooting at us. Several times Drake will scout ahead through a particularly treacherous area only to have his partner follow afterwards with enemies opening fire and Drake being charged with guard duty. The problem here stems from the NPC stopping while climbing so Drake could kill the enemies because the hardest target to hit is a stationary object.

Small things like this add up to drag Golden Abyss down and keep it from reaching the great experience we've had on the PS3. The story isn't that interesting, the set pieces are lacking, control issues with some of the new elements, and NPCs tagging along took what I expected to be a great game and made it just an alright game. This would not have been such an issue if Naughty Dog hadn't set the bar so high and given us so much to hope for from a new Uncharted. Hopefully next time Naughty Dog will head up development and Sony Bend can see how the Masters once again do it because having three shining examples to work from wasn't enough for them to pull this off.

Note this: This was the first ninja Gaiden game I've played. All the other ones look too tedious for me. But my brother bought this game and it looked interesting to me. I gave it a go and was mostly surprised by it. From what I can tell they strayed away from the previous games and took a new approach. I understand that most of these changes would probably make a lot of older fans mad. The changes include things like: less weapons, Quick time events, no costumes, and basically nothing special outside the story. Also They gave Ryu more of a character. From the little scenes I've seen of the Previous games, Ryu felt like a blood lustful killer guy who slays monsters and demons for no real reason. IN this game they gave him a lot more dialogue and a softer side. I couldn't picture the previous Ryu Talking nice to a little girl. This might make a lot of fans disappointed. I understand the feeling (Metroid: other M). As for me I like the new Ryu. Also the game has online Multiplayer. I haven't touched it. Not much of a multiplayer guy. I was able to beat the game little under a week. It feels like I might give it another go. It's seems like one of those games that has a lot of replay value.

Okay I've said the things I liked about the game. Now for the cons. As I said There is no extras what so ever. There is new sword DLC but as far as I know there will only be two new weapons. Compared to the number of weapons in the last games that is a big degrade. Also, you only play as Ryu. I was hoping you could play as others such as Ayane. And the difficulty: I played on normal mode. Not too hard. But If you lose consecutively times you get a choice of lowering the difficulty. Be warned. If you do this you'll be unable to raise it in the future. I believe this game was kind of like a Beta for a new Ninja Gaiden franchise. Took a new approach and wanted to see how the fans respond. I bet some time next year there will be a Ninja Gaiden 3 Sigma that is all of Ninja Gaiden 3 but with all the things fans complained about fixed. More weapons, Nippon, Costumes, etc.

Last thoughts: If you never played a Ninja Gaiden game, give this one a chance. If you have, come in with an open mind and know this won't be like your previous games. I'm sure if you can look past the faults it will be a fun game. Worst case just wait for the price to go down a bit, Judging by the reviews it won't be long...

This is definitely the best and most realistic MMA game on the market, however like graphics the uncanny valley comes into play, the closer it gets to a 1-1 simulation the more glaring the problems become. This game has an extremely detailed set of moves, with an incredibly steep learning curve, even after spending hours playing through the tutorial. After taking a character all the way through the career mode and feeling kind of like a bad ass, when I tried the higher difficulties for some of the achievements it was extremely difficult. Ultimately the lower difficulties are where most people will have the most fun, and most of the problems aren't so obvious. When you try the higher levels, the AI is almost prescient to your moves, and the previously extensive move set seems too limited for what you need to beat the opponent. There is one thing that sucks on every difficulty level, and that's the new submission system. I don't know if there was something wrong with my controller or my co-ordination, but I could never get the hang of it, and I maybe succeeded with one submission, and got out of only a few. I would maybe be okay with the system if it accurately represented the submission game in real-life MMA, but it doesn't at all. I would feel safe to wager that the submission system will be completely revamped for UFC 4.

For the Career Mode, I had a lot of fun with it, but I was disappointed to see very few changes from the previous games other than the addition of Pride rules (which were awesome at times). I would love to see more of a story added to this mode, and they could even use their Ultimate Fighter reality show as a great beginning to this mode. For the RPG stat increase system in career mode, there were a lot of problems. Personally I found some of the exercises to be fun and others to be incredibly annoying. However, the likeability of the exercises doesn't really determine which one's you'll use, as many of the exercises for some reason greatly decrease other stats (Equally or greater than the stats being improved!) so I really only stuck to two exercises especially towards the end of my career (the Heavy Bag and the Tire Flip). The create-a-fighter ratings were also screwed up, I think that I won the UFC belt before I broke the 80's, and I retired as the best fighter in history before I broke the 90's.

In the end, if you still have the previous UFC games, there's really no reason to buy this game. However, if you don't own them and want to play an MMA fighting game, this is absolutely your best option, and I would highly recommend it.

product_title: DragonPad XBOX 360 PC Wireless Gaming Receiver Black for Windows
review_body:
The Xbox 360 is an amazing product. Likewise, the wireless technology used in its controllers are top notched. You can literally be 20 feet away from the Xbox with your controller and still have full control over your games. With that in mind, I purchased this product thinking it would do the same thing for my PC. However, this was NOT the case.

The receiver itself is of course of lesser quality than an official Microsoft one, feeling light and flimsy in the palm of my hand and while I didn't expect the form quality to matter, I did expect it to work. Using official drivers from the Microsoft Games website, I was able to install the drivers using the method mentioned in other reviews. That being said, syncing the receiver to your PC and then controller to receiver was not very difficult. What is difficult is maintaining a connection through a good 5-10 minute play session.

More often then not, your controller will keep seeking the receiver instead of actually locking into the \\"Controller 1\\" (Top Left of the Xbox Logo) light. This happens so often that playing any game where jumping/shooting/moving/dodging is involved results in a negative experience. Just imagine playing an online game where you are disconnected all the time and you'll know what I mean.

In all honesty, I have tried all sorts of solutions to make this receiver work. I have bought a USB self-powered hub and even used the official Microsoft drivers. However, the connection from controller to receiver is usually lost when you are more than 6 feet away from receiver or if you move slightly 2 feet to the right or left. We all move somewhat during our game sessions and having the experience interrupted every time we slightly shift in our seats is more frustrating than not. Furthermore, even if you are 2 feet away from the receiver and a body part such as an arm or a person walking by gets in your way, the signal will disconnect. This is mainly because the receiver is no strong enough to emit/recognize/receive the signal from the controller and maintain a proper connection.

So there you have it. Is it really worth it to buy a product where you have to be a statue and extremely close? There much, much better options out there w/o the hassle. Save yourself the trouble and get what you need. You get what you pay for after all.

review_body:
I've been a gamer for over 25 years and have owned nearly every piece of gaming-related hardware released in that span of time. As I've gotten older I've seen my playing shift more from traditional consoles to portables. I'm still a fan of traditional console gaming but the convenience of playing anytime, anywhere is something only portable gaming can provide. For the longest time portable gaming necessarily meant a mild-to-heavily diluted gaming experience from what consoles offered or generally games that played to portable systems' strengths. With the PSP and 3DS the bridge in quality had narrowed between what portables and consoles could offer and now with the Vita we are getting very close to having portable games that are nearly on par with home consoles.

There are many games that are more portable oriented (simpler graphics, easier to pick up and play and put down quickly) for the Vita that look and play great. Lumines, Hot Shots Golf, and Super Stardust are perfect for on the road gaming or for an otherwise quick fix. For a more traditional game, Uncharted and Rayman Origins offer lengthy and high quality/high production values gaming that was previously exclusive to the consoles. In addition to the quality launch lineup there's also hundreds of games available for download that use the Vita's built-in PSP emulation. To be honest, I've enjoyed the Vita games I've played thus far but the bulk of my time on the system has been in playing these older PSP games. The screen and controls on the Vita make the PSP games look and play better than ever. Ha, I'm sounding like a bit of a fanboy. As I said before I've been gaming for a quarter century and I'm fond of the other systems I own, but the Vita is the first time I've felt compelled to share my thoughts in a review.

Make no mistake, there are some shortcomings with the system. My biggest issue is with Sony's insistence on using a proprietary memory card format that is both moreexpensive and apparently even slower than comparable MicroSD cards. This is especially perplexing because much of what makes the Vita a great system relies on having access to removable storage. Some other concerns have more to do with the future of the software library. For me, what's available through PSP emulation and in the initial launch window is enough to justify the purchase already but that doesn't deter from the concern that 3rd party software makers may balk at putting quality and/or exclusive games on the Vita. This is sort of a snowball effect - if the system or games don't sell well, game creators will be less likely to produce product for the Vita which will result in the system and games not selling so well...and on and on.

Anywho, my review is a bit sloppy, incoherent, and more akin to a forum post. Long story short - The Vita is a great and powerful piece of hardware that was designed for gamers to play virtually any kind of game thrown at it. The d-pad is the best I've used since perhaps the Sega Saturn (and I'm leaning on believing it's in fact better), the OLED touch screen is big and beautiful, the analog sticks feel and work well, and the whole package just feels solidly built. The only thing that may hold the system back is the software and terrible memory card situation (and the increasingly competent hardware by cell-phone manufacturers competing in the same market on some level).

review_headline: Phenomenal Multiplayer. Single Player is Lacking Depth
review_body:
It doesn't take a rocket scientist to know that StarHawk is a solid multiplayer game and has less of a focus on single player. Both aspects of the game are good, however the multiplayer is outstanding.

I bought this game from GameStop, not Amazon, simply due to the extra features and bonuses in the Limited Edition which is only available at GameStop. I feel ashamed because I am a very faithful Amazon shopper, but for this release Amazon did not offer what I wanted and what I would have expected.

First off the game takes up a good 2.5gigs, there's already a new update, and you need to have an online pass to play online, which is included. But keep in mind that if you buy it used you will need to purchase the online pass from SONY for $10.

Below are my pros and cons. Though every game has it's cons, I can tell that Starhawk is an instant classic just after my first few hours of game play.

PRO's:
+ Amazing Multiplayer! Probably the best, most unique I have ever played. A lot of fun!
+ The campaign story, style, and cut scenes remind me a lot of Infamous. Voice-acting is quite good.
+ Simple easy to use menu system. There are many options for online play. Everything is so very well integrated.
+ Graphics are quite good, very smooth and fast. Control and vehicle control are perfect in my opinion. They are tight and come very naturally.
+ Soundtrack rocks. Very unique classic, yet modern style. Meshes well with the game.

CON's:
- A little more attention should have been paid to single player, however multiplayer shines so well I can forgive that.
- You cannot play the entire single player campaign split-screen. Only multiplayer and co-op are available split screen, and a playstation Network account must be active for the second player.
- Single player campaign is 4 hours long at the most and the A.I. seems a little dated at times.

After my first few hours of playing I loved it, for the single player but most of all the multiplayer, which is intensely addicting. For those who didn't have the opportunity to play the beta, the style of Starhawk reminds me of a mixture of Halo, Infamous, and a 3rd person Borderland, but it also has a weird futuristic western style all its own. You can run on foot or use your power orbs to generate/spawn an array of land and air vehicles, walls, turrets, shields, or weapon bunkers. The more power you have the more vehicle and weapon choices you have, which is very helpful in multiplayer. It is a lot of fun and gives you different options of how to play. No, it is not a stealth game, however you can be a little sneaky at times. Or you can just fly your hawk in and destroy everything and everyone.

I must highly suggest this game for all of you multiplayer gamers out there, as this is a must own. I would not recommend this simply for the single player campaign, while it is good, it is not $60 good, or even $40 good. I would hold out a few months until it goes on sale, or simply rent it as you can finish the campaign in a weekend. review_headline: I played this more than Tetris or Dr. Mario
review_body:
If you played Final Fantasy Legend/SaGa 1 or 3, then you know the deal. If you are completely new to this series, I'll break it down. The story is that you have to travel the world searching for these things called \\"Magi\\" as well as searching for your Indiana Jones like father. If someone collects them all, you gain the power to become a god or something. The story is not the reason to play this. Infact, this game is so linear that when I replay this, I aliken the story to a Rocky Horror Picture Show viewing. The story is not the focus, the fun is found in some other aspect of this game. More specifically...

The gameplay- The combat is your typical turn based RPG fair. To the untrained eye, it looks like you are watching a stock tape ticker stream but you know what you are doing. You use swords, axes, bows, guns, millary ordinance, Martial Arts, magic, assorted monster attacks and even Nuclear bombs to kill your foes. You get humans and mutants that increase their stats spontaniously in tiny incroments. Robots stats are determined by their equipment. Monsters are determined by what meat they eat. If you play this for replay, you want humans. Balancing a budget early makes for a fun challenge that forces you to grind levels or accumulate money and stolen items in certain locations. This is why it is advised to bring humans on the advanced play through.

Presentation- When this came out, Caveman non back lit Gameboys where the hand held system of the day. The graphics were competant. The music delightful in places and loops in my mind, even to this day. Kids today may not understand any of these qualities or revere them in a yesterday context. Compared with the present this title shows its age. There was a remake back in 2010 but was not released in the states because the Japanese secretly hate America or thinks game enthusiasts are too stupid to appreciate a true classic.

Conclusion- Until Dragon Quest 9 came out, I played this the most of anything I owned since I bought it on its release. I played alot of RPG's and dungeon crawlers in my day and this is my personal favorite. If you done the same, then take notice because Square made magic here. If you enjoy a well put togather RPG and don't give a damn about graphics or metrosexual girly boy protagonists with amnesea or cute cockfighting cartoon monsters, then check this out. It may become your new favorite thing to play while you listen to your girlfriends insipid tv shows or chic movies on tv while you play this in a sub catatonic state. And let me know if you get a seven sword.

I just wanted to share my impressions of Duke Nukem Forever. The game has a few issues that caused me to set it aside after an hour of game play. I really wanted to like this game, but for 5 dollars I think I paid too much.  First are the skill challenges. Good games use things like level design and puzzles to pace the game play, poorly made games use skill challenges. Skill challenges are a cheap way for gamer designers to slow down game play so that a player does not finish the game in under an hour. Being able to hit the jump button at precisely the right time or you will fall to your death and have to restart at the last checkpoint. That's not re-playability, that's annoying. Games like Mortal Combat are skill challenge games and I wish skill challenges would stay in them.  Secondly, and it ties into the first are the mini games. Mini games are the creepy uncle/half brother of skill challenges. In the first hour I played I was forced to ride in a car jumping off ramps. If I had wanted a racing game I would have bought a racing game. It is again a tactic used by lazy developers to extend to feel of a game by adding a variety of play modes. I have always found it to be both painfully awkward and annoying when I encounter it.  Level design killed it for me. In the best first person shooter you almost get a sense of being guided though the level by the placement of enemies, the textures, the sounds and any number of things. You can tell in a game where the level design was a high priority it seems to flow from one room or area to the next. You never stop to think about where to go next, the game play draws you though the level. In Duke Nukem Forever I found myself wandering around several times considering where to go. It feels like reading a book and having people interrupt you to ask you the square root of 81. How am I supposed to be immersed in the game play if I have to stop playing consider where I entered a room, is there anything I missed, did I look in thiscorner?  And turning the lights out in an already poorly designed level...that's a low blow.  Only being able to carry two weapons. I can play Medal of Honor if I only want to carry two guns, I bought Duke Nukem for ludicrous gibs. I have ten number keys and I'm going to need them all for the weapons, that is what Duke Nukem should be about. I can let that slide, two weapons is the style these kids want today. All I'm saying is twelve years ago Duke carried a shotgun, a chaingun, a box of pipebombs and a rocket launcher with rockets while chain smoking cigars and wisecracking.  Those are some of the things I did not like about the game.  Other reviewers have pointed out

I am giving the game 2 stars because it is fun at first, but if I could give the endgame a negative rating for being a cynical mechanism for extracting the maximum amount of money and/or time from players in return for unpleasant and unrewarding gameplay, I would.

The details:
I played both D1 and D2, and while I have fond memories of them, I don't feel all that attached to the franchise. Nonetheless I was looking forward to it since Blizz announced its release and ponied up for the CE.

I was not one of the people who raged at release because of server crashes, glitches, bugs and frequent \\"maintenance\\" sessions lasting hours, sometimes with little or no warning. I figured that Blizz was fielding a lot of new ideas and processes with this game. I was happy with the game, despite huge numbers of reports of botting, duping, hacking, exploits, session spoofing, etc, I figured it didn't really affect me or the people I played with. I was wrong about that, but never mind.

Then two things happened: the Real Money Auction House (RMAH) and patch 1.3. I think others have probably gone into a lot of detail about why those two things proved real game changers for more casual players like myself, but for me the net change was that the \\"end game\\", such as it is, is now basically pay to win. You need not only to play skillfully, and to understand your class inside and out, which I would expect, but in addition you need really really good gear. Gear that, because of the way itemization works in the game, you will not get by farming. You must go to the AH, where you will need millions, yes millions, of gold per end game item (unless you want to spend hours surfing the terrible, horrid AH interface for the occasional deal). A little to much for ya? Well, off you go to the RMAH, where you can buy what you need for real money! Don't worry, there's a per-item cap of $250, so you can't go overboard.

Subsequent patches have only reduced the options of making in-game gold legitimately, and many of the changes seem to force players more and more to the RMAH as Blizz figures out where exactly players are managing to farm gold and items, and then nerfs those places one after the other.

Knowing what I know now, would I buy this game again? No, and for sure not the Collector's edition. The one nice thing I can say about the CE is that it did include a free copy of D2, which has been fun to check out again since I stopped playing D3...

Should you buy this game.? Maybe... I had fun with it through Hell Difficulty and Act 1 Inferno before the RMAH/patch 1.3/repair cost fiasco. If you feel that playing up through Hell Difficulty will give you $60 bucks worth of satisfaction, then it might be worth it. PersonalIy, I was hoping for a little more longevity, but oh well. *Goes off to play Path of Exile*

review_headline: A creepy sequel with a story that still doesn't make any sense
review_body:
The Good: Amazing atmosphere, stripped away the bad stuff from FEAR 1, awesome mechs, well balanced

The Bad: Mostly same weapons, a tad short, lame multiplayer, stupid cliffhanger ending (FEAR 3?), more or less the same as FEAR 1

FEAR was a hyped up FPS back in 2006 that started the whole \\"creepy girl with the black hair over her face\\" thing. FEAR was so great, not because of it's FPS action, but because of it's well executed disturbing atmosphere. FEAR 2 is no exception with everything bad stripped from the first and lots of new things thrown in. FEAR 2 is your basic FPS at heart, but if you look beyond the veil you'll see something truly wonderful and that's, once again, the incredible atmosphere FEAR 2 portrays. If you didn't already know, Alma is the creepy girl we are after that is somehow connected to soldiers called Replicas, whilst she can control them telepathically. While the story in the first game was almost impossible to follow the same problem infects FEAR 2 until toward the last few chapters where the developers stop playing mind games and finally spill the beans on what and who Alma really is.

The main thing here I need to talk about though is atmosphere, you walk through school hallways hearing lockers slam and things swirling around with darkness all around you. Disturbing ghostly apparitions appear that you must shoot, creepy super humans infect certain areas, and just overall the flashbacks you get of Alma are pretty damn creepy. The most scary parts in the game were when your flashlight somehow stopped working and all you can do is find your way around with flickering lights. While the atmosphere is great (especially with headphones on and the lights off!) FEAR 2 has some new gameplay mechanics that make the game even better. While new guns are added a lot of the older ones are improved (along with the difficulty toned WAY down). Most of your guns are average such as machine guns, shotguns, rocket launchers, sniper rifles etc. The only unique guns are the Hammerhead (shoots green needles that impale enemies to walls), the Laser rifle (a giant laser that shreds through everything), and the Pulse rifle (which shoots giant blue orbs that disintegrate everything in it's path). Of course these guns are harder to find and are rarer, but they have their uses.

My favorite addition are the mech sections...yes who would have thought FEAR would have mechs. Remember those annoying mechs in the first FEAR? Well now you can ride them! Hop into these heaping piles of metal and you get your standard machine gun and rockets, but the mech controls so well and the machine gun feels so powerful. It's great to see your enemies explode in a gory mess after a few machine guns rounds and you really feel you're more powerful for them for once. If your health starts running low hop out for a few minutes and your health will be restored. Included with old mechanics are the slow-mo, health injectors (that are really hard to find), easier to unlock achievements, and still lame multiplayer. I also have to mention how firefights are nicely balanced with just wondering around enjoying the atmosphere.

Everything is just superb cosmetically with great voice acting, beautiful visuals (although they could still be better), and great lighting effects. Of course the campaign is a tad short running in at about 6-8 hours and the cliffhanger ending is really retarded (aren't they all? *HALO 2*) Overall the game just builds up into a nice climax and that's what we usually love with shooters. While I recommend FEAR 2 for a great weekend rental it's nothing really more than that. review_headline: Buy it for the price per hour, and online community
review_body:
MindJack got a lot of grief when it came out, and it hasn't gotten much better. However, seeing it for under $5 one day, I decided to pick up a copy and see just how bad it really is.

MindJack tells the story of a man who's name I can't remember (and that I don't care enough to look up) as he tries to discover what he can, as within the first few minutes of the game he's treated as something of a traitor.

The voice work is pretty horrible at times, so expect to groan.

The mind hacking - taking over the bodies of friendlies or neutrals - is similar to The 3rd Birthday, with the exception of a pretty poor AI (although left alone for long enough they do a somewhat passable job most of the time) and you won't hear Aya's exclamations of ... whatever. This hijacking requires line of sight, however there also seems to be some percentage of body seen, in order for it to consistently work.

The game is mostly a third-person shooter, with a rather faulty hand-to-hand combat system (although taking someone as a shield seems to work fairly well).

All that said, it's about an eight hour game. However, I've put a little over 20 hours of time into the game. And it's for the same reason I'm going to give the game 4 stars.

The game allows you to play through by yourself, or like Demon's Souls (I apologize if anyone cringes my mention of that in regards to this game), blue or red hackers can jump in. Blue hackers can use any friendlies (and since you consistently have a partner through the game, at least one could play through with you), while red hackers can use any enemies. Red hackers can certainly have an easier time, since there are more enemies than friendlies at the start, but they're unable to jump into most bosses.

You can shut this off if you want, but the real enjoyment of this game comes through in the multiplayer.

Unfortunately there's not too many people playing the game (I'd say maybe a dozen at the time of this review), yet on the other hand they tend to be people that also just picked up the game, making it a fairly 'tight' group of people. In fact, thanks to MindJack I found someone who I'll be keeping an eye on, since we have very similar gaming tastes.

Had the online component not been active I would have given this game 3 stars. However, because of the great community, and the fun I had because of it, I'm giving MindJack 4 of 5 stars. It's certainly not one of their better games, but at $10 or less, it's worth the price, in my opinion.e a dozen at the time of this review), yet on the other hand they tend to be people that also just picked up the game, making it a fairly 'tight' group of people. review_headline: Good game console and multimedia platform
review_body:
I finally took the plunge and bought one of these for a few reasons. The price dropped, the hard drive got much bigger, and they introduced a whole series of new video streaming services. I figured I'd get a better console than my Wii and probably be able to drop cable and come out ahead in the long run.

So far, I haven't been disappointed. Microsoft has implemented a whole raft of new services for XBox Live subscribers. In addition to Netflix, there's Crackle (free ad supported video streaming), ESPN, SyFy, and assorted others. For a lot of people, this is a better value than conventional cable, and they seem to be planning to expand it again.

As a gaming console... well, I'm not a hardcore gamer, and for the most part I'm a PC gamer when I do play stuff. That said, there are a lot of very competitively priced XBox 360 titles out there, and I've bought a handful and enjoyed them. If you don't need the latest releases, you can really stretch out your entertainment budget this way. I also enjoy the old arcade titles they've got out for download. They don't cost much, and bring back some fun memories.

So, as a casual gamer and streaming video user, I have to say that the XBox 360 is a pretty good value.

review_headline: Saying this game was written by crack monkeys...
review_body: ...is insulting and unfair to crack monkeys.  This is by far and away the worst FPS I have ever played.  1.  The maps are 100% linear.  There is little to no exploration.  You know, the best part about Duke 3D ... yeah, they left that out.  2.  The controls are slow and kludgy.  I have the mouse acceleration turned up to maximum, and it still feels like I'm walking through mud anytime I try to turn.  You can only carry 4 weapons, and there is no quick-select method for the weapons.  You always have to cycle through them to find the one you want, and it takes about 3 seconds per weapon swap.  That's REALLY annoying when you're trying to fight a bunch of mobs.  Fortunately that doesn't happen very often.  See point #5.  3.  The AI is absolutely retarded.  Mobs will just blast happily away at a wall that you're behind never trying to flank you or establish line of sight in any fashion.  4.  The puzzles (if you can call them that) are just silly.  Think of the HL2 type puzzles then remove all the elements that make them novel and engaging, and you're left with the DNF puzzles.  You'll spend a lot of time kicking slimy alien balls into holes.  No, I'm really not joking.  I wish I was.  5.  Speaking of puzzles, there's actually very little fighting in this game.  Most of your time is spent on a combination of puzzles and jumping games.  I KNOW RIGHT!  You'd think the ONE thing they couldn't possibly screw up  in this game is the part about blowing up lots of aliens.  Nope ... nope ... somehow they managed.  This game is about 50% stupid puzzles, 40% jumping games, and 10% blowing up aliens.  6.  The whole hyper-chauvinism aspect of Duke is REALLY overused to the point that it just feels strained.  So yeah that's what 15 years gets you!

review_headline: ME3 BIOWARE FAILED TO HOLD THE LINE SPOILERS
review_body:
The game play up to the last part of ME3 was great, but the end of the game ruined the entire series and the franchise. The parts that ruined the game for me are listed below.

1.1. The endings for the game were horrible 3 choices that led to 6 variations of the same black. No variety like promised, all the endings shared 95% the same cut scenes. We were promised throughout the series that all our choices would shape not only our Sheppard but the galaxy and the final ending to the series; this was taken away in the final 15 minutes of the game. You can't just take an interactive game built on choice and make it into a linear game in the final moments.

1.2. Multi player content should have no effect on the single player campaign. There is a reason why no other game has implemented this, since not everyone like multi player. A player should be able to reach 100% galactic readiness without having to play multi player.

1.3. I did not like that after you make it clear to Cortez that you are not interested in him, that he still seems to push you towards liking him in future conversations. My personal beliefs I don't approve of the Homosexual lifestyle, and I don't feel I need to have that pushed on my in a game.

1.4. We want our endings more varied and distinct from each other like was promised, having all our choices taken into account in the final outcome.

1.5. Fill the plot holes give us a real back round on the Reapers, and their purpose, bring Harbringer into the picture more.

1.6. For those that ME3 is their first exposure to the ME universe, offer them a DLC that allows them to make the choices they would have had a chance to if they played ME1-ME2. This will make more revenue for Bioware in a DLC purchase, and give the player a chance to have a real full ME3 experience and a bump in galactic readiness to help with their ending.

1.7. The Rachni were always represented in ME1/ME2 as being an important part of ME3, and in ME3 they played a very small part. We had to save them again, and all they did was help build the crucible. We should have seen some Rachni ships in our fleet and so on.

1.8. We were also told in previous magazine interviews prior to release that Cerberus was going to be an enemy, and that we should make sure to destroy the collector base in our ME2 saves, This was so the illusive man would not get a hold of Reaper tech. Well I destroyed the collector base and the Illusive man still got a hold of Reaper tech. How he got acquired Reaper tech needs to be explained.

1.9. One of the pieces of feedback many of us asked for was the return of the Mako Tank and exploration missions. That feedback seems to have fallen on deaf ears since we have no Mako missions in ME3.

1.10. We had Loyalty missions in ME2 and it would have been nice to have them with the new squad members of ME3, it added immersion into the relationships with the characters.

1.11. A helmet toggle option similar to what we had in ME1 would be nice, especially with the custom sets of armor we got from pre-orders, and import saves.

1.12. If you are going to have 6 variations on the ending fine. But You could cut that to 6 endings and make them so varied and different it would make a more complete experience, with a excellent, very good, good, neutral, bad, very bad ending. The key thing being that it takes our past choices and actions into account, not just war assets and galactic readiness.

I know that if at least the endings are not redone I will no longer purchase products from Bioware, and the ending DLC should be free, since we already paid for a proper ending to the game we purchased. People make the argument that the game is Art and not subject to pressure to change.

I make the argument that an Interactive game like the Mass Effect series, in which certain promises and descriptions and player game shaping was established by the company makes it a Commercial product , with art aspects, and a ever changing storyline, Due to the players participation in the creative

What should have happened is the squad with Sheppard barely makes it to the beam and teleports to the Citadel. Have the illusive man knock out everyone but Sheppard and Anderson with his new powers keep basically the whole dialogue between them, except make it easier for Sheppard to use a paragon or renegade option for the illusive man killing himself.

After the illusive man's death, have Harbinger reanimate his body as an avatar of Harbinger, and have a interactive dialogue between them leading to a final one on one battle between the two. At the end of the battle have Sheppard use the crucible in either a passive way that destroys the reapers, or as a massive thailix cannon to assist in killing the Reapers.

Have our choices throughout the series determine what ending we have. Keep the ending diverse into for example 6 possibilities, including great, very good, good, neutral, bad, very bad. If you want to make more money on DLC create a DLC that offers players new to the franchise to use an interactive comic like you did with ME2 and have them quickly make the choices they would have if they had played the entire series.

The key thing here is we just want was promised in interviews and articles prior to release, nothing more. A proper set of endings to up till now a Epic game franchise worthy of being called the 21st century Star wars saga.

It really pains me alot to have to write a negative review about this controller. I really really wanted it to work, and for a short while, it did. But the design and construction of this thing are just too poor to recommend it to anybody.

Bear in mind that I only had this contoller for FIVE DAYS before some of its issues became too much to put up with.

Pros:

Analog stick resistance worked perfectly, for a little while, at least. The resistance could be adjusted to where I could aim with more precision than ever while the sensitivity ingame was set to 10. I was able to tweak the resistance til it felt just right after about an hour or so of adjusting to the feel of the controller.

The face buttons feel great when you get used to it. Their use of the mouse click mechanism makes it effortless to press the buttons, and it's going to be hard to go back to regular buttons after using this.

The overall feel of the controller in my hand felt good. The multifunction shoulder button was a little awkward to reach up for, but I didn't use it much at all, so it didn't turn into a big issue. The triggers also felt fine, contrary to some of the other reviews I'd read.

Cons:

This is where it gets bad, and these are deal breakers, in my opinion. I really gave this controller the benefit of the doubt, even though I'd read plenty of negative reviews before purchasing.

Bear in mind that these were happening withing FIVE DAYS of receiving it in the mail.

The most unworkable problem came when the face buttons simply stopped working. I was a little confused at first, trying to figure out just what went wrong. After a few minutes like this, it just sorta fixed itself, so I shrugged it off. But then it happened again a couple days later. And it didn't just fix itself this time. After several hours without a controller, I took a closer look and figured out that the \\"remap\\" function was stuck on. When I was pressing the buttons they were just remapping themselves to the shoulder buttons every time, instead of doing what they were supposed to. This was because of a loose/broken solder on the remap switch.

The second con came from one of my favorite features. The analog stick resistance worked great for a couple days. But in order to maintain the same level of resistance I started with, I had to occasionally increase the tension a notch or two. Within three days I had reached the maximum level, but the stick was still losing its resistance. There was still some tension, though, so I continued using it.

But apparently there's another negative side effect of having the resistance cranked up. You CANNOT push your stick all the way to the edges to get the full turn you need while you're aiming/driving. In Halo Reach, I was able to still aim fairly well (even if it was a little too slow on the edges), but when I would switch to a vehicle it was literally unsteerable. I pushed the analog stick hard enough to where it felt like it was going to break, and it still wouldn't register the full range of motion. So basically, I was stuck in vehicles and it would literally take me 6-7 seconds to do a 180 degree turn. So then... I switched the resistance down about 10 or 15 notches to where the vehicle turns would finally register. This worked for a good 15 seconds. Then my vehicle blew up... So I had to crank it back up to max resistance while I was on foot. After about 10 or 15 times switching back and forth, the clicks between settings became less distinct, and the stick resistance was becoming less effective.

Lastly, I couldn't use my old mic(the one with the two plastic tabs) on this controller. It won't work without dismantling the mic.

Bottom Line:

I liked every idea that went into designing this controller. On paper, it's what I would consider to be the perfect FPS controller.But the durability and quality of this thing is so poor that it becomes simply unusable after a short time. I'd hate to imagine what other kinds of problems would come up if I'd had it for longer than a week.

review_body:
Since they're two seprate games I'll rate them seperately:

Operation Anchorage (2/5): I had some fun with Operation Anchorage mostly using the silent pistol and stealthily taking out the Chinese, however after awhile it got stale and boring, and I had to take mutiple breaks before I could beat OA. Fallout isn't well known for being a cheap CoD knock-off, it's better known for being an immersive sandbox RPG. Operation Anchorage is about as immersive as an arcade rail shooter. The strategic elements are simply not true, the whole war is very linear with the same goal, \\"go to this camp, kill these people, plant bombs, *yaaaaawn*, sure is Call of Duty around here...

The boss fight at the end is a joke, I chose the sniper class earlier on and loaded up on ammo prior to the boss fight. Basically you walk into a court yard where some guy you've never heard of named Lt. Wang chases you around with a sword while the other Chinese soldiers ignore you. I once threw a grenade between two opposing soldiers and only the American's turned hostile and started shooting at me. With full ammunition and playing the sniper class on very hard without 100 unarmed or 100 speech it is impossible to kill Wang unless you want to be there for hours doing well timed punches which pick a tiny fraction of his health off. Really it's just sloppy on Bethesda's part, and people say the only redeeming quality is the powerful stuff you get; wow so you're saying for $10 and 3 boring hours of wannabe COD I get to have the game completely unbalanced? Gee thanks!

The Pitt (3/5): I heard there were major bugs and glitches with the Pitt but I'm a bit late so I never experienced that but I'll just take everyone's word for it. The Pitt's whole experience felt like I was in Alien 3. Most of the time you were in an orange-tainted steel mill fighting things that looked like the monsters from the Descent. You get a new weapon here which was sorta cool I guess, it was like a weed whacker with axes instead of plastic wires. The whole story was supposed to be some grey moral choice, but how can you not resist kidnapping children? So that was a no contest decision for me. Entering Pittsburgh through the bridge was pretty cool though.

One thing that mildly annoyed me about the Pitt is when you release the mutants into the town I got the impression that you'd basically break the lock on a gate and start running like hell, which sounded like a lot of fun! Unfortunately it's not the case, instead the mutants spawn in front of you so when the character earlier in the game said \\"here take this stealth boy, you may need it *wink*\\" they really give you no other choice. Crouching and walking through the city just doesn't seem as exciting as running with a horde of those mutants chasing you, maybe that's just me though.

review_headline: Diablo 3 - Review after about an hour's or so of play.
review_body:
Long time fan and patron of Blizzard. There last couple of years though has been somewhat of a dissapointment in terms of what I expected versus what was given. That being said I have so far very much enjoyed the new game and am trying to become accustomed to the new system.

The biggest con to this game from what I have read has been that you need to have the internet to use it. I understand Blizzards side, even if it is legitimate or not. Had there been zero warning about the necessity of the internet, I would have been greatly upset and distressed to say the least. But, as a sensible gamer, and frugal with money I like to commit some forms of research before making a purchase. If someone had looked about reviews by the \\"pros\\" who were able to do walk-throughs before release, and any information from Beta's, no doubt they would learn an internet connection is required. I know D2 was not this way, as are some games marketed out there that are hack and slash, but before you bomb a game with only 1 star, make sure you have a legitimate reason. Flaming on a game you didn't do research on (for instance not having the video card to run a game, and then screaming about it and thumbs downing it) is your own fault. To the average player though, or to a mass marke, I will agree this does hinder your overall base, and some people truly enjoy just playing the single player (example..Call of Duty and its ever continuing trend to slack on the single-player co-op aspect versus online play only but I digress).

Game-play so far. I've seen people talking about over-simplified or too simplistic I agree and disagree with the sentiment. It is very much structured for blizzard to maintain a great deal of control over skills specifically and the customization of those skills (rotations and such) is highly limited. The rune system is pretty cool and as you level each skill can have a small bevy of compliments based on your needs. I am a Demon Hunter foran example and right now my hungering arrow (first primary skill) I have a rune that allows the arrow a chance to pierce more enemies. As I level my next rune will allow me to change that rune if I so chose to do fire damage, but lose the added piercing target bonus. So initially I am pretty hamstrung by Blizzard in terms of customizing my character, but the runes will make characters unique, albeit not near as unique as previous games. I will note that although people seem to greatly miss D2 and it's talent point system. If you truly got far in that game, you were sinking 20 points in 3 or 4 true skills in each class, if you wanted the full potential. Yes you could customize, but your skill set was still pretty lopsided with what you had versus what you used. I will say outright that I do miss assigned my stat points, but I can live without that, as a messed up stat placement can be a crusher later-on and with no eraser I would rather play a different class. The game-play is very smooth, graphics are solid. I enjoy the new orb system (similar to dark-spore) for healing. At least speaking for Demon hunter I enjoy the already growing rotation of trap, run, arrow with my 3/4 skills I currently utilize. I will try to comment more as I get further. Storyline seems decent as well, and I love the new journal aspect. Added flare with lore for sure. I think I'm just rambling now.

I would recommend this to friends, if that's what this all points to. Will it change hack and slash games forever...no. Will it give me lots of fun through playing it through it's difficulties. You betcha. Can't ask for too much more out of a game than an enjoyable storyline and some quality game-play and graphics.

review_headline: Fantastic Game, Well Worth The Money!
review_body:
Back in 2007 \\"Mass Effect\\" won over gamers and is considered by some to be one of BioWare's best games. In 2010, The sequel, \\"Mass Effect 2\\" hit store shelf's and again defined RPG's.

***WARNING, THERE ARE SPOILERS***

PROS:
+ Combat is excellent and improved upon since ME1. I felt as though combat was a big issue in ME1 and I'm glad it feels a lot smoother in this game.
+ Plenty of replay value for such a campaign driven game. You can search undiscovered planets, complete \\"loyalty\\" missions which basically gives background on each squad mates, search planets for side quests, or just go around and search stores and upgrade weapons, the Normandy etc...
+ Voice acting is superb as with ME1 and ME3. Each alien species offers a unique voice and it keeps me wanting to talk to aliens I see.
+ Plot is very good and it connects to ME1 but at the same time it strives to open up the universe even more, like \\"A New Hope\\" to \\"Empire Strikes Back\\" did or \\"Alien\\" to \\"Aliens\\".
+ ME2 also borrows a lot from other Science Fiction franchises. I deffenitley see connections to \\"Star Wars\\", \\"Star Trek\\", \\"Alien\\", \\"Planet of The Apes\\", and many others!
+ Soundtrack is great, its science fictiony and gripping.
+ The amount of squad mates certainly differentiates this game from other RPG's due to the number of them that you can have. To each squad mate there is a \\"loyalty\\" mission which provides background and furthers the story a lot more.

CONS:
- Where is the gun customization that was prominent in ME1? That was a huge part of that game and could of been done really well here.
- Sometimes voices don't sync properly and for some reason sentences cut in and out.

Final Score: 4.5/5

While \\"Mass Effect 2\\" has its problems, the game delivers and is a fun and unique experience which will satisfy most gamers.

review_headline: 2-D Platformer Adventure With a Whole Lot of Fun!
review_body:
A lot of times when a video game system is almost defunct, some really good games come out for it near the end of its retail life. That is typically because video game developers get really good at exploiting the system's capabilities to the fullest because it's been around for so long. Unfortunately, during that time, most players' eyes are on the next new system, and these little gems of games tend to get underappreciated and overlooked. While all eyes are on the Nintendo 3DS, there are still some really cool games coming out on the ol' NDS. And \\"Monster Tale\\" is one of them.

THE STORY

A colorful 2D action-platformer with flashy sprites, at first glance the game might appear \\"cutesy\\" and geared toward younger gamers. But I am adult, and I found the game challenging and entirely entertaining. A young girl, Ellie, is awakened one night to a commotion in the forest and goes outside to investigate, finding a mysterious bracelet. The bracelet not only allows her to shoot energy balls a la Samus Aran of Metroid fame, but it also transports her to a faraway land. Ellie happens upon an egg that hatches in her presence into a monster she dubs \\"Chomp,\\" who begins voluntarily following after her. From that point on, the two are inseparable, and Ellie goes on to explore multiple kingdoms and complex dungeons, uncovering more of the story as she searches for a way to get back home. The story is just a vehicle to progress the game, but the characters are humorous if not a tad cliched, and they are only a minor part of the game.

THE GAMEPLAY

The first thing I thought of while getting into Monster Tale was how much it reminded me of the Castlevania games for GBA and NDS. Ellie has a basic, unlimited whip attack (she is slinging her shoulder pouch) and a charged energy shot attack which varies in power depending on the charge bar. She can jump and (eventually) roll, climb, make multiple-hit attacks, etc., acquiring these new abilities that come to her in the form of orbs that are sitting on pedestals around the dungeons. Each one grants a new ability that enables Ellie to reach previously unreachable areas. Ellie is also able to purchase upgrades for herself (with money she picks up from monster kills) from a recuring seller, like making her whip attack more powerful or upgrading the efficiency of her bracelet's energy usage.

And of course Chomp can assist in a variety of ways. As you progress, you will acquire items (either as monster drops or that Ellie can purchase) that level up Chomp's stats. For example, if you pick up a book, Chomp will read it and his intelligence will go up. A bicycle will increase his speed. Some items not only benefit Chomp, but also can assist Ellie in the form of a short-term attack effect, like a catapult that launches rocks up into the gameplay screen, randomly hitting enemies, or a frisbee that flies up and acts like a shield. Eventually Chomp will level up enough to unlock new forms, which you can opt to transform him into, giving him particular strengths (and weaknesses) and even a new look. You can also change Chomp back into any previous forms at any point as well, which can be beneficial depending on the attack style or element of your enemies. If the enemies' element is, for example, water, then you wouldn't want to be using a fire-form of Chomp against them (fire-water-earth = rock-paper-scissors). You can further customize Chomp by setting what attributes you would like him to have. He has slots for a variety of collectible skills, and specific attacks can be assigned to the shoulder buttons.

The game is played on the upper screen, and the lower touch-screen is Chomp's recharge/learning/dining area when he's not assisting in attacks, the screen for setting up skills for Chomp and looking at Ellie's abilities, and the screen for checking your maps, very similarly to the Castlevania games. Even the save rooms are just like those in Castlevania, as are the shop seller rooms that appear here and there. Your progress is rated by percentage of completion and the way new areas open up as you trigger events. The maps fill in as you go along, and places you haven't been to yet are blank areas.

Often, before you can gain access to a new kingdom, you need to defeat a full-screen sized boss. It is not difficult to learn their attack patterns and start whittling away their health bar, but the attack patterns can be quite clever and sometimes requires Chomp to attack parts of the boss in the lower screen. As new areas become accessible, enemies become progressively more difficult - either faster, by shooting more accurately, or simply because there are more of them, and it really benefits to have Chomp assisting. Occasionally Chomp is needed to get through various obstacles, such as spike pits. There are also a couple unique enemies that jump off the upper screen to Chomp's lower area, and begin launching attacks at Ellie from there, and it's up to Chomp alone to squash them.

MUSIC

The music is great! It's brash and exciting, matching up perfectly with the theme of each area. For example, one area is a dance club and of course there's house music. I usually don't have the sound cranked up all the way; in fact if it's repetitious, I tend to mute the whole thing. But that didn't happen with Monster Tale. Nothing was repetitive or nerve-wracking. Much of the music had a somewhat gothic sound to it (again - like Castlevania).

DIFFICULTY & CHALLENGE

The difficulty level of Monster Tale is not as high as that of the Castlevania games, but I wouldn't call it \\"easy,\\" either, especially in the later levels where the monsters are quick and precise, and instead of just wandering back and forth, they target and come after you. One thing the game does to assist the player is to indicate on the maps where Ellie needs to go next in order to progress further - either by highlighting what exit you need to take to another area, or, if you're on the correct map, what room you need to go, with a pulsing orange dot. You are free to run around endlessly through previously-covered areas (if you like grinding for levels/money/treasure drops like I do), and the game does require quite a lot of backtracking, being that there are areas you initially cannot get to but can access later, once you have the ability to get past specific obstacles. If you pay close attention to the storyline, which plays out during little character exchanges between Ellie and a few other human kids who willingly or unwillingly step up to stop her, you can figure out where to go next. But why bother, when the game basically points to where you're supposed to go next? I kind of wish you could opt to turn off the \\"you go here next\\" indicator, or at least give the option to play the game in a more difficult mode that doesn't assist in direction. It would give the gamer more of a sense of accomplishment than just chasing a flashing pointer around. I'd say that was the game's only real weak point.

LENGTH OF PLAY & REPLAYABILITY

Other players have said that this game can be finished in around 10 hours. However, it took me a little under 15 hours to get 100%, as I have never been one to rush through a game. I prefer to be thorough, and unlock every skill, form, item, etc. That is faster than I ever spent on a Castlevania game, but that's still decent for a 2D action-platformer. Still, I found myself wishing there was more. In a way I suppose that's a good thing, it indicates it was a good game. Once I completed the game thoroughly, however, I just didn't feel like any more could be done with it, because I had done so much backtracking the first time through, there was simply nothing unfinished about it to draw me back to it. You can continue by leveling up every form of Chomp to the maximum, but it's pointless when there's nowhere left to explore, really.

RATING 8/10

Overall I give Monster Tale an 8 out of 10. It's a great game with some minor flaws, mainly: a little too easy because of the direction indicator, and over a bit quicker than I wanted. But the music and graphics are awesome and the play dynamics have excellent flow and a great feel. It is, simply put, fun to play. Even though you're slaying monsters, there's nothing dark or scary about it, no blood or gore. And if you like Castlevania &/or Metroid, the feel of this game should be very familiar to you.

review_headline: FEAR 2 - ORIGIN: EVERYTHING A GREAT VIDEO GAME SHOULD BE AND THEN SOME!
review_body:
I can be a hard judge of Video Games and that is a fact! But have no Fear, I found F.E.A.R. 2: Origin to be the most awesome video game, I have successfully completed. I have cerebral palsy, among other disabilities so playing video games is difficult for me. F.E.A.R. 2: Origin set on Easy Mode was still quite the hand full for me to play. However F.E.A.R. 2: Origin had none of those extremely challenging hurdles or mini games tucked inside that made it impossible to finish. Not to say F.E.A.R. 2: Origin was not challenging because; it was indeed the most challenging video game I have ever played. F.E.A.R. 2: Origin was intelligently designed so it did more to challenge your senses. F.E.A.R. 2: Origin never got old or boring either. Using the Mech's to lay waste to the enemy was an awesome experience. Mech's are very powerful robots driven by humans that can wage destruction on a massive scale. Because the Mech's regenerated their abilities during times they were not fired on was an awesome touch that let me figure out unique awesome ways to win that were compatible with my brain and limited physical abilities. The weapons in F.E.A.R. 2: Origin were a lot of fun to use. The enemies died in so many unique ways with lots of blood spatter and gore thrown in. F.E.A.R. 2: Origin was a real festival of blood and gore if you had the gore option engaged. Of course if you want your enemy to die a less gore filled bloody death you have the option to turn Gore \ Realism feature Off in the games control center.

F.E.A.R. 2: Origin is not just another shoot em' up gore fest, F.E.A.R. 2: Origin was a LOT of fun but it was also different in so many interesting ways. I wished Snake Fist hadn't gotten killed because; I liked him he was a true scruffy geek \ nerd like me minus the disabilities of course. The locales where the action takes place looked so real down to the signs in the buildings especially the school scenes. That school cafeteria was so real I could almost smell the over salted fat rich unhealthy rubbery food they serve students. I am trying hard to find one bad thing to say about F.E.A.R. 2: Origin and nothing huge comes to mind. The graphics were awesome. The sound was first rate not as good as the original Bioshock BUT still awesome. The audio set a creepy or frantic mood well whenever needed. The city scenes and subway interior scenes were equally well done. The unusual thing about F.E.A.R. 2: Origin was the attention to detail and the overall quality and attention to detail that was invested in every interior shot. F.E.A.R. 2: Origin had a fair share of destructible objects sprawled throughout the game. Nothing destroys the mood set by a video game more than an object easily destroyed in the real world that is impossible to destroy in the game.

F.E.A.R. 2: Origin also had some funny dialogue for the enemies as they got ready to kill you. I laughed my head off when an enemy would say, I've got him just the instant before I blew his head off. I loved it when a frustrated enemy would say he is moving too fast, or I need back up here. The timing of some of the enemies lines is pure comic genius. You have to be deep into the game to really enjoy the enemies funny one liners and assorted quips, I have heard some people say the character in F.E.A.R. 2: Origin has some pretty lame friends given that whenever the going gets rough they fade out. However I enjoy being a LONE WOLF when hunting things on video games. The most infuriating video games are those that pair you up with an inept but affable side kick you must continually get out of jams not of your own making. I know F.E.A.R. 2: Origin was a good video game because even on Easy Mode I died a lot in some places and not at all in areas where I am stronger like sniping. Despite lacklustre performance in other areas of video game play rare is the video game with good snipping guns that I do not get the expert trophy. F.E.A.R. 2: Origin's sharp shooter trophy is called \\"DEAD EYE\\" and Yeah I won it. Gun aiming in F.E.A.R. 2: Origin is so much better in F.E.A.R. 2: Origin compared to the truly stupid sideways reticle only gun aiming in the original F.E.A.R. Button layout was much improved in F.E.A.R. 2: Origin although some minor additional fine tuning to make some things flow better is needed.

review_body:

This SNES clone really feels cheap in your hands, but to my surprise it actually works well.

The only two games that I could not get to work were Star Ocean and Street Fighter Alpha 2. These two games were the only ones out of the SNES library that have the S-DD1 chip. review_headline: High hopes, but Crystal Dynamics has screwed up a legendary franchise
review_body: First I have to say that the graphics and scenery in this game are breathtaking. If it were an animated full-length feature film (rather than a game that requires active participation), this review would have rated at 5 stars all day long. Here's the problem: Crystal Dynamics (and Eidos Entertainment, collaboratively) have lost sight of the gaming experience, and have chosen to focus more on cinematic presentation of their games than playability. What I'm talking about here is the maddening \\"active camera\\" that has been present since TR: Chronicles, and unlike other games in the genre, they neglected to create an option to disable, so you're stuck with avirtually unplayable (although cinematically gorgeous) experience. For those of you not familiar with this process who might be considering this game, this means that every time you are in a scenario (and there are a LOT of these in this game) where you must jump backwards onto a ledge that is about to retract, fall, etc., and then quickly jump onto another ledge, the camera angle will rotate around while you are in mid-air (to create a more dramatic effect I suppose), then you have to counteract by toggling the right stick to center the camera again before jumping. There are several parts (Midas' tomb for example) where you just don't have the time to do this before falling to your death. Save your money and buy TR1. Same game, way less frustration.

In the lead-up to Mass Effect 3's release, the developers at Bioware made it a point to emphasize how the decisions players made over the course of the trilogy would culminate in a highly personalized and conclusive finale. \\"We wouldn't do it any other way,\\" they said.

All lies.

The reality of the situation is that all of those decisions get thrown out the window as the player is railroaded into one of three (very brief) ending sequences - with the most significant difference between them being the color they are tinted with. Seriously.

With player influence over the story being the defining quality and major selling point of the franchise, it's baffling how Bioware could drop the ball in such a way. When the last 10 minutes of a 100+ hour series manages to cast a shadow over everything that came before it, it can only be described as a catastrophe.

The 1st two Metal Gear games from the 80s, which came bundled with the two disc version of MGS 3 Subsistance. I know. The price seems steep, but I really wanted the artbook, and that's one of the main reasons I purchased the Limited Edition. If you can do without the artbook, I'd go with the regular edition (no sleeve and no book), which goes for less than $40.
