review_headline: Could be better, but better than most
review_body: Compared to other available RPG's on Xbox, this is as good as it gets, but it could be better.    First, The graphics seem pretty dated, though I forgive this because the game is pretty large.  The magic doesn't really effct the environment (like freezing or burning stuff, other than bad guys doesn't happen) and the spells overall are... not visually pleasing.  Also on the negative side the story is pretty predictable (but recycling is good right?)and linear.. you can do the quests in differnt order, but it's not a sandbox game like fallout, or oblivion.  The positive quality of this game is building your character.  If you enjoy building your guy and trying to beat the game with differnt characters you'll probably enjoy it.  I like that you can use differnt parties (like no magic, or all thieves) and character classes and they're actually differnt, in some games, every character feels the same.    I don't really like the WoWish combat system, but it works.  The dialogue was amusing for the first 2 hours, now it's close to being annoying (One thing I love is that you can press a buton to skip the dialogue but it's a differnt button to pick your answer, so you don't accidentally chose a response you don't want! Thank you for that!)  So while not ground-breaking, I think DAO is one of the better attempts on the market right now, worth renting or buying if you enjoy RPGs.

DO NOT BE DECEIVED!  This item is falsely advertised, plain and simple.  Do not buy this item if you intend to use it for the Genesis 2.  It claims to fit \\"all 3 models of the Sega Genesis\\", but this is a mistake or perhaps an out and out lie.  This converter does NOT work for the Genesis 2.  It is designed for the Genesis 1.  I can not say for sure whether it works for the Genesis 3 or not.  Technically, the hardware IS compatible with the Genesis 2, but the design makes it impossible to fit over the Genesis 2 system, since the piece of plastic on the back of the converter gets in the way, so unless you want to take a chainsaw to the back piece of plastic and ruin the item, then it absolutely can not be used on the Genesis 2.    I give this a 5-star review here because the item itself is wonderful -- the problem is with the false advertisement, not the item itself.  If you have a Genesis 1 and want to play Master System games then this is a great item, and I highly recommend it, but do not buy it for the Genesis 2.  If you have a Genesis 3, then do your research and find out if it works for that, because I don't know.    If you do want to play Master System games on the Genesis 2, then there is a Power Base Converter 2 that was released outside of North America and was designed to fit the Genesis 2 since this one was not; however, it is very expensive (I've never seen it for under $75, and up to $200), and it's not easy to find (they don't have it on Amazon at the current time).  If you want to play master system games, I recommend either buying a Sega Master System, or buying a Genesis 1 along with this Power Base Converter.  The Genesis 1/converter combo is preferable to the original Master System console since the picture quality is better from what I have read, however there are a few games that the Power Base Converter can not play (I think it's only like 5 games or something), so if you want to play one of those games, then you may want to consider a Master System console, otherwise the Genesis 1/Power Base Converter combo is probably the better choice, or you can look for the Power Base Converter 2 for the Genesis 2, but like I said, it's generally more expensive then both the other two would be combined.    I hope this review was helpful.  It is a shame that people feel they need to falsely advertise items to sell them, but then again, it's always possible that it was a genuine error.  In either case, be forewarned -- this item will NOT work on the Genesis 2.

When I bought this game, I also purchased Modern Warfare 2 and Left For Dead 2 all within weeks of each other. Let's put it this way: I haven't even opened the packaging on the latter two and my girlfriend hates me for it (maybe because I named my level 46 siren after her and spend more time in front of a television than in front of real people).    Borderlands is a non-stop loot-collecting, face-shooting, treasure-hunting experience that will appeal to everyone (FPS and RPG fans alike). And that's just the single player option. With 2-4 people (XBOX Live or offline) you can enjoy all of the above with a co-op experience. Enemies are harder in co-op play, loot is better, and the ability to yell at your friend from across the room (or on headset) for taking an amazingly rare face-shredding machine gun adds to the over-all appeal to the game.    The story does lack, however. Most of which is told through textual interfaces on the mission screen. The only person that really speaks to you (involving plot progression) is a disembodied female voice that pops up from time to time. Fallout this is not, but that is not a bad thing. The games stands alone among a sea of FPSs.    DLCs are on the way as well. Right now, \\"The Zombie Island of Dr. Zed\\" is available and receiving good reviews. Expect the same amount of inventory management and fast paced gun-play, but now with ZOMBIES.    Can't wait to see how this franchise continues.

The Show 09 is everything I could ask for in a game. The best thing about it is that it is actually two games in one, Road to the Show and Franchise. Both are equally compelling and offer a completely different experience. In the first you play as a young ballplayer working your way up from the minors. The experience is so transcendent that it's eerie. You really FEEL like you're the young player vying for the Show. The coach wants you to work on fielding even though you'd like to spend those precious training points on power. You're stuck in Durham, North Carolina just because some past-his-prime veteran has come off the DL so there's no more room for you in the bigs. Then just when you've accepted your lot, BOOM they've traded you to the Twins. Brilliant!

The franchise mode is very similar to other BB games with extremely intricate owner tasks. Luckily, if you're more interested in playing and less interested in selling your team, you can just turn those modes over to AI. Gameplay is extremely fluid, player movements are uncannily realistic, and the AI has a slew of adaptations to account for momentum switches.

Now a word about difficulty hitting. It's hard. It is so hard to hit that there is an infinite future for fine tuning my skills. But the sliders allow you to custom-downgrade the difficulty to where anyone could hit a fastball if they wanted to.

I think I know why people get so upset about the difficulty of the game even though they know they can make it easier if they play on rookie with altered sliders. It's a matter of pride. Most people can't like a game they suck at without \\"cheating\\". But come on. This isn't your career or your love life or parenting or even real-life golf with people watching you. It's a VIDEO GAME. So if you can't hit a curve ball change the sliders until you get better enough to do it.

review_headline: The Thief Series is my All-Time Favorite
review_body: First off, let's talk about what's in the box.  There are three games.  The first two were created by Looking Glass Studios, and are EXTREMELY well-made games.  The third was made by Eidos and was fine, but not as enjoyable as the first two.  To those who started with Thief III, you have no idea how \\"open\\" the city was in the first games.  That said... after Looking Glass folded, at least the third part of the story did get told, albeit in somewhat \\"consolized\\" form.    THIEF came to me, originally, in my sound card's bundle.  I didn't think I'd care for it, but it was free, so I tried it, and fell in love with the game.  It's not about stealing...  not exactly.    Yes, your way of making a living is a bit disreputable, but hey, you end up saving the world...  so I guess that can be forgiven!    The original game was called \\"Thief - The Dark Project.\\"  This \\"collection\\" box actually holds \\"Thief Gold\\" which is a subtly reworked version of that game (with several new levels, new creatures, and so forth... stuff that was supposed to be in there but got cut for time in the original release).  The other two games are the original releases, albeit fully patched.  There is a small problem with these game and later operating systems, where the video codec (INDEO) becomes unregistered from time to time.  This is an easy fix, of course, and I believe that they have installed the (fan-derived) fix into this package.  (This is a slightly odd circumstance where Microsoft originally carried Intel's INDEO codec, but dropped it after some sort of conflict with someone at Intel, and not only removed it but seemingly caused it to malfunction on occasion if you install it yourself!)    There are some issues with video cards... particularly nVidia cards running recent drivers.  Any video card with more than a certain amount of memory will not run the first two games without some \\"tweaks\\" being put into place.  This is not the fault of the games, it's the fault of the shifting \\"DirectX\\" definitions over the years, and the fact that nVidia changes their supported features without regard to \\"legacy\\" coding.  Again, this can be fixed, but you'll need to spend a brief period of time searching the 'net to get the fix (which, as far as I know, was not incorporated into this package, oddly).  The best place to look is at a website called \\"Through the Looking Glass\\"...  [...].  Any questions about how to make these games work if you have problems, you'll be able to answer from there.    (I understand that ATI cards don't have the same issue that nVidia cards do, but I don't know that from personal experience.)    ANYWAY... once you get the games up and running, be prepared for an experience like no other. (I'll mainly discuss the first two games, since the third game is significantly different in terms of game mechanics.)    If you want to fight... get another game.  Yes, there is combat, but your character is really pretty weak, compared to most enemies.  Go toe-to-toe with an enemy and you'll be reloading your game momentarily, as often as not.  No, the trick is patience, stealth, and tactics.  Know your environment.  Study your enemies.  Think, don't just \\"run and gun.\\"    On the harder difficulty levels, you are often prohibited from killing anyone, and if you do, you fail the mission.  In a few cases, you're required to avoid ever being detected at all.    Thief I is a bit less polished, graphically, than Thief II, and Thief III has more \\"polish\\" overall, but really doesn't look better than Thief II in my opinion, since you're seldom going to get \\"in the face\\" of your enemies.  But if you expect modern graphical photorealism, you're playing the wrong game.  These games look good, but they're not graphically up to modern standards.  And that's OK, honestly... the gameplay makes up for it.    Your best weapon isn't a machine gun, or a \\"mega-sword.\\"  It's a blackjack.  A blackjack is basically a little leather pouch filled with lead shot... useful forknocking out (without killing) guards.      You need to read scrolls and books to learn what's really happening throughout the story.  And it's a REAL story, not just a framework for a few missions.    Yes, you steal treasures throughout the game.  Whatever you steal during a mission becomes the money you get to spend to support you while you equip yourself for the next one.  So... if you steal very little, you have very little cash to buy required equipment the next time around, and gameplay becomes harder.  Oh, and on higher difficulty levels, you are required to steal a certain amount of loot in many missions.    There are NPCs you interact with.  They're well-written, for the most part, but not \\"Alex Vance\\" type characters.  And they're merely polygonal, without moving lips, for that matter.  Just remember, technology has advanced rapidly, but creativity hasn't... so don't let that bother you.  (By the way, the closest current equivalent to this is \\"Dark Messiah - Might and Magic,\\" which could, with minimal effort, be used to create further Thief games...  they even have \\"rope arrows,\\" with Eidos left out of Thief III, but which were fundamental to Thief I and Thief II.)    I've played the first two games through several times, but only played the third game through once, though I expect I'll give it a second effort sometime soon (I've restarted the series recently, with the release of this \\"collection\\" package).  It's still my all-time favorite gaming experience... and I think I'll wrap up here and head off to rescue my fence, Cutty, from Cragscliff Prison.  Want to join me?

review_headline: Don't Believe all the Negative Press..This is a good Game
review_body:
One of the highlights of all the Tekken games has been a lot of the crazy characters. Maybe they aren't as over the top as other games, but they have a personality all their own. Right when you pop Tekken 6 into your system, you may seem overwhelmed with the HUGE character roaster. All of the over 40 Tekken characters are unlocked right from the get go. You will see some old favorites, as well as a few new comers. Most of their moves are similar to previous Tekken games, so if you were a champ at Tekken 5, you should have no problem here!
Beginner Friendly:
Not many fighting games will let you be good right from the get go. In Tekken 6 even if you have never played a Tekken game before, you will have no problem getting onto the groove of things. Whether you are button mashing, or pulling off the crazy 10 hit combos, you are going to find yourself having a great time.

Sense of Style
Like most fighting games, they try to make themselves flashy in some way. Tekken 6 may not have any super special moves in games like Street Fighter, but the combos are extremely in-depth, and have a deep sense of satisfaction after putting a chain of moves together. It isn't just the fighting that has style either. If you know anything about the Tekken story-line, you will know that it is just simply ridiculous. The endings for each character have their own sense of craziness and all Tekken fans will enjoy them.

Balance
No character in Tekken 6 really seems over powered or unbeatable. Each character has they're advantages and disadvantages, but there is not one single useless character, or one God character to be found. So if you see someone who looks cool and you just want to play as them, practice makes perfect kiddies. Become an unbeatable master with Jack-6, or destroy everyone with one of the Mishimas, it's all up to you!

More than the fight:
Fighting games need to have more than just fighting now a days. Tekken 6 offers a large form of customization for all characters. You may not be able to make your own custom character, but with all the options to change the appearance of one of the Tekken 6 fighters, you will think you did! Tekken 6 also sports a single player story mode which can sometimes be enjoyable, and this will last you a good number of hours.

The Bad:
Lag

Online matches are great in Tekken 6...except when you encounter lag. In all fighting games lag can simply kill you, the same can of course be said for Tekken 6. When you encounter lag, you will find yourself having a hard time putting together combos, or trying to perfectly time your attacks.
The Verdict :
If you are in the mood for a solid fighter that has PLENTY to offer, Tekken 6 is for you. Even if you have never played a Tekken game in your life, this is something to be experienced. Lengthy single player, cool characters, customization out the wazoo, and an ever growing online community make this a must own fighting game.all characters. product_title: Littlest Pet Shop Friends: Country - Nintendo DS
review_body:
My 11-year old sister loves Littlest Pet Shop. I think she is too old for it, but then again I am in no hurry for her to mature either and they are adorable little animals! A few weeks ago I wrote a post about the New Littlest Pet Shop Friends game and Littlest Pet Shop Online. When my sister saw that I received the New Littlest Pet Shop Friends \\"Country\\" to review, she was beyond excited! She opened it and put it in her Nintendo DS faster than I could ask her if she wanted to play it!

Littlest Pet Shop Country Friends is not just a game where you tae care of animals, it is jam packed with mini-games, dress up, and actually has a task to accomplish! The point of the game is to get your pets ready for a big celebration, so you have to deliver invitations, pick up food, and explore towns. The cool part of this game is that you can play two-player multi-player via a Nintendo Wi-Fi connection (unfortunately we weren't able to try this feature out.)

Your child may think they know all the Littlest Pet Shop pets, but Country Friends contains six exclusive country pets to collect! I think my favorite part was styling my pets, as I always loved dress up and accessories! My sisters was exploring and the mini-games. Now I have never played a Littlest Pet Shop game before so I don't have anything to compare this to, but I think the game is cute and fun. It is perfect for any Littlest Pet Shop fan and really for all ages. There are also a few other versions of the Littlest Pet Shop Friends Collection that include: City and Beach. All of the Littlest Pet Shop Friends games feature new pets to play with, enjoy, and have a story line.

I received this game to review it but this opinion is 100% mine.

I've played these games since the very first Tomb Raider, and I've enjoyed watching them get better in the last few years. After reading scathing reviews of Underworld, I rented it instead of buying it just to see for myself what was going on. I have to agree that this game is a joke to the Tomb Raider series. After re-energizing the series with Legend and Anniversary, I expected the games to just get better and better and was excited that there was going to be yet another one. But I am very disappointed.     The quality of the graphics on this game is nowhere near as pristine and beautiful as the aforementioned Legend and Anniversary, and the swim controls are so screwed up in comparison to the others, including the original, that it's very difficult to get anywhere! The camera is all jacked up, too, and doesn't stay behind her or move like it should, even when changing the settings. And that's just the beginning of the troubles for the PS2 version.    It seems like in an effort to continue the success they were riding high on, the creators didn't put a whole lot of effort into the game, instead opting to fast-produce it and count on the fact that die-hards would buy it without second thought. Well, my advice is to take a second thought, check it out from a rental store, and then decide for yourself. Chances are, you'll be disappointed like I was. I hope that if there's another game coming, they'll take these reviews into count and make it amazing like this one could have been.

I managed to play this game the day it came out thanks to Amazon's Launch-Day Shipping Option (very inexpensive at roughly $5) and immediately proceeded to beat the campaign and continue onto the multiplayer experience. The first Modern Warfare was known for its very dramatic and untraditional storyline and new setting for the Call of Duty franchise and this reputation would prove difficult to uphold. However, Infinity has pulled it off. While the campaign is short at around 5-6 hours, the experience is worth every second. The single player campaign was well-formulated and kept me entertained throughout the whole time. While there was no real \\"high\\" point in the experience, I didn't feel any low points either or levels I absolutely detested. The Co-Op aspect of the game, \\"Spec Ops\\" proved to provide more gameplay time than the singleplayer campaign itself. You will find yourself trying to beat each mission on the hardest difficulty \\"Veteran\\" and formulating strategies of your own to succeed. Most of the missions can be done by yourself but a few require a teammate. The experience was solid and some of the later challenges were some of the most difficult I have taken part in with recent games.     The two aspects of the game mentioned above only account for about 50% of the game, the other 50% being focused on the Multiplayer aspect. The majority of first-day owners of this game went immediately to multiplayer, skipping the campaign and spec-ops entirely. The mutliplayer experience provides a solid experience and proves that MW2 is the true successor to COD4: MW. With already over 4 days logged in on multiplayer I have still yet to get \\"sick\\" of it. The amount of customization that one can put into their classes is pretty much endless and the addition of the killstreak rewards reward new and veteran players alike. It's a great game to play with your friends, always trying to trump your friend in your K/D or score ranking and that is one of the key reasons this game will never get old for me. I patiently await the third installation of the Modern Warfare \\"series\\" and am unsure how they are going to trump this game.

review_headline: As much frustration as fun due to steep learning curve
review_body: I wanted to like this game. I gave it 20 hours of my time and it keeps frustrating me. The main problem with Grand Slam Tennis is that it's too difficult to learn and the AI is too good. You can't consistently hit solid shots. The AI rarely makes mistakes so playing the computer even on easy isn't fun at all.    The controls are simple you swing and depending on how you swing it determines whether the ball goes straight, slices, or has topspin. Lobs and drops are done with the a+b buttons. The problem is that they aren't consistent it is very difficult to hit the type of shot you want when you want it. You can with the wi motion plus direct the balls direction. This system is very touchy as well. A great deal of shots will go where you weren't intending. The AI is mistake proof other than a few double faults on serves so this creates lots of frustrations. I had a 53 hit volley in a match. You have the option of using the numbchuck but this makes things harder. Using the Wi motion plus with the WI remote works best.    The serving is easy however I have yet to get a single ace. I am sorry but players like Roddick get a few aces per match. This missing aspect makes this game a bit unrealistic. Graphics are what you'd expect on WI which means decent nothing special.    The crowd and the venues are done quite well and you do feel like you are at center court in Wimbledon. The sounds and player movements are very realistic. The mini games are fun and provide a change of pace.    Another disappointment was the lack of tournaments or a detailed career mode. Like the title says it's Grand Slam so you play those 4 tourneys and that's it. Instead of playing the full tounrament you play an exhibition match and a couple of matches against pros to gain abilities that help your game in the beginning you only can use one so they are not much help early on.    The bottom line, If you are buying a WI motion plus just for this game don't.

Just finished very first play-through of this game-very interesting re-imagining. This very much reminds me of the conversations I was having back when the original SH came out for the PSone. What if Harry is really....or Cheryl....what about Dahlia? I don't want to spoil ANYTHING, so I will stop there so you get the idea.

Graphics-pretty ugly for a such a late PS2 title. I really wish they would stop just scaling down the engines and dragging them onto the PS2 without optimizing it first. Some textures cut in and out when viewing them, particularly posters. Also, can we at least try to anti-alias this thing. Some areas, with our swinging flashlight painfully illuminating the lack of A-A, were pixelated nightmares. Also, I noted that the top and bottom of the screen had some distortion-was this intended to make it look like video tracking or a graphical glitch. Dunno. Finally, FMVs were washed out, faded, with an obvious resolution shift.

Deep Breath....that's really my only complain for the moment, though

Gameplay-Wow. A game that responds to how you play it? Balderdash. I couldn't believe this was even possible. But it is-you can have a completely different experience depending on how you play, and how you respond to the \\"good doctor's\\" questions and exercises. There are a few places where you will notice obvious forking-you can only take one of two paths-and it is clear that this transforms the scenes ahead, and of course the ending. I really liked exploring each area for these markers, as they set up a great binary opposition in terms of your path-good or evil, easy or difficult. For some reason, all my scenes, interactions, and even scenery was vaguely sexual. Gotta wonder if that was intended or just \\"my play-through,\\" but that is a digression. I plan to go through it again and try for a different scenario. Side note-you also have collectibles that come up in various spots-mementos-that just give you a little bit more to do.

Now for my last gripe-the \\"dog runs,\\" or at least that is what I call them, the scene's where you are running for your life from your enemies, pulling down objects to get them between you and your attacker. I really liked the visceral sense of combat in the older games-stalking your enemy with a lead pipe and beating them to death in brutal fashion. I was very disappointed that this was missing. The new feature-running and hiding, with an occasional flare to keep enemies at bay-frustrated me to no end, but I felt that this wasn't the whole of the game, so I can let it slide. Plus, it gets you EVERY time when one of the ankle biters latches onto you and have have to time your button presses just right to get them off of you. Try this on when you have three of the things trying to give you hickeys. Not fun. Thankfully, the game is forgiving if you die during this, and restarts you at the beginning of the run.

All in all, I REALLY enjoyed this game. I believe that for such a late title, the graphics could have been polished/optimized a bit more for the system (I hear the Psp version is the best one to get), but I am not dissatisfied with my purchase. It's not going to be for everyone, but it is a worthwhile entry and new direction for the series.

review_headline: PC version crippled; COD4 had better multiplayer
review_body: The single player is not nearly as fun and exciting as MW1 (COD4).  However, the price is now only $20 on PC, so it's definitely worth buying (was questionable at original $60 release price I had paid).    BAD:  The PC version didnt' just get relegated to the back seat in favor of consoles; it got shoved in the trunk.    The \\"removal\\" of lean (Q or E to peek around corners, in use since COD1) in PC version is a travesty (why not just remove from only console versions?).  You now have to walk/run Rambo around corners and get shot up, without any idea of what enemies or terrains lie ahead, which really detracts from the gameplay and realism.  I guess we're \\"lucky\\" they didn't remove crouch and prone as well.    You HAVE to install Steam, and MW2 installs in its subdirectory.  If you prefer to install to a non-system hard drive partition (ex. D:), but have Steam installed in C:, you're out of luck (and 11GB) and will want to reinstall Steam to the other hard drive/partition.    MUCH less graphic and audio tweak options than previous COD and other PC games.  It's officially a console port now.    Other posters have already detailed the multiplayer issues with MW2, but the much smaller gameplay and no server mods are especially disappointing.  No kick/ban now, so you can't play for 30 minutes without cheaters/hackers ruining the game.  I'll stick with original MW1 for multiplayer.    GOOD:  Graphics are quite good, but sometimes skips frames once or twice per stage (I have Core 2 Quad Q6600 + 8800 GTS).  Interesting use of snowstorm (obscures vision) and ice-climbing mechanics; snowmobile's fun and new, but the \\"heat-seeking\\" handgun bullets while riding is ridiculous.    New weapons to try out.  Dual-wield with left & right buttons controlling them individually.  The riot shield is an interesting addition (blocks bullets but you can't shoot, although you can melee with it).    CONCLUSION:  I'd still have purchased this regardless (had pre-ordered months ago), but am quite disappointed in Infinity Ward's shafting of the PC customers.  If there's a next release, I'll definitely wait until all the customer reviews are out.    PC was where MW1 (COD4) shined with betters graphics, customizations, and servers, but I'd definitely rate MW2 below MW1 (COD4), and perhaps even COD5.  They could've just kept MW1 mechanics and multiplayer, used this new storyline and new maps with improved graphics, then shipped it, but decided to cripple it.

review_headline: Lots of action, but not for long.
review_body: The Conduit is a non stop action FPS, and very satisfying. This game probably would not stand out on any other console because games like this on the PS3 and Xbox 360 are a dime a dozen and The Conduit offers nothing game play wise that isn't available on other consoles. BUT good FPS games are severely lacking on the Wii so this release is quite notable.     That said, the Wii offers the best game playing experience for first person shooters. The ability to point and shoot rather than controlling decade old technology that is the dual analog stick method adds unspeakable tremendous value to the experience and story of the game. It really does pull you into the game more.     In The Conduit, you will die and die a lot. The action is non stop from the beginning. The story line is decent and it is easy to follow the twists and turns that the plot takes. My only real complaints about the game are that the enemies are too redundant, boss battles are repetitive, and the game is WAY too short. I was expecting this game to last me a good month to play (20-25 hrs.), which is quite common for a $50 game. I received this game on a Tuesday and played it for about an hour each day (Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday) and on Friday I played it for a little over 3 hours and beat it. So it was probably between 6-7 hours long. The game is extremely linear, as in not a lot of exploring is even possible and you can't really back track much (there really isn't even much point). The PLOT however is very non-linear. You NEVER know what is going to happen next. I liked this but at times the game felt like it didn't even know where it was going. That fact made the ending very abrupt. I didn't even know that the last boss battle was the last boss battle until the game was over. Seriously.     The puzzle aspects of the game are at times frustrating and I did have to look up walk-through videos on youtube at places where I got stuck. You really do have to think outside the box at times to advance the game. The weapons are fun to use, and I like the fact that you frequently run out of ammo which makes you try other guns rather than sticking to the same one the whole game. The controller is completely customizable as is the HUD, which helps make the game more playable.     The multiplayer modes are decent, if you like that kind of thing. There is really nothing special about it. There is some sort of ranking system, but it's only used to match you to other players of your skill level (if there is even anyone online that matches your skill level, otherwise you are playing with people who are pros and know the levels inside out when you are playing for the first time). The ranking system is nothing like the Call of Duty ranking system where you unlock weapons and upgrades as you fight online. The online play feels like a FPS version of Mortal Kombat. All you do is vote where you want to fight, how long you want to fight, what guns you want to use and then just duke it out. I could also never figure out how to get out of a game without turning my console off, the Home button didn't even work.     Replay value - not much. I don't think I will be playing this game a lot, especially the online play. Call of Duty World at War is probably the best FPS Wii game to date. It has tremendous replay value. I can't wait until Modern Warfare gets ported to the Wii. Game developers really need to take a close look at what it does with the online multiplayer modes and mimic it. The Conduit keeps it interesting but not for long. I like that the plot of the game turns a lot, but it's kind of like a \\"who done it\\" movie where once you know the ending there isn't much point in watching it again. Kind of like The 6th Sense. Once you know the ending, watching the movie the second time isn't as much fun. They needed more intriguing side stories and areas that you could explore to keep you coming back to the game to find more and more in it, or give some incentive to doing so. Reallywhen you think about the plot of this game, if it's about an alien invasion, you would think there would be MANY things going on at once and though the story turns, it is still a pretty basic plot. What are the aliens trying to do? How can one man stop them? How can one man stop all of their efforts? Games like this tend to have one singular protagonist who defeats a vast army of enemies. Where are the other good guys?     The bottom line, 4/5 stars (for the $[...] I spent buying the game used). If I had paid full price ($[...]) for this game I would have been VERY upset and felt like I had been mugged in a dark alley and left bleeding in a pool of feral cat urine. I probably would have only given it 2/5 stars, but for the price I paid it was worth every penny. 7 hours of enjoyment is not worth $[...].

product_title: Pinball Hall of Fame: The Williams Collection
review_headline: Takes me back to the arcade
review_body: With the absence of real pinball machines in most arcades, this game is a real treat.  I have both the Wii version and the PS3 version of this game, that's how much I like it.  When you don't want to get spend a lot of time in gunfight, racing, or the other types of games for those systems, this is so much fun just to pick a pinball machine and flip the ball around.  I like the controls a little better on the Wii version of the game, but the graphics are better on the PS3.  Also there are more pinball machines on the newer PS3 version.  I'm a 47-year-old gamer who likes many new games but sometimes I yearn for the games I used to play back when a person had to actually go to an arcade to have this kind of fun.  I like how you can change the camera angles -- on some games, it helps to be able to follow the ball around the table, and on other games it helps to have an overhead view without the camera moving so that you can aim to hit targets.  I only hope they do another version with more tables.

Maybe if I made a game I'd shut the hell up, but I only play them.  This is an action game and nothing, nothing else. First, the game's graphics are great and the unique way of telling the story through still art, the cross on his chest, the angel that you reach at certain stop points and ask questions is really entertaining.  Riding on the beasts back and playing with a beast to make him jump up walls and breathe fire seemed pretty unique also and I liked it.  Fighting the bosses was fun and the way they make you fight Lucifer is pretty creative and great.  The part that drove me crazy was when I learned I seemed to be doing the same thing. I'm not complimenting Heavy Rain but I respect it trying to change gameplay a little. I don't want gameplay to change for every game I play, but let me let me fool myself a little that I'm not playing a weaker version of God of War or The Darksiders.  Even though the game forces you to press more than just square, I don't feel involved with the game. This is my biggest problem. I just don't feel my character.  Especially on that board where it was like the 9 stages of where I had to beat things in under a minute for a bonuse and then kill all enemies in the air at first, then kill all enemies (as enemies continue to multiply) with one single combo, then kill all enemies with magic, then keep two random placed humans in the pit of hell from being killed, and this went on like I said for 9 stages back to back.  I only wish things made more sense.  You can't say \\"for the sins of gluttony\\" and label a board or section this or that, yet when I fight I am doing the same thing for \\"the sins of adultery.\\"  There were very few puzzles and the puzzles they did have would make me do things like push a boulder here to cover up fire, or run from one portal to bring me out on another in a world that made no sense within the game to make me feel like it mattered.  I give this game a three because the graphics are far to good to get a 2 but notbetter than some other games. Don't get me wrong they did not short you on background detail (the images in the pools of hell, and in the prisons of people's hands and faces was tight as....tight as Dante's hell) but it's just nothing different than your average \\"good\\" game. THE OTHER REASONS FOR 3 STARS:  The other reason I give it a 3 is b/c when it comes to character and story being cohesive I just didn't feel it.  I felt like they were going to make the game play similar to God of War no matter what and the character/individuality of Dante just in no way came out through gameplay.  Maybe if they took the story deeper with me doing things within the story instead of being separated from what I am actually doing then I would write different things.  Uncharted is good for this.  Someone says something that has to be done, or that he hopes isn't done and you do it and see the consequences of your actions.  Noone expects a damn game to be more than a game (although a few games have blown my mind, but when you have all types of quotes through gameplay, and titles referring to things in which make no sense to what you are actually doing then I have to think like this.  I'm bout to ramble.  Why didn't the game give us riddles, or more informative fights?  For example, lets think like this and take this for example: If we're in hell take my mind to hell and hell's order. Let me be lied to by a demon, let me catch someone who says this the truth yet that person is known for being a liar.  Do this on a section that deals with lies. When a section says lies (let it be Silent Hillish in how I have to figure something out), or when a king is announced to have killed this many people and to have set up trials for his brother's wife, why don't I as Dante have to find friends within the game that I can consider allies to set this king up (like Assassin) and then fight the imphs he has in his possession, or why don't I in stealth kill a leader that I over hear talking about his/her devilish plans and use the information I hear from him to later use as a lie to tell a minion, demon, devil in hell to get me past a gate or some barrier; and if the lie I collected is rated strong enough then I pass; if not I have to go listen to another better lie.  Make me fight for information, that's how you involve a character in a game with a story like this. Let me swim, fly ride a vehicle or move very fast or control another character like a clone; I'm rambling but you know.  If your audience has to be 18 to get the game then it's okay to challenge the gamer a little mentally.  So for the mental aspect, the character's involvement with story, graphics not being better than 4 star games or as good,and not giving the gamer variety with character's interaction with other characters in the game or fighting style; I give it 3 stars. I'm not asking for Heavy Rain or Silent Hill or God of War but if you're copying other games anyway, why not splice a lil here and there too?  Play the game it's fun don't let my harsh criticism scare ya'.  I'm just saying what I thought. This game was really fun.  It is an action game and I guess not a successful adventure game and definitely not a mystery game like the old Resident Evils or Silent Hill or God of War or Darksiders.

review_headline: A monumental achievement for the rail-shooter genre and a quality prequel to boot!
review_body: Dead Space Extraction is definitely one of the diamonds in the rough of 2009, right there with MadWorld, Half-Minute Hero, Resistance: Retribution, and MotorStorm: Arctic Edge.    However, there are probably two preconditions that add some bias to my review and may determine the level of enjoyment you have while playing DS:E.    1. Have you played through Dead Space (360, PS3, PC)?  2. Do you like light gun shooters to begin with?    Now, if you answered \\"yes\\" to the above questions, as I would have, you will most likely adore this title.  The game picks up LITERALLY in the same exact location where Dead Space closes, adding a clever reverse-bookends to the series (or the series thus far; Dead Space 2 is expected to arrive late 2010).  If you've played through Dead Space with an eye for detail, Extraction will put many a grin on your face during its 6-hour or so thrill ride, as you will notice that almost every location is borrowed from the original while adding something new or intricate.  The same goes for the story:  Whereas Dead Space's storyline was sometimes muddled (most likely due to the onus on background info left to subpar animated film Downfall and the wonderful motion comics... which few people actually viewed), Extraction shines a very clear light on the mythos underlying Dead Space, including the series' allegorical religion, Unitology.    The voice acting is phenomenal, adding a very mature tone to the cinematic sequences and admittedly lengthy dialogue portions that occur amidst the shooting.  It sounds professional without ever becoming particularly cheesy or inappropriately placed.    The graphics--WOW!  By far the best looking Wii game released so far.  My jaw practically dropped as I thought to myself, \\"The Wii should not be able to do this.\\"  The game is on rails for the most part, yes (you do get a few moments of control as to the direction in which you move), and that obviously helped the developer to free up some space, but the graphics arestill stunning and the enemy models and environments are easily on par with the original game.  The atmosphere is genuinely scary (let's say there is a particular sequence at a tram terminal that made me literally jump) and is never once wounded by the Wii's technological limitations.    Music, stunning.  Controls... extremely creative.  You hold the Wiimote sideways to access a gun's alternate fire, and while this may sound awkward, it turns out to feel really, really cool.  And it's also surprisingly accurate.     Now, if you haven't played the original Dead Space and/or do not like light gun games in general, you're either going to feel a little lost or the game's very linear style just won't appeal to you, period.  Otherwise, the only complaints you may have:    - It's somewhat short, although long as light gun games go.  - Thought not nearly as anticlimactic as many reviews stated, the intense ending lacks a true \\"boss fight\\" sequence and may feel somewhat abbreviated.  - Some weapons are more useful than others.    A note on co-op: I played through much of the game on co-op, which is unobtrusive, and I have to say, Dead Space: Extraction is a co-op treat.  The devs obviously kept co-op players in mind when designing the game, and nifty little touches, like having one player unlock a door while the other player fends off hordes of monsters, makes for an incredibly intense and enjoyable co-op session.    All in all, Dead Space: Extraction is a treat for light gun fans, Dead Space fans, and it's one of my favorite games of the year.  An extremely pleasant surprise and highly, highly recommended.

Sweeeeeeet! I am loving the Wii Fit Plus! Just got it in the mail yesterday from Amazon and I'm impressed with the improvements Nintendo made.

Here are some of my favorite features:
1. My biggest complaint about the original was that I had to use my remote between every exercise and scroll through the menus to what I wanted, making a 30-minute workout into more like 45 or 60 minutes. You can now choose from suggested workouts based on your goals (like shedding some extra calories, slimming your figure or relaxation), or you can customize your own using yoga and strength training. You still need the remote when you use the suggested workouts, but if you make up your own, there is no button pushing so you can put the remote down for the whole time. Plus, it saves the workout you designed so you can use it again and again, or you can easily swap out an exercise or two. **The only thing I'm not crazy about is that the suggested workouts incorporate the balance games and aerobics, but you can't include them in your own customized workout. Still a big improvement, especially since doing the yoga feels more like a flow now instead of pose, stop, pose, stop, etc.

2. I love that there's a multiplayer mode so it's easy to play with other people -- but don't get your hopes up too high: You only get to pick from nine games (soccer heading, ski slolam, ski jump, balance bubble, hula hoop, obstacle course, Bird's-Eye Bull's-Eye, driving range and snowball fight).

3. I'm really enjoying most of the 15 new games on the Plus, such as rhythm kung fu, the obstacle course, snowball fight, rhythm parade, Segway circuit and a more challenging table tilt. You also get three new strength exercises and three new yoga poses.

4. The Plus tracks the approximate number of calories you burn. It also lets you set a goal of how much you'd like to burn in a session as well as a chart to help you see how that might compare to the calories in common foods.

5. In the Favorites section, it not only lists the activities you do the most, it also lists what you've done more recently and what you have done the least so you can mix it up more if you want to or stick with the ones you like.

6. The Body Test has additional tests that challenge both your balance and your mind. Glad to have a few more things it might throw at me after doing the same tests for the past two months now.

7. Under the Chart menu, it not only tracks your BMI, Weight, Wii Fit Age and Fit Credits (where you can record outside exercise), Nintendo has added a place to record your waist measurement and your steps.

review_headline: True Japanese Game Fans will love this game !!!!
review_body: For many years, Arc System Works quietly earned a fan following with the flashy 2D fighting action and totally over-the-top characters of the Guilty Gear series. The studio has started anew with BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger, a new game with new characters and an evolved fighting system that adds to Guilty Gear's basics. Unfortunately, there are only 12 playable characters in this one--a smaller number than most conventional fighters. Still, they're all very different from each other--and as you might expect from Arc System Works, a few of the characters are completely insane. While you may have trouble wrapping your head around the game's crazy cast and its many different gameplay nuances, which have such esoteric names as \\"drive attacks\\" and \\"guard libra,\\" you'll find plenty to do with the many different offline play modes--plus robust online play that works great. BlazBlue may not be the easiest fighting game to get into, but it still has a lot to offer. If you have ever lived in Japan playing their games we don't get here in the states, you will love this game.    Enjoy

Bioware has yet again made another stellar game.  Their story-telling and cinematic plot immersion is matched typically only by Square's omnipotent Final Fantasy series, in this gamer's humble opinion.    If you haven't played the first Mass Effect, I cannot recommend playing this sequel; although stand alone, this game is superior in most aspects to its precursor.  It's just that you would be robbing yourself of the greatest assest of the galaxy of Mass Effect, its story!  The Godfather In Space is what I've dubbed it.    Numerous upgrades and improvments to number 2 have been made over the first installment, along with (it pains me to say) some glaring weaknesses.  Many of the improvments come in the form of much more immersive and challenging encounters with enemies, (especially on higher difficulties) [SIDE NOTE: For veterans of the first game, those who breezed through it in particular, I highly recommend your initial playthrough to be on 'Veteran' difficulty to enhance the challenge, no pun.] also more diversive envirnments that are unique in every facet.  Gone are the tons and I mean TONS of cookie cutter spacecraft, bunker, and enemy layouts.  Each encounter feels and looks different.  Also improved is party and enemy AI, making each fight alot more fun, and not something you can just plow through without breaking a sweat.  Stratigic use of cover and you own abilities is necessary for the most part.  You also have more freedom of movement on the galaxy stage, physically moving your craft through the cosmos to your destinations.    The pitfalls of ME2 are not glaring at all for the most part, just an annoyance if you let it get to you, and if you lose sight of the 'big picture'... I will explain.  ME2 takes a MAJOR step back (or forward depending how you look at it) in terms of inventory managment, item gathering, resource gathering, weapons and armor procurement, and customizability.  In fact, you do not even have an inventory, and anything you could possibly get, takes an intangible spot on your ship or is a passive upgrade you can purchase for Shepard, his allies or the entire squad, which you will typiclly always buy with resources you gather (more on those later)  Outside of the passive upgrades, there are BARELY a dozen different weapons in the game, with a few different heavy weapons sprinkled in for some variety.  There is also no armor to be had, tinkered with, or bought outside of maybe a half dozen pieces you can get for Shepard which for the most part, have a minimal impact on gameplay.  Every squad member shares the weapons that you DO collect, and automatically are equipped with the strongest version of whatever weapon they are capable of using, making outfitting your unit for an encounter completely nonessential, everything is typically done for you.  Building your characters abilties are also incredibly linear and basically comes down to wanting one ability more than another, out of the maybe 4-7 you get TOTAL from game's beginning to end.    Now these different things can be seen as making the game seem to lack depth; a true and valid arguement.  But does it affect the game in the 'big picture' we talked about earlier?  No it does not.  Some might say getting all of impractical nonsense out of the way paves the way for you to just concentrate on the real grabber of the game, its story, rich with character development.  On the other end of the spectrum, some may argue that this game lacks attributes that makes a game an RPG, things that most RPGers know are staples of the genre: buying new and exciting weapons, magics, abilities, items for everything from healing to camping (lol), and statistic building.  As I alluded to you earlier, I am of the former opinion; yes it aggrivated me early on, but just get past it, what does it really matter in the face of one of the best stories out there in this increasingly controversial, competitive, and cutthroat enterprise that is video games.  I just like to show both arguements so those who want to may draw their own conclusions.    Nothing needs to be said of the actual story of the game, its plot, characters and locales; because any who are reading this article would be more than proficient in these catagories already.    So, like The Godfather I & II, both Mass Effects are not without some flaw, but masterpieces all the same, and are definitely worth the purchase.    Lets hope the last leg of this trilogy is better than Godfather III though. ;)

review_headline: Not even close to what I was hoping for...
review_body: I LOVE Empire:Total War....after about 40 patches and they got it (almost) right.  The A.I. is still totally weak.  What I read about Napoleon:Total War with the supply changes...well...that was about all I expected for change, aside from the Uniforms of course.  Naturally, it's a bit crash happy at the moment and this will take...based on E:TW...about 4 or 5 months to fix.  But that's still not my problem with it.  Okay, if you want to play France, you have to unlock campaigns beginning with the 1796 Italian Campaign (which I won with Massena and not Bonaparte, but naturally Boney gets the credit) and then move on to the Egyptian/Levant Campaign of 1798, which has a HORRIBLE set up.  No French navy.  None.  Am I wrong in thinking there was a \\"Battle of the Nile\\" in which Admiral Nelson got his fame?  Well anyway, after you trudge through this awful mess, THEN you can play Imperial France on the big map from 1805-1812.  You win that one and then you get to go have your ass handed to you at Waterloo.  One little battle.  And it was little by previous campaign standards.  It's just super-famous.  Okay, what's the problem?  It's completely linear!  Remember when you had to defeat other countries in Rome and Medieval II to unlock other countries?  Well now you have to win campaigns just to play a proper large-scale campaign.  UNLESS!  Unless you want to play someone other than France and you get four, count'em, FOUR choices.  Austria, Prussia, Russia and the United Kingdom.  That's it.  I started up with Britain and noticed how completely lame their navy was for January 1805...not even close to proper strength...and Wellington was in play.  Nooooooo, Wellington was in India at the time.  (Do some research, CA!)  The off map links to trade ports like from E:TW are one move away from various Western European ports, actually any port because there are trade ports in the Med, too.  Lame.  And the first time I did a naval attack...Crash!  Just when I turned my Line and started to board Dutch ships!  Next part.  You know how you have choices as to how to develop your regions' economies as towns grow in E:TW?  Not in Napoleon.  Totally not your choice.  Each town has a destiny and there's nothing you can do about it.      So...necessary unlocks to play a \\"full\\" campaign with France (which only goes to 1812, also weak).  Four whole choices of other countries to play (How can you leave out Spain or the Ottoman Empire or even Sweden?).  No choice whatsoever how your regions develop.  Inaccurate force and leader set ups.  Stupid trade port system.      Now about the Supply system, I like it.  But I didn't expect it to be so static.  I thought you would have choices (see above) where you can build army depots.  I also thought raiding enemy supply points would result in faster replacement rates (purely from stealing war materiel and medicine).  Nope.    Really, the only thing I like about this so far are the uniforms and the voices.  Bunching your artillery en masse and pounding the Austrian formations as your attack columns advance is totally satisfying, especially with all of the French shouting and marching music.    But I play E:TW exactly the same way Napoleon fought once I have the proper sciences anyway.  Hey, the guy won battles for a reason.  You can start emulating him just as soon as you have ring bayonets, fire-by-rank, and mobile artillery.  Oh and while we're on the topic of sciences.  The science tree in this game is more like a science shrubbery.  Another disappointment.    Final summation...good to see the period in TW format but the game needs help, badly.  And it won't get fixed, aside from the bugs.  They aren't going to redraw the map and include more nations to play.  So basically, it sucks.

product_title: Fallout 3 Game Add-On Pack: Operation Anchorage and The Pitt
review_body:
Operation: Anchorage was the first downloadable content available for Fallout 3. Fallout is far too complex a game to explain here; suffice it to say that the paranoia and jingoistic patriotism of the 1950s became a permanent way of life due to the escalation of nuclear war between communist forces and America. Operation: Anchorage fills in the back story of the game by thrusting the player into a pivotal moment in Fallout's history: the liberation of Alaska from communist China.

This isn't really an addition to Fallout so much as it's a complete mini-game more in the vein of the Tom Clancy sneak-and-shoot games. The mission involves a series of escalated attacks against Chinese forces in a windswept arctic climate. There are soldiers that can be commanded to fight on your behalf, enabling some rudimentary squad tactics. There are no mutations and therefore no mutants, no irradiated wasteland and thus no radiation concerns, and only the equipment Anchorage supplies you. It's a completely different game with a similar interface.

And sneaking is critical here. It was a shock for my 20th-level Fallout character, stripped of his huge arsenal of drugs and equipment, to be regularly outmatched by sharpshooters who often had a tactical advantage. In fact, all of the opponents are considerably more difficult, including the invisible Crimson Dragoons. I faced down several threats by staying near a health dispenser and clicking it every few rounds as I was pounded by Dragoon fire. There were several points in the game where I died multiple times using the brute force approach, eventually forced to sneak my way through much of the content. In short, Operation: Anchorage gave me a good dose of humility.

Anchorage provides two items that will change your Fallout 3 experience. The first is the Winterized T-51b Power Armor. One of the most powerful armors in the game (DR 45), it never gets damaged. The other standout item is the Gauss Rifle, which has a scope, uses microfusion cells, and causes creatures to be knocked down for four seconds on a critical hit.

Words can't properly express how satisfying it is to hit a Deathclaw full in the face and watch it go flying off a cliff. Those four seconds can be a lifetime on a battlefield, bestowing a critical combat advantage to the player's companions who continue to pound away at the prone target; players using VATS and the right perks can knock an opponent around like a hockey puck.

Operation Anchorage isn't like the rest of Fallout 3 and that might be a turn off for some. But the Gauss Rifle and Power Armor make it all worth it.
'
Part of the genius of Fallout 3 is that it mixes 1950s sensibilities with post-apocalyptic atrocities, striking the perfect balance between humor and horror. With the Pitt, the balance definitely shifts towards the nihilistic, more The Road and Swan Song and less Beyond Thunderdome.

Like Operation: Anchorage, the player enters former Pittsburgh stripped bare of weapons and armor. He is pretending to be a slave. Mingling among the slaves, the player must fight his way through The Hole, a series of arena battles against increasingly difficult foes. My high-level character tore right through them in record time.

Surviving multiple rounds in The Hole grants an audience with Ashur, the head slaver and a former Brother of Steel. Indeed, this title may be more apt, because Ashur has created a bustling economy using Pittsburgh's steel mill to churn out weapons and armor.

It soon becomes clear that things are a little less black-and-white than in the rest of the Fallout wasteland. With the population largely sterile due to the Troglodyte Degeneration Contagion, Ashur settled on slave labor as a short-term solution to his manpower difficulties. Those who are tough enough ascend to join the slavers in bullying slaves and raiding other communities. The twist-ending requires a sadistic choice with no real winners or losers. It's as grim as it sounds.

Also like Operation: Anchorage, The Pitt provides one of the best melee weapons: The Mauler. An auto-blocking, persistent damage-inflicting beast of a weapon, The Mauler gets blood and guts everywhere, but then, killin's messy work.

review_headline: FFCCtCB - yes that's the abbreviation for this game
review_body:
Overall this was a pretty solid game. The story was decent but what excelled most was the game play and the music.

Story/characters: Basically at the start of the game you are thrown into the story, which is kind of exciting, but right after you are still left with little background information. Supposedly Keiss is one of Layle's best friends but it never quite explains deeply enough your past or why they became friends. What happens is a mysterious being attacks a ship Layle is supposed to be guarding and it sets off to light these crystal beacons. The mysterious being (Amidatelion) is part of one of the long lost tribes called the Yuke. Layle charged with stopping her, but as he learns more about her and her story he begins to think about this whole situation more. Then there is Belle. Belle is a girl with a knack for stealing things. She is being hunted down by Keiss and Layle's employer because she has a secret picture on her camera.She is supposed to be the main female character but she and even Keiss aren't seen as often as I expected for main characters. This game is mostly a solo game with brief run ins with the other characters. This is what I found lacking is that Layle doesn't seem to develop proper relationships with these characters because he rarely sees them. Specifically the back story between Layle and Keiss is lacking. The other characters include Althea, the princess of the Lilty (plant-like people) and Cid (yea, there's a Cid in almost every final fantasy game) who is an engineer for the Lilty Kingdom. Then there is Jegran, the commander of the Lilty Kingdom and Keiss and Layle's original employer. (You can tell this guy is a bad guy from the start).

Game Play: This is where it gets interesting. The combat revolves around pointing the wiimote at a target in real time and locking on to it. Then you can throw the object or enemy at walls, other enemies, or carry them above your head. Later you can also do rolls to avoid enemyattacks. It's pretty simple but it is also very fun. You can do this to random villagers in towns or guards without many repercussions. There are no random battles exactly, but something similar to it. When travelling the world these big purple thingies float from the sky and summon monsters. You have to kill the monsters and then destroy the purple thing. When you do you get an increase in maximum life. I honestly only did this twice in the entire game, but if you have trouble with bosses later in the game you should consider killing them to increase your life. The purple things spawn randomly in specific spots, and if you wait long enough they will despawn and go away.

Music/Sound: The music is amazing for this game. Whether your wreaking havoc throwing Lilties around for fun in the Lilty Kingdom or just chilling on the Selkie Beach, you will always have some really catchy tune playing. product_title: Jillian Michaels Fitness Ultimatum 2010 - Nintendo Wii
review_headline: Okay for die-hard fans of Jillian; for others, there are much better options.
review_body:
After the fiasco that was Fitness Ultimatum 2009, you might be hesitant to buy the 2010 version. I was too. I've had the game for a while now and thought I'd break out the good and the bad.

The Good:

1) The exercises are definitely more intense than the ones you'll find on games like Wii Fit Plus or EA Sports Active. There's are nine exercises that use the Wii Remote (water pump, sledge swing, hip twist, oblique, side lunge, back kick, jumping jack, squat jacks, running) and nine that use the balance board (boat pose, crunch, swing kick, lunge kick, bicycle, side plank, pelvic thrust, push-up, closed push-up). Use of the balance board is optional.

2) The game is fairly well organized into three main sections:

a. \\"Workout Area\\", contains four choices: \\"Island Overview\\" allows you to quickly do one of 18 random exercises in one of 9 different environments, ranging from a cascading waterfall to a sunset on a pier. Great for if you want to exercise in a hurry. \\"Single Exercise\\" allows you to choose the specific exercise, location, music, and number of reps. \\"Circuit Training\\" lets you choose from five combinations of exercises that Jillian herself recommends for Total Body, Abs, upper or lower body. You can also customize five of your own circuits. \\"Resolutions\\" allows you to create a customer workout schedule over time for up to six months, or use a schedule that Jillian herself made.

b. \\"Jillian's Locker\\" is very obviously something that the programmers stuffed into the game to make it appear more substantial. It isn't substantial at all. \\"Outfits\\" contains outfits that you can dress your on-screen Jillian in. More of a gimmick than anything else, and the interface is confusing to navigate. \\"Diet Tips\\" and \\"Exercise Tips\\" contain a total of 14 one-line tips. Obviously put in here by a programmer in a vain attempt to make the \\"information\\" look more substantial.

c. \\"My Info\\" is an interesting area where you can set your profile (height, weight, age) and then see your stats (how much you exercised using the game and a chart of your weight loss over time). Overall I actually prefer the more \\"professional\\" presentation of this over the cartoony approach of Wii Fit, but again, the user interface is atrocious, with non-intuitive buttons and difficult controls.

3) While you're doing each exercise, the game will show an animated Jillian performing the exercise, showing you exactly how to do the exercise, complete with the Wii-mote or the Balance Board. You can use a 3-D camera to rotate and view exactly how to do it from any angle. This is a neat feature that isn't available on other games.

4) For the Wii, the graphics are not bad. The environments have rich graphical experiences and great background audio. When you're running through the jungle behind Jillian, you really feel like you're there running through a lush jungle. When you're on a dune overlooking a beach, you can see the wind and hear the surf pounding against the shore.

5) There is something cool about having Jillian as your \\"personal trainer\\", leading you through intense exercises, shouting out positive and negative reinforcement depending on how you do. The game does capture her intense, all-out style quite well.

The Bad:

1) The game is still extremely spotty in its use of Wii-Mote or Balance Board to measure how well you're doing the exercise. While marginally improved over the 2009 version, it's still not very accurate and a lot of it is \\"trial and error\\". In most cases the controller really doesn't add much to the experience and you're on the \\"honor system\\" to do the exercise right. Sometimes just flicking the remote lightly will trigger compliments from Jillian; other times you'll swear you're doing the right thing, but Jillian will berate you for not doing it right.

2) For any given exercise, once you press the \\"Start\\" button, the on-screen Jillian will start doing the reps for the exercise very rapidly, regardless of whether you are doing them properly or even doing them at all. Sometimes before I even get set, she's finished with the exercise already! Worse, there's no ability to \\"Restart\\", your choices are just Pause or Quit.

3) The overall user interface is horrific. There are a number of awkward or non-standard ways that controls and interface elements are programmed. Sometimes navigation through menus is unresponsive, sometimes buttons are so small you can hardly select them.

4) There are a limited number of exercises (9 balance board, 9 Wii-mote). This pales in comparison to the exercises provided in The Biggest Loser.

To sum up? I'd give it 3 stars out of 5. If you're committed to exercising, you'll get some benefit out of this, but there really aren't any huge innovations here. You'll find that Wii Fit Plus is more fun, EA Sports Active is more precise in its controls, and The Biggest Loser for Wii has a much larger variety of equally intense exercises. The main audience for this one are die-hard fans of Jillian Michaels who enjoy her no-hold-barred style and love the idea of her acting as your virtual personal trainer, even at the expense of a very polished video game experience. Wow, this game is something alright. It has managed to steal the dubious honor previously held by Spider-man 1 as having the absolute worst camera in any video game I've ever played. This is the first and only game I've ever played which actually gave me motion sickness. I don't even get sick reading while I'm riding in a car and have never been sick on a plane, so it's really quite an accomplishment.

You'll be fighting the camera the whole game. I couldn't find any way to zoom in or out and when I focused the camera on Laura it would slowly pan out on its own. Trying to do a jumping puzzle, sometimes the camera will lock in place making jumps much more difficult than they need to be; get used to making many leaps of faith. If you move around near walls, especially on your motorcycle, the camera will whip to other angles of its own accord. If you lock on an enemy to attack them, even if you were facing them already, the camera will whip out to another angle once you've finished them off. Why? who knows.

The camera makes things so bad that the only reason you can still play the game is because there are very few enemies and you have time to keep moving the camera back to where it should be. The presence of a button to snap the camera behind your would have been appreciated. For an unfathomable reason, while you're moving the controls change to what the current angle is. In other words, you end up going in a direction other than where you're actually pointing to go. Say you're holding left, suddenly the camera shifts and you're moving down or whatever. Left may not be left anymore. You keep having to stop and start.

The controls are the most twitchy I have ever seen. Laura moves like she's on an ice skating rink. Then you use her motorcycle and you're skidding around like you're oiled up out there on the ice. It's also wierd to see her sort of hovering a half inch above the ground sometimes when you're pushing things. Another problem is you will push the controller to go one direction and Laura will fail to move at all or you'll aim in a direction to jump and she'll jump (often to her death) in an entirely different direction. They try to guide you a little bit with the direction she's looking, but sometimes even that is misleading. Reading other reviewers I thought they must be exagurating, but no the controls are really that horrifyingly bad.

Combat is very limited. There may be as few as 1 or 2 enemies in an entire level. You have unlimited ammo, heal fully in a few seconds if you keep away from them, and really enemies don't do all that much damage anyway; it's rare if ever you'll be challenged by them. One note, the Thrall things (flaming hounds) will keep coming back from the dead unless you shoot them, then go over and press a button to stomp on them while they're down. The game only tells you this once, and the tip is hard to read.

Laura looks really good, though a lot of the game is MILF attire; nothing wrong with it, but if I'm stuck looking at her rear the whole game make the outfits skimpy. The cut scene movies were semi-plentiful and well done. The story was compelling enough I wanted to finish the game. Maybe other games had better graphics, but as this is my first encounter with Tombraider I can only say I found the graphics to be perfectly acceptable.

All I can say about this game is that I didn't know you could possibly produce something so sloppy, so glitchy, so painful to control, which still manages to be somewhat fun to play. This review is necessarily split into two sections, each addressing the game differently.    AS A DJ SIMULATION: a good start.  The game is quite good about replicating a ton of elements of real mixing, such as eq/fader effects, dynamic crossfading, etc.  There are a few notable areas where it makes some compromises, though.  The crossfader is pretty much the polar opposite of a feather fader, and it requires a ton of effort to move back and forth.  In-game, the crossfader plays are only 3 point recognition, not analog, a simplification that strikes me as necessary to make the game fun.    The buttons being ON the record is an interesting idea (and necessary, in order leave a hand free for fader/fx), but because the scratching is always paired by holding down one of the three buttons, the simulation breaks down, as trying to scratch near the center of the record is awkward and pretty unrealistic.  The solution is to platter scratch, which is terrible, but one does what one must.  It also introduces a dynamic not found in real life: intricately (and rapidly) switching fingers mid-scratch, which doesn't make a whole lot of sense to me.    There are some obvious compromises that a lot of DJs seem to be griping about but I think make perfect sense.  The single turntable, for example: sure, it's less accurate (what exactly are you crossfading between...?) but the game needed to be MANAGEABLE to the average human being.  The platter doesn't move on its own, so you don't get the same sensation of fighting direct drive torque when scratching, but motorized parts = higher cost, more frequent breakdowns.    I appreciate that the game's \\"star power\\" allows you to ignore the crossfader temporarily, which lets you concentrate on tooling around with the effects knob.  This pretty accurately recreates the idea of being a bad-ass in the zone, where the basic elements of the mix are handled so well that you can devote your time to the fun stuff.  I just wish there were more samples/stabs available more often.  Maybe the sequel could feature more Rock Band drum type freestyle sections.    Despite the technical inaccuracies, the game does a very good job of simulating the excitement and power of club DJing.  I think anyone griping about the game's realism should play locate a copy of Beatmania in an arcade, then come back and heap praise on Activision.    AS A VIDEO GAME:  The game is relatively forgiving and easy to get in to at lower difficulty levels, and the craziness ramps up rather quickly.  The higher difficulties still make sense (you don't get the GH3 sensation of \\"those jerks did this just to screw with me\\"), although expert is incredibly challenging.  The music is fantastic, and there's something for everybody.    Even if you've played rhythm games before -- even if you've specifically played a DJ rhythm game before, e.g. Beatmania -- I think you'll find that DJ hero is a totally fresh addition to the genre.  It provides the departure from the \\"guitar & rock\\" formula the genre desperately needed.    I can see more casual music gamers getting frustrated with DJ Hero quickly.  The mechanics of manipulating a crossfader are strange at first (although anyone with ANY mix experience will feel right at home), the multitude and variety of input styles with the scratch hand can be overwhelming.  One suggestion, especially for those who got into music games because they like guitar: start at lower difficulties, even if you don't feel like you need to, and work your way up.  The game's greatest learning curve difficulty comes from the fact that the mixes are new, and people without a lot of background listening to remixes and mashups may find the timing of a lot of the stabs, transitions, etc. bizarre.  Expect to play with your eyes for a little while.    One last suggestion for newbies: when using the crossfader, resist the temptation to grip it between two fingers and wiggle it back and forth.  Instead, try holding your hand flat on the controller and putting the fader between your pointer and middle fingers.  When you move the fader, slide your fingers over, then move the \\"inside\\" finger back to center position (i.e. if you slide the fader to the left, move your pointer finger back to the middle position).  This way, your \\"inside\\" finger acts as a stopping guide when you move the fader back, and you avoid accidentally sending it too far.
